Combined with almost guaranteed clear skies across parts of North Africa and a path that crosses ancient temples, Mediterranean coastlines and the Nile Valley, it’s easy to see why it’s already known as the “eclipse of the century.” Few eclipses in modern times have combined such exceptional duration, reliable weather and globally significant cultural landmarks along the path of totality. Total Solar Eclipse 2028 The trilogy concludes in spectacular fashion on July 22, 2028. Totality will sweep across Western Australia before crossing New Zealand, with Sydney witnessing its first total solar eclipse in more than 170 years. Remote parts of the Australian Outback will enjoy more than five minutes of totality beneath some of the clearest skies on Earth. For eclipse chasers, it provides a fitting finale to one of the richest three-year periods for total solar eclipses in recent history.

item.title: When To Cancel Your Summer Vacation Because Of Wildfires
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.99
The list of vacation destinations burning this summer reads like a bucket list itinerary: Bordeaux, Crete, the Aegean coast and Bend, Oregon. Fires across Europe have killed at least 17 civilians, six firefighters and two helicopter crew, and forced roughly 330,000 people from their homes in France and Spain. France has already passed its worst fire year on record and is running at 6.2 times its 20-year average, according to the data research firm Ranking Atlas. If you have a trip booked, you're probably doing arithmetic you didn't expect. Here's where the fires have already forced the call: - Central Oregon. The Akawa Butte fire northeast of Sisters reached 27,491 acres before evacuation notices eased. Visit Central Oregon, the tourism marketing agency, has been promoting a hyperlocal smoke map this summer, partly to prevent unnecessary cancellations in towns that weren't affected. - Spokane, Washington. Three fires broke out around the city on August 1 and are now managed together as the Spokane Area Fires. Roughly 65,000 people have been evacuated, and more than 600 structures were hit. An air quality alert covering 13 eastern Washington counties warned that fine particulate levels could reach the "very unhealthy" range. - Gironde and the Arcachon Basin, France. About 40,000 visitors at 45 campsites in Gironde and the neighboring Landes were evacuated, and the prefect publicly asked tourists to stay away. On the Cap Ferret peninsula, the summer season has been effectively canceled. - Crete and the area west of Athens. Authorities moved about 8,000 residents and tourists out of the coastal resort of Agia Galini, Crete on July 29. The fire that started west of Athens on July 31 destroyed more than 100 homes and drove out over 1,000 people, more than 250 of them evacuated from the beaches by boat. Every one of those flare-ups has travelers asking the same question: Should I cancel, and if so, when? But you won’t find the answer on the TV news. More often than not, it comes down to air quality, whether anyone has ordered an evacuation and how your travel insurance policy defines a disaster. Get that wrong and you'll cancel a trip that didn't need canceling—or forfeit a deposit you can't recover. When Should You Cancel Travel Because Of A Fire? Headlines aren't always enough to prompt a cancellation, according to experts. Daniel Grainger, founder of Ranking Atlas, ran a country-level analysis of the European Union's fire records. He says cancellation decisions are based on a specific destination's fire trend rather than this week's news. He points out that in Portugal, wildfires have burned the equivalent of 23% of the country's land area over 20 years, yet this year's fire activity is running at only 0.35 percent of the seasonal average. Most Mediterranean coastlines see some fire activity every August. Karen Clay, professor of economics and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University, says the common error is treating one number as the whole story. "The air quality index can worsen by 100 points across a short distance as smoke plumes move," she says. Those index categories are built around healthy adults, she adds, so anyone with asthma, heart disease, a pregnancy or a young child needs to react sooner. She also points out that people check the forecast the week before instead of the morning of, which is when advisories and smoke shift. The index itself is slipperier than travelers assume. Colleen Rosales, strategic partnerships director at OpenAQ, a nonprofit that publishes open air quality data, says air quality indices are calculations rather than physical readings, and countries build their own to match their own health standards. A fine particulate concentration that reads "good" in Mongolia can read "moderate" in the U.S. Providers don't always disclose how they got their number. Air quality indices don't mean the same thing everywhere. Also, a fire in one part of town doesn’t mean the entire destination is closed. My U.S. home base is in Spokane, and the fires there illustrate this point. Nearly half the city’s neighborhoods were evacuated or at risk. The images were terrible. But Visit Spokane’s latest advisory says the region remains open to visitors, with many events and attractions continuing as scheduled. Hotels are taking reservations. Several are discounting rooms for evacuees and first responders. Bottom line: A fire in the news doesn't necessarily mean the destination has stopped functioning, or isn't open for business. Does Travel Insurance Cover Wildfire Cancellations? "When severe weather or a natural disaster causes an extended delay so your travel carrier can’t get you to your destination for at least 24 hours from your original scheduled arrival, that can be a covered reason for trip cancellation," says Daniel Durazo, director of external communications at Allianz Partners USA. "To travel insurers, a heat wave, smoke or a bad forecast alone are not covered reasons for cancellation. Yet widespread evacuations, destroyed accommodations or an official order preventing access can change the equation." Durazo says the wildfires near Bordeaux were a clear case of a destination becoming uninhabitable rather than simply unpleasant, and that people with travel insurance policies could be reimbursed for unused, prepaid, nonrefundable trip costs, subject to their policy terms. Allianz Partners’ 2026 Global Travel Confidence Index, conducted by Ipsos, found that 68% of American travelers now weigh environmental risks and extreme weather when choosing where to go. Terry Boynton, president of Yonder Travel Insurance, draws the same line. "For heat, wildfire smoke and other extreme weather events, the key question isn't whether the conditions are unpleasant," he says. "It's whether they directly disrupt your travel plans in a way that is covered by your policy." If smoke cancels or badly delays your flight, trip cancellation, trip interruption or travel delay benefits may apply. If you simply decide not to go, they generally don't. Chrissy Valdez, senior director of operations at Squaremouth, says standard trip cancellation coverage on travel insurance policies responds to mandatory evacuation orders, uninhabitable accommodations, airport closures and supplier cancellations. "Where it falls short is when a traveler feels uncomfortable going unless there is an evacuation order or uninhabitable lodging," she explains. "Most standard policies don't treat high temperatures or poor air quality as covered cancellation reasons." In those situations, a more expensive "cancel for any reason" or "interruption for any reason" policy provides more flexibility, she adds. The timing can be tricky. Buy insurance after a fire is burning, and you’ve bought nothing. The U.K. insurer InsureandGo designated the current European wildfires a known event as of July 22. Every carrier sets its own date, and once it passes, that fire is no longer an unforeseen event on any policy sold afterward. There’s also a category of disruption nobody’s policy addresses. Nick Cavanaugh, CEO of Sensible Weather and a climate scientist, says traditional coverage is built for low-frequency, high-severity events. Smoke and heat tend to ruin the trip without canceling it. His company's survey of 600 U.S. leisure travelers found 78% have had a trip negatively affected by bad weather. That gap between what people assume is covered and what's listed in the policy can be frustrating, according to Joe Cronin, president of International Citizens Insurance. But some gaps are wider than others. "Travel medical coverage generally does apply if you go anyway and end up needing treatment for heat exhaustion or respiratory issues," he says. Do Hotels And Vacation Rentals Offer Wildfire Refunds? Here you have more leverage than you think, at least in some places. If your hotel, campsite or rental is evacuated by local authorities, French law treats it as force majeure, and the provider is generally required to refund the unused portion of the stay. Under EU package travel rules, travelers who booked a package can cancel before departure when unavoidable and extraordinary circumstances hit at or near the destination, with a full refund and no additional compensation. The platforms moved during the Gironde fires. Airbnb told the French newspaper la Voix du Nord that it extended the scope of its policy to cover the entire Gironde region in light of local advice against traveling there. Many suppliers waived cancellation fees, even on nonrefundable rates, when access was impossible or a property had closed. SNCF, the French railway system, allowed free changes and cancellations on trips to Gironde and Landes. Pay attention to the fine print. Airbnb's Major Disruptive Events Policy covers unforeseeable natural disasters and severe weather, plus mandatory government evacuation orders. Weather common enough to be foreseeable in a given location is usually excluded. For example, during the January 2025 Los Angeles fires, one guest with a rental near Pacific Palisades was told her cancellation didn't qualify. Ask for everything in writing, too. Keep the evacuation order or prefectural notice, and enclose it with any request for a refund or rebooking. Suppliers with no legal obligation to refund will often move a booking rather than lose the customer, and Sensible Weather's Cavanaugh says booking direct rather than through a third party usually buys you a real person to ask. How To Plan A Trip During Wildfire Season The season isn’t finished. Above-normal significant fire potential continues this month in much of the Northwest, northeast California, the northern Great Basin and the West Slope. Washington has already seen more than 1,000 fires burn about 425,000 acres this year, the most since 2021, according to the state Department of Natural Resources. Experienced travelers aren't panicking, though. "Despite another summer marked by record-breaking temperatures and increasingly severe weather events worldwide, most experienced international travelers are not overly concerned about extreme heat or weather-related health risks when planning trips abroad," says Bill McIntyre, a director at Global Rescue. Its survey found only 12% are "extremely or very concerned," with 52% "somewhat or slightly concerned." What distinguishes them is preparation. "Experienced international travelers understand that unpredictable weather is one of many travel risks that can be managed with preparation," says Jeff Weinstein, a paramedic and medical operations manager for Global Rescue. "They recognize that staying hydrated, adjusting itineraries and understanding local conditions will significantly reduce the likelihood of heat-related illness." Weinstein says their real concern isn't avoiding every risk. It's knowing they'll have access to quality medical care and, if necessary, medical evacuation. Check your destination against its own seasonal average rather than the country's latest news headlines. Take a look at the local air quality reading the morning of your departure. Ask your lodging about air conditioning, filtration and backup power. Build in a buffer day. Book rentals or hotels with flexible refund policies, which costs less than a "cancel for any reason" rider and pays out faster. Remember, canceling your vacation is the only decision here you can't reverse. Smoke will eventually clear—and maybe soon—but a forfeited deposit stays forfeited. So this summer, make the call as late as your refund window allows.

item.title: 7 New UNESCO World Heritage Sites Worth Traveling For In 2026
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.53
In July 2026, UNESCO added 25 new World Heritage Sites (19 cultural, five natural and one mixed) bringing the global list to 1,273 sites across 173 countries. This year’s additions also marked a milestone for Comoros, São Tomé and Príncipe and South Sudan, which gained their first-ever World Heritage Sites. South Sudan entered the list with a natural site, the Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape, which is home to one of the largest known terrestrial mammal migration in the world, with millions of antelope moving across its savannas and wetlands. While South Sudan is among the countries under Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory, here are seven new UNESCO World Heritage Sites that are worth visiting in 2026. Beaches of the D-Day Landings, Normandy, France UNESCO recognized the D-Day beaches in Normandy for their direct association with the Allied landings of June 6, 1944, which marked the beginning of the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi occupation. The site stretches across roughly 50 miles of coastline. It includes five D-Day landing beaches, such as Utah and Omaha, where American troops arrived, as well as Pointe du Hoc, a 110-foot cliff stormed by U.S. Rangers and the American Cemetery at Colleville‑sur‑Mer. Since it lies between Caen and Bayeux, the easiest way to reach it is via direct trains from Paris. Bayeux is particularly convenient for Omaha Beach, Pointe du Hoc and Colleville-sur-Mer. The Wider Area of Mount Olympus, Greece While Mount Olympus combines one of the most recognizable stories in Western mythology, it is also an impressive natural destination. UNESCO highlights not only its association with Zeus and the Twelve Olympian Gods, but also its limestone cliffs, deep gorges, unusual geology and importance as a Mediterranean plant-biodiversity hotspot. Mount Olympus rises in northern Greece, between Macedonia and Thessaly, close to the Aegean coast. Litochoro is the principal gateway for exploring the mountain and is accessible by road and train from Thessaloniki or Athens. Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, U.S. Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is the only U.S. site added to the World Heritage List in 2026. Okefenokee protects the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the world’s subtropical zone. Its total area is 680 square miles, which also contains about 92% of the wider Okefenokee Swamp. Its vast wetlands can be explored by canoe, kayak and boat, offering close encounters with alligators, birds and an ecosystem UNESCO recognizes as globally exceptional. The refuge lies in southeastern Georgia and northeastern Florida, with its main visitor entrance near Folkston, Georgia. Jacksonville is a convenient major-airport gateway city, close to the refuge. Aqaba Marine Reserve, Jordan Aqaba brings a completely different experience to the list: snorkeling and diving in a newly UNESCO-recognized coral ecosystem. UNESCO calls it the world's northernmost tropical coral reef system, with more than 150 hard-coral species and 500 fish species. Its corals have developed unusual resilience to high temperatures and marine heatwaves. The reserve lies along Jordan’s short Red Sea coastline at Aqaba, at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba. Travelers can fly into Amman's Queen Alia International Airport and connect to King Hussein International Airport in Aqaba via domestic flight or reach it by car. Village of Sidi Bou Saïd, Tunisia Sidi Bou Saïd is arguably one of the most visually appealing of the 2026 additions, with whitewashed buildings, vivid blue doors and windows, narrow streets and Mediterranean views. But UNESCO’s rationale goes deeper and stems from a history shaped by Sufi traditions, distinctive architecture, and generations of artists drawn to the village. Sidi Bou Saïd sits on a cliff overlooking the Mediterranean just outside Tunis, next to Carthage. Travelers fly into Tunis-Carthage International Airport and can easily reach the village by taxi or by train. The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros Comoros is a little-known island nation between East Africa and Madagascar with three main islands: Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Anjouan (Ndzuwani) and Mohéli (Mwali). 2026 is the first year a site in Comoros was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage destination. The inscription includes six historic towns: Moroni, Itsandra, Ntsoudjini and Iconi on Grande Comore (Ngazidja), and Mutsamudu and Domoni on Anjouan (Ndzuwani). These medinas trace how settlements dating back at least to the 11th century became sultanate capitals shaped by African, Islamic and Indian Ocean trading networks. International travelers generally enter through Prince Said Ibrahim International Airport near Moroni via Nairobi, Kenya or Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, India Sarnath is one of Buddhism's most significant sacred places and one of Buddhism's four principal pilgrimage sites with stupas, monasteries, archaeological ruins and living pilgrimage traditions. It is believed to be where Buddha delivered his first sermon after attaining enlightenment in the 6th century BCE. It is also a Buddhist monastic community, or Sangha, that effectively began with his earliest disciples. Sarnath lies just outside Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, making it particularly easy to add to a northern India itinerary. Lal Bahadur Shastri International Airport in Varanasi is the easiest getaway for international travelers.

item.title: Nantucket’s Greydon House Expands With New Lounge And Suites
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.38
Nantucket may be a tiny island, but the 48-square-mile island just got more space to stay overnight. Greydon House, the 10-year-old boutique hotel in the center of town, just opened a new lounge and four individual guest suites, as part of an ongoing expansion. Connected to the original 1950s era Broad Street property by a brick pathway, the expansion continues Greydon House’s commitment to Nantucket’s architectural legacy. Designed by a Nantucket-based team – Emeritus designers and interiors by Natasha Willauer – the addition includes a ground flour lounge called The Green Room, now open to the public Thursday through Monday from 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. The Green Room’s soft loungers and wraparound 14-seat bar offer an intimate setting for cocktails, light bites, and conversation in a seagreen colored space. Decor and finishings were sourced from local Nantucket antique shops, vintage markets across New England, and independent artisans who crafted on-site furnishings. “The goal was never to replicate the original, but to create something that feels like a natural extension – more like a cousin than a twin,” said Willauer. “We wanted each space to feel individually lived-in, while still connected to the larger story of Greydon House.” The four new guest suites are each unique, and designed to embrace Nantucket’s coastal landscape with soft blues and greens layered with warm woods, brick hues, and brass accents. Some of the suites have Gothic windows overlooking North Water Street and select bathrooms feature dual shower systems, marble finishes, and custom walnut vanities. Set in a former sea captain’s home and originally designed by Roman and Williams, the 20-room Greydon House has become a luxury destination on Nantucket over the past decade. The property is consistently named one of the best hotels on Nantucket and is home to the Venetian restaurant Via Mare. Next up in the expansion is a patio and garden slated for this fall. Visiting Nantucket Nantucket attracts nearly 2 million annual visitors. Despite reports that Nantucket has seen an explosion in tourism, data from the ferry operators and airlines (the only ways to reach the island, which is not connected to land by bridge or in any other way), indicates that tourism rates have remained steady in recent years. Census data shows that Nantucket has a year-round population of about 14,ooo residents, though around 80,000 people reside on the island in July and August. Lodging is a consistent topic of conversation for locals and visitors. The island has fewer than 1,000 standard hotel rooms and strictly regulates short term rentals and secondary platforms, like Airbnb. Nantucket’s Culture and Tourism office offers free referral services for overnight stays and lists vacancies, if available, daily. Hotels rarely open on the island. Most recently, Blue Flag Capital reopened the renovated Beachside Hotel in 2025.

item.title: Canadian Visitors To U.S. Were Up 10% In July—But New Steep Tariffs Threaten Tourism Lift
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.11
Topline The number of Canadian visitors to the U.S. was up 10% in July compared to a year ago—the fourth consecutive month of improvement—but tourism leaders warn the Trump administration’s new round of 50% tariffs could reverse the trend. Key Facts Roughly 10% more Canadians traveled to the U.S. in July, according to data released Tuesday from Statistics Canada. This was driven by a 13% increase in car trips, while trips by air were down 1% compared to July 2025. Overall visitation from Canadians remained down 29% compared to July 2024, driven by fewer trips by car (-29%) and by air (-27%). Crucial Quote “Right now, there are some good indicators that the bleeding may have stopped,” Amir Eylon, President and CEO of Longwoods International, told Forbes, before adding a caveat: “We’ll see this fall if the new tariffs have a negative impact.” What We Don’t Know Whether Canadians resuscitate their travel boycott of the U.S. to protest the sweeping new 50% punitive tariffs slated to take effect on August 19. The additional duties will apply roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, including a wide swath of items like wine, hockey sticks, cement, dairy, furniture, swimming pools and wigs. Most Canadian Visitors Still Won’t Travel To U.S. The increase in Canadian visitors to the U.S. in July was “largely due to a base-year effect,” Statistics Canada said, referring to a statistical distortion occurring because 2025 visitation was extraordinarily low. “When you hit rock bottom, a little bit up looks like a big improvement,” Eylon told Forbes. Inbound travel into the U.S. “declined sharply” in spring of 2025 “following geopolitical tensions,” Statistics Canada noted in the latest report. After President Donald Trump began calling Canada “the 51st state,” then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau told Canadians not to vacation south of the border, kicking off a travel boycott that has continued for 15 months. In the Longwoods survey, which was fielded before the new tariffs were announced, 56% of Canadians said U.S. policies made them less likely to travel to the U.S. Last month, Brand USA, the marketing arm of the U.S. tourism industry, launched a new campaign to woo back Canadian travelers. “Canada has always been essential to the United States’ travel economy,” Fred Dixon, the organization’s CEO said in a statement. Big Number $4.5 billion. That’s how much the drop in Canadian tourists cost the U.S. economy last year, according to the U.S. Travel Association (USTA). Historically, Canadians have comprised the single largest cohort of inbound tourists to the U.S., making up about a quarter of all foreign visitors, according to the U.S. Commerce Department. In 2024, Canadian visitors spent $20.5 billion in the United States. The USTA warned in early 2025 that even a 10% reduction in Canadian inbound travel could translate to $2.1 billion in lost spending. The actual drop was more than double that hypothetical. Further Reading Canadian Visitors To U.S. Nudged Up In June—But Remains Down 29% Since 2024 (Forbes)

item.title: Private Jets Are More Popular Than Ever. Here’s What To Know Before You Book One.
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.03
Christine Landis regularly takes a private jet from San Diego to Mammoth Mountain with two kids and an 80-pound chocolate Lab. The drive is eight hours, including the stops you make when you're traveling with children and a large dog. The flight is about one hour. And time, as they say, is money. "That's seven hours of my day I'm buying back," says Landis, who runs a home management platform. She booked through Wheels Up at first, then moved to NetJets. The cost runs roughly $9,000 each way. Landis is part of a group that has grown a lot bigger than most people realize. WingX Advance counted 3.9 million business jet departures worldwide in 2025, up 5% and the highest annual total on record, breaking a mark set in 2022. Back then the surge was a pandemic story. This time there's no pandemic. There's something more durable going on. But before you click "Buy," consider this: Private aviation is sold like a consumer product now, but it isn't regulated like one. Reserve a seat on a commercial carrier, and somebody has already vetted the airline, the airplane and the pilots. Book a private flight and that work is yours: figuring out which way to buy, who's flying you and whether the trip is worth it at all. Why private jet travel is surging A few things have converged recently. Corporations loosened up their travel policies. In Morgan Stanley’s recent survey of 160 corporate travel managers overseeing about $5 billion in annual travel spending, 10% report more permissive private jet policies for 2026. That’s up from 4% at midyear and 2% the year before. The continuing decline of customer service in commercial air travel has helped push that number higher. Washington helped, too. The One Big Beautiful Bill restored the 100% bonus depreciation for private aircraft, a tax treatment the American Economic Liberties Project says is giving a boost to private aviation. Its recent report counted a record 348,000 private jet departures globally in a single month, about 70% of them in the U.S. And booking a private jet got easy—really easy. "Technology has collapsed the booking friction that used to be the real barrier, not price alone," says Joshua Lowton, president of Surf On Demand at Surf Air Mobility. "When someone can see available aircraft, get transparent pricing and book in minutes rather than hours of phone calls, private flight becomes a practical comparison to a crowded commercial flight with connections." Surf Air’s on-demand charter revenue hit $10.1 million in the first quarter of 2026, a 77% jump and the best quarter that business has had since it launched. In June, Wheels Up signed on as the first outside customer for Surf Air's broker software, a deal worth up to $12 million. Lowton says electric aircraft are next, with BETA's ALIA flying demonstration missions in Hawaii. How much does a private jet cost per hour? If you're budgeting for a charter, the hourly rate depends on the size of the aircraft. Expect to pay between $2,500 and $5,000 per hour for a light jet, which seats up to seven passengers. Midsize jets run between $4,000 and $8,000 per hour, offering more cabin space and a longer range. If you need a heavy jet or ultra-long-range aircraft for cross-country or international flights, rates start around $8,000 and can exceed $15,000 per hour. Those base rates don’t cover the entire bill. You have to account for federal excise taxes, landing fees, crew overnight expenses and repositioning charges if the operator has to position an aircraft with no passengers on board to reach you. Experts say you should get an all-in quote in writing so you understand the total cost before signing a contract. Private jet options: Charters, jet cards and memberships If you're thinking of switching from commercial airlines to private jet travel, you have a lot of choices. On-demand charter. You book a specific aircraft for a specific trip. There’s no long-term contract, no initiation fees, and no long-term commitment. "First-time flyers should start with on-demand because of the flexibility it provides," says David Gitman, CEO of Monarch Air Group in Fort Lauderdale, Fla. Jet cards. You prepay for flight hours at a fixed rate. Sentient Jet invented the format in 1999. "Card owners purchase flight hours at a fixed hourly rate, with guaranteed availability, no hidden costs and hours that never expire," says Alan Walsh, its president. Memberships. Annual or monthly fees buy access to a fleet and, usually, better pricing. Fractional and co-ownership. You buy a share of an aircraft. Partners in Aviation matches two owners on one plane instead of dozens. "Our focus is on operators flying 50 to 150 hours per year," says Mark Molloy, its president. Per-seat. You buy one seat on a scheduled flight out of a general aviation terminal. JSX runs 30-seat jets under public charter rules. Cirrus Aviation Services launched Theos to reach the same customer. "There was a growing segment of travelers who valued the efficiency and personalized experience of private aviation but didn't necessarily need, or want, to charter an entire aircraft," says Eric Grilly, its president. Jet cards and memberships usually require a minimum purchase, often 25 hours a year or more. "Occasional users don't benefit from cards," says McLean Robbins, founder of Lily Pond Luxury, a travel agency. Most of her clients book individual charters instead. Irakli Litanishvili, co-founder of Mirai Flights, goes further. Don't buy a block of hours first, he advises. It ties you to one or two aircraft types, so the trip that needs something bigger, smaller or a turboprop into a small airfield ends up costing you more. Learn the market first. How to check private jet operator safety records Most companies selling you a private flight don't own the airplane. They're brokers. For example, while Surf Air Mobility does own aircraft that operate through its scheduled commercial services on Mokulele Airlines and Southern Airways Express, it discloses on its website that it doesn't operate aircraft for its On Demand service. There's a gap between the brand on your invoice and the company whose pilots are flying you, and it raises an important question about safety. "People often lump all of private aviation together, which is misleading," says Greg Raiff, CEO of Elevate Jet. “If you're talking about weekend pilots flying small planes, the accident rate is meaningfully higher than commercial. Full stop, commercial is still the gold standard. But if you're talking about professionally operated, crewed business jets, the safety record is excellent.” The real divide isn’t private versus commercial. It’s operators who are well established and professionally managed by aviation experts, versus fly-by-night carriers where the pilot is the owner and the owner is also the entire complement of office staff. Fewer than 5% of operators carry the industry's top-tier, independent safety certification, and only a handful of those have sustained a perfect safety record across three decades. That's the group worth paying attention to. The regulatory line is Part 135 versus Part 91. (Part 91 is general aviation, and Part 91 operators aren't licensed to fly you for money.) Operational requirements for Part 135 are less stringent than for Part 121. "Most small aircraft accidents are Part 91," says Bob Bacheler, managing director of Flying Angels, a medical transport company in Philadelphia that moves several dozen clients a year on private jets. Third-party audits like ARGUS, Wyvern and IS-BAO close some of that distance by rating operators above the FAA floor. "Consider charter suppliers that undergo third-party audits," says Susan Sherren, founder of Couture Trips. "Prioritize equipment and crew credentials over amenities or menus. Luxurious amenities such as caviar can't replace strong safety standards and professional qualifications." For example, Surf On Demand earned ARGUS Certified Charter Broker accreditation in March. There are more than 400 ARGUS-certified operators. There are 16 certified brokers. Raiff has a field test. Ask a broker who its director of safety is, then search that person's name. "More often than you'd think, you'll find out that person is also the director of marketing." When flying private makes sense - You’re splitting the cost. Divide a charter among four to eight people and the per-person cost drops, especially against multiple business-class tickets. - The airlines don't go where you're going. Scheduled carriers serve fewer than 500 U.S. airports. Private aircraft can use more than 5,000. Landing 10 minutes from a small town beats flying into a hub and driving two hours. - You can turn a two-day trip into one day. The savings show up as a hotel night you don't book and a workday you don't lose if you're getting there and back on the same day. When flying private doesn't make sense - You're treating it as a pure upgrade. Landis, who flies private regularly, draws her own line: "We don't fly private when there is a reliable commercial nonstop available." - You're chasing a fantasy. First-timers expect luxury and get logistics. "What actually impresses them is arriving 15 minutes before departure, walking straight to the plane, and being in the air within minutes," Lowton says. - You haven't looked at the airplane. Litanishvili says the two things you'll feel are cabin height and baggage space. A Citation Mustang cabin runs about 4 feet 6 inches, so you stoop. A Global 7500 runs 6 feet 2 inches, with a bedroom. - The quote you're comparing isn't the price you'll pay. Bacheler still remembers his first charter and the $350 catering fee nobody mentioned. How to book a private flight the right way - Ask who operates the flight, not who sold it. Get the certificate holder’s name and the tail number, the aircraft’s registration mark. Kate Scott, vice president of SELECT Private Jets by Internova, points out that air charter brokers are required to disclose the operator. - Demand an all-in quote in writing. Fuel surcharges, catering, de-icing, landing and handling fees, repositioning, overnight expenses and taxes can all add up when you're flying private. Scott says every foreseeable cost belongs in the quote so you're comparing the same thing across bids. - Check the third-party audit, not the website. Research the reports by ARGUS, Wyvern or IS-BAO. A polished app proves nothing about a maintenance program. - Confirm the baggage limit before you book. Capacity differs by aircraft, passenger count and route. It's the single most common first-time miscalculation, and luggage restrictions are tighter than most travelers expect. - Ask what happens when it breaks. What happens if your flight is delayed by a mechanical failure? Robbins says her broker sells coverage that guarantees a comparable or better replacement aircraft. - Read the cancellation terms before you wire anything. Most charter is paid by wire transfer, which means no chargeback protection. - Ask about empty legs if your dates are loose. Repositioning flights sell cheap. They also disappear when the primary itinerary changes. Private aviation sells itself as freedom, and for the right trip it delivers. But it also hands you the responsibility that an airline normally carries for you. Nobody vets the operator on your behalf, and nobody guarantees the reserve aircraft or crew. That's something to consider before you book your own jet.

item.title: This British Port Wants Bigger Cruise Ships. Not Everyone Is Happy
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.99
For cruise guests exploring the British Isles, Falmouth offers something quite different from major ports such as Southampton or Liverpool. The Cornish town combines a historic waterfront, beaches within walking distance and access to some of southwest England’s best-known attractions. Yet despite sitting on one of the world’s largest natural harbors, Falmouth remains a relatively small player in the British cruise industry. That could be about to change. A proposed £150 million ($202 million) redevelopment of Falmouth Docks would allow much larger cruise ships to berth alongside, potentially helping increase annual cruise visitor numbers to as many as 200,000 by 2030. Supporters see an opportunity to secure the future of a historic working port while bringing more tourism revenue into Cornwall. Opponents question the environmental impact. Behind the debate is a question facing many smaller destinations: should ports reshape themselves to accommodate ever-bigger cruise ships? Falmouth’s Growing Cruise Business Cruise tourism is nothing new to Falmouth. The port welcomed around 60,000 passengers across 42 cruise calls in 2025, with passenger numbers expected to increase again in 2026. But there is a significant limitation to further growth. Larger vessels generally need to anchor offshore and transfer passengers into town by tender boat. The redevelopment would change that by extending and upgrading existing wharves and dredging areas around the docks. The aim is to accommodate so-called 'Excellence-class’ cruise ships measuring as much as 345 meters, or 1,131 feet, in length. These are enormous vessels. Ships built on the platform typically carry around 5,400 passengers at standard occupancy and can accommodate considerably more when full. Planning documents envisage approximately 11 calls from such ships annually if the redevelopment proceeds. More Than Just Cruise Ships Although cruise ships have attracted much of the attention, the proposed redevelopment is not simply an oversized cruise terminal. The wider project includes repairing aging infrastructure, improving cargo facilities and creating capacity to support the emerging floating offshore wind industry. The British government has backed the plans, arguing that modernizing the docks could create skilled employment and help Falmouth compete for new maritime business. Cruise tourism forms one part of that economic case. Project projections suggest increasing cruise traffic to 200,000 passengers annually by 2030 could bring an additional £13 million ($17.5 million) into the local economy and support more than 350 tourism-related jobs. Falmouth is also a gateway to Cornwall, with shore excursions taking cruise guests to attractions such as the Eden Project, St. Michael’s Mount and other destinations around the county. Environmental Concerns Over Dredging The strongest objections concern the dredging required to accommodate larger ships. Cornwall Wildlife Trust has submitted a formal Holding Objection to the Marine Management Organisation, arguing that more evidence is needed before the environmental impact can be properly assessed. The Trust says the project would involve dredging around 643,000 cubic meters of sediment from the Fal Estuary, with potential risks to seagrass, kelp, maerl beds and the area’s native oyster fishery. It has also questioned whether existing sediment testing is extensive enough to identify pockets of contamination. “We do not want to see the Docks decline, but redevelopment must be done carefully,” said Dan Barrios-O’Neill, Head of Marine Conservation at Cornwall Wildlife Trust. Developer Balaena says the proposal involves targeted “pocket dredging” rather than dredging the wider estuary, and that material considered unsuitable for disposal at sea would be taken inland instead. The Marine Management Organisation is the lead environmental regulator for the project. What Happens When Thousands Arrive At Once? Annual passenger totals can disguise one of the biggest challenges created by modern cruise ships: the concentration of visitors into a few hours. The project’s environmental assessment considers a worst-case scenario in which two ‘Excellence-class’ ships are alongside simultaneously. Such a situation would be unusual, but potentially striking. Two large ships could mean more than 10,000 cruise passengers arriving in or passing through the area on a single day. The assessment also considers the additional coaches, shuttle buses, taxis and other vehicles required to move passengers around. For businesses, that influx could mean thousands of additional potential customers. For residents and other travelers, it could mean a very different experience of the town. Ppart of Falmouth’s appeal as a cruise port is precisely its relatively small scale. There is a legitimate question over whether attracting substantially larger ships could begin to change some of the qualities that make Falmouth attractive in the first place. A Bigger Question For Smaller Cruise Ports Cruise ships have grown dramatically over the past two decades. Ports that once comfortably accommodated mainstream vessels increasingly face a choice: invest in deeper water, longer berths and upgraded infrastructure, or accept that a growing share of the cruise fleet may be unable to dock. There are benefits to adapting. Allowing larger ships to berth alongside is easier for passengers than tendering ashore and could make Falmouth attractive to more cruise lines and itineraries. Doing nothing also carries economic consequences for a working port trying to secure its future. Yet bigger ships do not automatically create a better destination, either for residents or for cruise guests. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Why China Worries About North Korea
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 7.29
For China, Northeast Asia remains the weak spot in its attempt to secure its immediate borders. Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are mounting, which raises the possibility of conflict that could spill beyond the Korean Peninsula. Security coordination among Japan, South Korea, and the United States is also becoming stronger, putting pressure on China, and North Korea’s entrenched nuclear status has made Japan and South Korea anxious about their own security and could even motivate them to eventually pursue nuclear weapons themselves. China is increasingly worried about North Korea’s role in creating and intensifying these risks—and about the need to adjust its North Korea strategy to manage them without inflaming tensions and further destabilizing the region. Pyongyang has grown more unpredictable as it has become emboldened by its nuclear program. Decades of international sanctions, condemnations, and isolation have not forced Pyongyang to denuclearize. Instead, they have made North Korea even more determined to hold on to its nuclear weapons program. And although North Korea still depends on China for economic support, Pyongyang’s expanding security relationship with Russia has made it less exclusively dependent on Beijing than in the past. If a crisis involving North Korea were to break out, China fears that it could be marginalized as conflict spirals out of control. For nearly eight decades, Beijing’s relationship with Pyongyang has leaned on historical ties, symbolic friendship, and informal coordination. But Pyongyang’s unpredictability has made such an approach inadequate. China’s new strategy, symbolized by Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to North Korea in June, aims to draw Pyongyang back into its orbit and make the bilateral relationship more stable and manageable. Beijing does not want North Korea—one of the world’s few remaining communist states and a potential showcase for how China can effectively manage its relationships with allies—to fail. Nor does Beijing want to abandon its push for long-term denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula. But it realizes that it needs better ways to avoid surprises from Pyongyang, which could be destabilizing for China or trigger expanded military deployments by Japan, South Korea, and the United States. Beijing is working to establish structured high-level communication channels so it can receive earlier warnings about potential North Korean provocations, have greater opportunities to intervene before a crisis escalates, and improve its ability to predict North Korean behavior. It is also shifting its approach from treating denuclearization as a precondition for engagement with Pyongyang to reducing risks that might lead to conflicts. With global uncertainty on the rise, China hopes that closer contact and clearer communication with North Korea can serve its most important goal—keeping its immediate neighborhood calm. SETTING BOUNDARIES Although China and North Korea share a border and are both communist states, their relationship has fluctuated over the nearly eight decades since the two countries were founded. China’s connection with North Korea has traditionally relied on diplomatic friendship, shared revolutionary memories, and the personal networks of elder leaders. During the Korean War, for example, the two countries drew close. But at other times, tensions have pushed them apart. After Kim Jong Un became North Korea’s leader, in late 2011, the country’s relations with China plummeted because of disagreements over Pyongyang’s actions, including Kim’s pursuit of nuclear weapons and the arrest and execution of Kim’s uncle. Beijing’s frustration with Pyongyang reached new heights in 2017, when North Korea conducted a nuclear test and many missile tests that revealed that it had mastered hydrogen bomb technology and was rapidly improving its nuclear capabilities. The test not only flew in the face of China’s stated opposition to North Korean nuclearization but was also politically embarrassing for Beijing: it occurred while China was hosting a summit for BRICS leaders. That year, China voted for five UN Security Council resolutions to impose crippling sanctions on North Korea and tighten monitoring requirements. China’s concern about a potential escalation of conflict between North Korea and the United States even led Beijing to invite U.S. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Joseph Dunford to China for discussions about the North Korean nuclear program and regional security. Soon after, when a U.S.–North Korean rapprochement appeared possible, China changed course. In early 2018, after U.S. President Donald Trump and Kim started discussing a potential summit, China worried about being excluded from discussions about how to manage tensions on the Korean Peninsula. In the run-up to Kim’s meeting with Trump, which ultimately took place in Singapore in June 2018, the North Korean leader wanted to consult Xi about his experiences dealing with the U.S. leader. Beijing quickly extended an invitation for Kim to visit. Kim went to China in March and again in May and June of that same year. After Xi returned the favor and visited North Korea in the summer of 2019, border trade flourished and bilateral ties recovered. But when the COVID-19 pandemic struck, in the beginning of 2020, North Korea closed its border and suspended all passenger and freight train services and flights to China. The abrupt termination of the main channels of connections and contact left the Chinese–North Korean relationship in a shambles as trade ground to a halt and economic ties were mostly cut off. At the same time, North Korea drew closer to Russia, leaving China again worried about being the odd man out. FROM RUSSIA WITH LEVERAGE Today, China remains economically irreplaceable to North Korea. China is the source of over 70 percent of North Korea’s total foreign trade, approximately 60 percent of its food, and 75 percent of its consumer goods. China annually supplies North Korea with approximately 520,000 tons of petroleum and between 500,000 and 800,000 tons of grain and fertilizer (all within UN exemption limits). This is a foundational arrangement for sustaining North Korean livelihoods and stabilizing China’s northeastern border. In the past few years, however, Russia has drastically increased its support to North Korea. Following the signing of the North Korean–Russian Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty, in June 2024, Moscow has provided security guarantees, military technology, energy supplies, labor export markets, and sanctions evasion support to Pyongyang. North Korea, in turn, has sent ammunition and soldiers to fight for Russia in its war in Ukraine. Russia’s closer relationship with North Korea relieves some of China’s obligation to deliver economic aid and security guarantees to its northeastern neighbor. But it has also given North Korea greater bargaining power and changed its relationship with China. Previously, China was North Korea’s sole provider; now, it is merely the largest among multiple pillars of support. North Korea’s external strategy has evolved from one in which it leaned on China to balance pressure from the United States to a three-pronged arrangement in which it uses China to stabilize its economy, Russia to supplement its security, and U.S. pressure to justify its nuclear program. By simultaneously strengthening ties with China and Russia while maintaining its nuclear deterrent against the United States, North Korea has made clear its desire to replicate the Cold War–era pattern of maneuvering between China and the Soviet Union, which allows it to maximize the benefits it can receive. China remains economically irreplaceable to North Korea. For Beijing, the biggest risk of closer North Korean–Russian cooperation is that it provides an excellent pretext for Japan, South Korea, and the United States to accelerate the integration of their bloc. If North Korea and Russia continue to work closely on nuclear weapons, Japan and South Korea will use the North Korean threat to justify boosting their alliances with the United States. They could push for more trilateral intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, and weapons integration. This will ultimately create an institutionalized military deterrence alliance directed not only at North Korea but also at China, which will impose pressure on China from multiple fronts and exacerbate military tensions around flash points such as the Taiwan Strait. Moreover, the great-power competition between China and the United States increases the chances that frictions with Pyongyang could escalate into direct U.S.-Chinese confrontation. The Korean Peninsula is an integral component of Washington’s Indo-Pacific strategy, its alliance arrangement, and its efforts at regional deterrence. China’s priority is to avoid unnecessary military conflict with the United States, but North Korea’s continued nuclear and missile provocations, its deepening military cooperation with Russia, and its growing unpredictability risk dragging China into a crisis. Beijing’s wish to avoid instability in the Korean Peninsula reflects its desire to stabilize its relations with the United States and avoid any potential for escalation that could lead to direct conflict. TALKING IT OUT China can no longer rely on historical sentiment, personal friendships between leaders, and ad hoc diplomatic coordination to maintain its influence over an increasingly unpredictable, confident, and assertive North Korea. Rather, Beijing needs a way of managing its relationship with Pyongyang that is more stable, is built on consistent and normal interactions, and enables China to set enforceable conditions on the aid it provides. In other words, China needs an institutionally driven approach—one that puts greater weight on formal cooperation mechanisms and communication channels. China is focused on establishing more emergency lines to connect leaders, expanding regular diplomatic and security consultation, and improving official notification mechanisms for border incidents and missile tests. Such efforts have already started. In the past four months, China’s foreign minister and the head of its top political advisory body met with Kim in Pyongyang, and North Korea’s premier visited China and met with Xi. Beijing further hopes to include North Korea in multilateral platforms such as the Greater Tumen Initiative, an intergovernmental economic cooperation framework for Northeast Asia, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and to develop regional dialogue mechanisms under China’s leadership in which North Korea can participate. China still does not welcome a nuclear North Korea and does not believe its nuclear status should be cost free. But Beijing increasingly realizes that immediate denuclearization, or a clearly defined step-by-step road map to denuclearization, is not feasible. A nuclear North Korea is hardly ideal, but pressuring an unpredictable Pyongyang in ways that could lead to outright conflict is far worse. Crisis prevention and the need for stability are now China’s top priorities on the Korean Peninsula. Beijing can also leverage North Korea’s economic dependence on China to push for specific acts of restraint from Pyongyang, such as refraining from provocative actions that could trigger expanded military deployments by Japan, South Korea, and the United States. Economic support is not just a price China has to pay to maintain North Korean stability; it is also a practical tool to shape Pyongyang’s actions and prevent Beijing’s own marginalization in the region. China can link humanitarian assistance, openness to border trade, energy supplies, and the provision of infrastructure to North Korea’s willingness to restrain its military threats. Only by conditioning incremental cooperation on tangible evidence that North Korea is effectively lowering the risks of conflict can China convert its economic advantages into substantive regional influence. The high-level meeting in Pyongyang in June was the first step toward realizing this strategy. Chinese–North Korean relations will have to follow a new logic: if North Korea desires broader cooperation with Beijing, it has to meet China’s requirements on border stability, crisis communications, and military restraint. In return, China is willing to provide greater economic support, expand trade and investment, assist with infrastructure development, and offer international political backing, especially because it wants to see a stable and economically viable North Korea that neither poses a security threat to China nor becomes a pawn in great-power competition. With a changed North Korea, emotional ties among fellow travelers can no longer sustain regional stability. Beijing is counting on the possibility that more connections and clearer boundaries can transform its influence over Pyongyang into effective crisis management tools. item.title: China’s Legal Weapon
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 5.20
In May, China’s Ministry of Commerce took an unprecedented step: it ordered Chinese firms to disregard U.S. sanctions against five domestic refiners processing Iranian crude oil. Weeks later, China’s Ministry of Justice issued another first-of-its-kind order, declaring that the European Union’s antisubsidy probe into a Chinese security firm was an improper assertion of foreign jurisdiction. These measures might seem like ordinary bureaucratic retaliation, the latest moves in a familiar cycle of sanctions, investigations, and countermeasures. But they are part of an important shift in the terms of global rivalry. Traditionally, assessments of a country’s ability to shape events beyond its borders have focused on its military strength, economic size, and cultural reach. Today, an understanding of national power must also include what countries can obtain through the law. Beijing’s recent moves to resist extraterritoriality flow directly from a strategic, state-led project to improve China’s legal power. The United States led the construction of the postwar legal order, and for decades, it has had a disproportionate ability to shape global outcomes through legal instruments. In the early 2010s, for example, Washington leveraged various jurisdictional advantages to cut Iran off from oil markets and global banking, pressuring it into negotiations. The United States’ legal power has rested in part on wealth and military strength, but it has also depended on the capacity of American legal personnel, the credibility of U.S. legal institutions, and the jurisdictional control the United States has retained over key nodes of the global economy. These advantages have not gone unnoticed in China. Over the past decade, Beijing has mobilized ministries, courts, law schools, and bar associations around a shared goal: enabling China to use the law more effectively beyond its borders. Beijing has invested in building a cadre of lawyers who understand foreign and international law. It has advised Chinese entities on how to defend themselves more effectively in foreign courts and international tribunals. It has promoted Chinese courts and arbitration bodies as alternatives to Western forums. It has expanded its use of sophisticated legal tools—including sanctions, blocking rules, export controls, and national security reviews—to police foreign actors’ conduct. And it has sought greater influence over global norms, from technical standards to rules governing sea-lanes. China’s bid for legal power has enjoyed real success. Past a certain point, however, China will struggle. It is relatively easy to enact new laws and train better lawyers; it is harder to reproduce the institutional credibility and economic indispensability that made the United States a dominant legal force. But the United States cannot simply assume that its inherited advantages will endure. It must work to preserve the legal institutions, professional expertise, economic relationships, and international commitments from which U.S. legal power has long derived. If, instead, Washington dismantles the legal structures underpinning its power—as it has begun to in recent years—Beijing may be well positioned to step into the void. BUILDING A CODE Washington’s extraordinary legal power traces back to the central role the United States played in designing the post–World War II international order. Even before the war, the country had already developed a large legal profession, sophisticated corporate firms, and distinctive constitutional institutions, although European legal systems retained greater intellectual prestige. The United States’ wartime ascent allowed it to marshal those domestic capacities into building U.S.-centric international rules and institutions. Washington helped shape the UN Charter, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and the Bretton Woods system, embedding U.S. influence into institutions governing international security, trade, and finance. The United States continued to accumulate legal power over the second half of the twentieth century. Its law schools, law firms, and government agencies helped develop a pipeline of talented lawyers expert in national security law, cross-border disputes, and international law. Today, the State Department’s Office of the Legal Adviser employs roughly 200 attorneys—nearly three times the approximately 70 lawyers employed by its British counterpart—and divides them among more than 20 specialized units that handle treaty negotiations and cases before international tribunals. At the Justice Department, the Office of Foreign Litigation protects American interests in thousands of proceedings around the world. These and other offices have given Washington unusual capacity to advance its interests abroad, in both courts and diplomatic forums. A combination of legal credibility and economic leverage has also cemented the United States’ global legal reach. Washington has built on these advantages over decades, applying antitrust law to foreign firms, prohibiting bribery abroad, and using sanctions and export controls to shape the behavior of overseas actors. The country has evolved a distinctive form of jurisdictional power—the ability to bring foreign actors and activities within the reach of U.S. law. Parties to legal disputes often choose U.S. courts because they regard them as sophisticated and impartial. Foreign firms, meanwhile, may come into U.S. jurisdiction if their transactions clear in dollars, their products incorporate U.S. software or components, they seek to acquire an American company, or their conduct affects U.S. markets. These connections give U.S. lawmakers, courts, and regulators substantial reach in fields as varied as sovereign debt and terrorism financing. These same advantages have strengthened Washington’s ability to shape global legal norms. American approaches to commercial law and corporate compliance have spread widely, often because foreign firms voluntarily conform to preserve access to U.S. markets. Global banks, for example, have built extensive sanctions-screening systems around rules administered by the U.S. Treasury. The United States is not the world’s only hub of legal influence. English common law still governs substantial rules on cross-border finance, shipping, commercial contracts, and international arbitration. The European Union exercises great influence in fields such as data protection, competition, and food safety. But through legal talent, legal reputation, and economic dependencies, the United States has remained a focal point in global law. LAW AND A NEW ORDER As China emerged as a global power, its leaders began to see law as an instrument of statecraft and to recognize the country’s vulnerability to other countries’ legal power. Pressure applied by Washington through sanctions, export controls, and prosecutions targeting the Chinese corporations Huawei and ZTE only underscored the urgency of building China’s domestic legal power. As early as 2014, Beijing began to stress the necessity of “foreign-related legal work”; at the Communist Party’s 2019 Fourth Plenum, leaders made strengthening China’s legal power part of a broader plan to modernize China’s system of governance. In 2023, the party devoted a Politburo study session to “foreign-related rule of law.” At that meeting, Chinese leader Xi Jinping identified strengthening China’s legal capacities as a “long-term need” for advancing the goal of national rejuvenation. Chinese officials condemn American legal hegemony while closely studying the institutions and techniques that sustain it. One top priority has been to cultivate legal talent. Before Xi came to power in 2012, China already had more law schools than the United States, but they were of uneven quality and lacked systematic approaches to teaching foreign law. Chinese law schools have since launched several dozen programs, institutes, and degrees dedicated to training lawyers in international law and the legal systems of other countries. In 2024, Beijing designated 51 university-led partnerships that bring together law schools, government agencies, courts, law firms, and arbitration bodies to train students for international and cross-border legal practice. Since 2012, Beijing has added extraterritorial provisions to more than 20 laws. The government itself has established a dedicated Foreign-Related Rule of Law Bureau in the Ministry of Justice, a specialized international commercial court, and nationally designated research centers. Scholars and practitioners now advise Chinese entities on responding promptly to foreign litigation, avoiding default judgments, and presenting Chinese legal positions through expert testimony and amicus briefs. China has also invested in narrative power—the capacity to present its conduct in legal terms that foreign audiences will find intelligible and persuasive. As the party secretary of a major Chinese law school wrote in the People’s Daily, “enhancing propaganda ability” is key to Chinese legal ambitions. Chinese law schools have accordingly placed greater weight on teaching Chinese students to argue using the vocabularies of foreign legal systems. One leading school’s course on U.S. foreign relations law examined students by asking them to develop arguments based on the U.S. Constitution against a hypothetical change in American policy toward Taiwan. Beijing has become especially concerned with foreign laws that reach Chinese actors. In a 2023 report, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused Washington of constructing “a massive, mutually reinforcing and interlocking legal system for long-arm jurisdiction.” China’s 2021 blocking rules sought to protect Chinese citizens and firms by authorizing the Chinese government to forbid local parties from complying with particular foreign laws and official measures, and regulations issued in 2026 by the State Council, China’s cabinet, created a broader mechanism for prohibiting Chinese parties from complying with improper foreign assertions of jurisdiction. In May, for instance, Beijing barred Chinese parties from complying with U.S. sanctions levied against five refiners accused of purchasing Iranian oil and from assisting with the EU’s antisubsidy investigation into Nuctech, a Chinese security-equipment firm. Other measures have extended Chinese law outward. Since 2012, Beijing has added extraterritorial provisions to more than 20 laws. The 2020 Hong Kong National Security Law, for instance, claims jurisdiction over certain national-security offenses committed abroad against Hong Kong. China has expanded its offensive legal arsenal to export controls, foreign investment and cybersecurity reviews, and entity list and licensing regimes and used those tools to freeze assets, prohibit transactions, or restrict access to strategically important materials such as rare earths. Chinese courts have also widened their reach over cross-border disputes, particularly in global patent litigation, by ordering parties not to pursue or enforce competing proceedings abroad. Ultimately, Chinese leaders believe their country must become a more active participant in international rule-making and a leader in institutional reform. Party directives call for greater Chinese influence over rules governing the oceans, polar regions, cyberspace, outer space, nuclear safety, anticorruption efforts, climate change, and international finance. They also urge more Chinese representation within international organizations. At the World Trade Organization, China has become an active litigant and coalition organizer. Chinese institutions have also gained substantial influence in developing international technical standards in areas such as telecommunications, e-commerce, and emerging technologies—even as Beijing creates and promotes alternative bodies, most successfully the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which has developed into a major multilateral lender. THE JURY IS OUT China has not sought to emulate or disrupt every aspect of U.S. legal hegemony. It has concentrated on building a legal infrastructure that protects Chinese trade and investment and strengthens China’s capabilities in international rule-making. Its ambitions to export Chinese legal practices have been more selective, focusing on discrete tools and techniques—such as AI-assisted adjudication—rather than transplanting its legal practices wholesale. These investments in legal power have paid real dividends. But China’s legal ambitions also have political limits. Beijing has tried to make its courts and arbitration bodies more attractive, creating specialized commercial courts and inviting foreign experts to participate in advisory roles in cross-border disputes. These reforms, however, remain embedded in a judiciary that is subordinate to Communist Party leadership. The China International Commercial Court, for example, is not a special island within China’s legal system; it is composed of Supreme People’s Court judges operating within the ordinary, party-led judicial hierarchy. To make Chinese legal institutions more appealing, Beijing would need to grant them genuine autonomy rather than merely expecting professionalism in routine cases. But as China’s 2018 detention of two Canadian citizens after Canada arrested a Huawei executive showed, the party readily interferes in the legal system when important interests are at stake. The credibility of Chinese law is further undermined by Beijing’s messaging. Xi has stressed the importance of projecting an image of China as a rule-of-law country. Yet China increasingly uses the law to signal resolve and threaten retaliation. A legal system marketed as welcoming becomes less attractive when it is also advertised as a weapon of national struggle. As China expands its legal power, the United States is willfully eroding its own. And China’s legal ambitions face economic constraints. The global dominance of the dollar and the United States’ market size and technological leadership bring many outside actors within the reach of U.S. law. China has sought to build comparable leverage by promoting the renminbi in cross-border trade, developing alternative payment systems, and dominating critical supply chains. But financial market restrictions have kept the renminbi’s share of global foreign exchange reserves to low single-digit percentages. China remains outflanked by the United States in many metrics of legal power. A Chinese sanction may bar companies’ access to China, but it generally cannot induce banks and companies around the world in the way a U.S. sanction can. As China’s own Ministry of Foreign Affairs lamented in 2023, the United States remains “the only sanctions superpower in the world.” Beijing has also struggled to make China a preferred forum for international disputes. The China International Commercial Court has handled less than 50 cases since its creation eight years ago. In 70 to 80 percent of the cases heard by the London Court of International Arbitration, both parties are foreign. By contrast, such cases make up less than two percent of the caseload of China’s leading commercial arbitration institution. The United States still enjoys dominant legal power, and as things stand, China will be slow to catch up. But even as China seeks to grow its legal power, the United States is willfully eroding its own. The Trump administration’s attacks on judges and civil servants weaken confidence in U.S. legal institutions and the U.S. government’s capacity to pursue complex legal strategies beyond its borders. Washington is also surrendering influence in the forums in which global rules are made. After the United States withdrew from the World Health Organization and abandoned negotiations over a pandemic accord, the remaining WHO members adopted the agreement without Washington, and China pledged $500 million to help fill the resulting vacuum. The U.S. government’s aggressive use of export controls, technology restrictions, and financial chokepoints has encouraged other countries to reduce their exposure to U.S. jurisdiction. If Washington continues to undercut its own advantages, China has established the foundations to provide at least some plausible replacements. Party supremacy may limit the credibility of Chinese courts, but it does not prevent China from winning cases abroad or from shaping global legal norms. China need not embrace a liberal rule of law to become a formidable legal power.
