item.title: A Middle Eastern NATO?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 6.55
A Middle Eastern NATO? What’s behind the defense pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. Over the last several decades, the Gulf states have used their oil and gas riches to transform their economies into global powerhouses. Many have built gleaming new cities and some of the world’s best airlines—and turned to the United States for security to make sure the party kept going. The Iran conflict has thrown most of those plans into flux. The latest example of this state of uncertainty could be the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a pact between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia to treat an attack on one of them as an attack on them all—language that is reminiscent of NATO’s Article 5. On the latest episode of FP Live, I dug into the nature of this new defense agreement and how the Gulf countries are rethinking their security and economic frameworks. I spoke with Allison Minor, a director at the Atlantic Council who previously served as a U.S. deputy special envoy to Yemen and also as a director at the National Security Council focused on the Arabian Peninsula. Over the last several decades, the Gulf states have used their oil and gas riches to transform their economies into global powerhouses. Many have built gleaming new cities and some of the world’s best airlines—and turned to the United States for security to make sure the party kept going. The Iran conflict has thrown most of those plans into flux. The latest example of this state of uncertainty could be the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a pact between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia to treat an attack on one of them as an attack on them all—language that is reminiscent of NATO’s Article 5. On the latest episode of FP Live, I dug into the nature of this new defense agreement and how the Gulf countries are rethinking their security and economic frameworks. I spoke with Allison Minor, a director at the Atlantic Council who previously served as a U.S. deputy special envoy to Yemen and also as a director at the National Security Council focused on the Arabian Peninsula. The full conversation is available on the video box atop this page or wherever you get your podcasts—on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or anywhere else. (Follow the FP Live podcast to automatically download it for free.) What follows here is a transcript of an excerpt of our discussion. Ravi Agrawal: So let’s just start with what’s being called the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. How do you see this? Is it an attempt at building a regional NATO, or is it not as significant as that? Allison Minor: I think it’s a very significant development, but I don’t think it’s going to translate into the truly operational security alliance that we see with NATO and particularly the NATO Article 5 condition. There is a mutual defense commitment in the Mecca Agreement, but I don’t think it’s going to look like what we would expect a NATO response to look like for an attack on a NATO member. RA: Yes, and the Article 5 clause you’re pointing to, of course, is that an attack on one is an attack on all. And the added factor that makes this more interesting is that Pakistan is a nuclear state. AM: Exactly. But Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have had a defense agreement, including a mutual defense pact since September of last year. That was before the Iranian attacks on the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia. And Pakistan’s response to those attacks have been relatively muted from the pure security perspective. They sent about 8,000 troops and air defense support. It was not game-changing. What was very significant from the growing Saudi-Pakistani relations was the way that Saudi Arabia leaned on Pakistan for negotiations, both to help de-escalate directly between Riyadh and Tehran and so that the Saudis could help shape negotiations between the United States and Iran—because Pakistan was serving as a mediator—without actually having to be directly involved in those negotiations themselves. So when you add Turkey, another regional heavyweight and a NATO member, into this grouping, it becomes quite significant, and it projects this position—particularly for Riyadh, who is the host of this agreement—and their ability to demonstrate that they are a force for stability in the region. So I think that’s significant, but viewing this as a discrete military access, or a new camp that is forming in the Middle East, would be shortsighted. In reality, the situation is much more diverse. The Saudis also have the Gulf Cooperation Council defense agreement, which also includes a mutual defense commitment with all of the other Gulf states. We’re looking at this diversifying web of relations as all the countries across the region try to navigate a very turbulent period, and this idea of diversification on all levels is part of that strategy. RA: I’m curious how you see its posture. Is it anti-Iran in posture? Clearly, it is at least partly in response to the events of the last few months. Is it anti-Israel? Is it an indictment of U.S. policy in the region? Many of these countries have U.S. bases. What is this exactly? AM: Officials have said that negotiations on this agreement have been ongoing for over a year. So it’s not immediately a response to just this most recent confrontation with Iran that escalated earlier this year. But it isn’t surprising that it happened after Operation Midnight Hammer last year, which kicked off this escalation that we’re seeing now. It’s not a surprise that it’s happening after the Israeli strike on Doha last year as well, which really shook the Gulf region to see Israel conducting a strike directly on a Gulf capital. So it’s not necessarily an alliance against Iran or Israel; it’s a new security grouping that’s just trying to manage what they know are going to be shifting regional threats. As it comes to the United States, this is a reflection that the idea of a U.S. security guarantee is just not as appealing or credible as it was before. For a long time, the Saudis’ strategy was to pursue an explicit U.S. security guarantee, an Article 5-esque commitment from the United States for Saudi Arabia. There’s been this sense of an implicit U.S. security guarantee in the Gulf going back to the Carter Doctrine, and that was reinforced in the past with the U.S. response to things like the Gulf War. But in recent years, it’s become increasingly clear that the United States is not necessarily willing or able to provide that kind of security guarantee. And Gulf countries have become increasingly uncertain about whether or not they want to hitch themselves solely to U.S. policy in the region. All of these factors have been fluctuating for some time now, and the Iran war has escalated that conclusion—and unfortunately exposed the limits both of U.S. deterrence in the region and of U.S. capabilities. Because we’ve seen not just U.S. military actions against Iran but even earlier, in 2024 and early 2025, U.S. attempts to push back against the Houthis’ attacks in the Red Sea that did not purport to be conclusive. There’s a growing recognition that you need a diversity of security partnerships. The United States is going to be part of that, and perhaps the Mecca Agreement could actually be consistent with the U.S. effort to recalibrate its role in the region and lean more on partners to take the lead in their own defense. I hope that Washington can view that in that way, but it will require us to change our assumptions and how we operate because we’re no longer selling a U.S. security guarantee for pure Gulf compliance with U.S. policy. RA: I have to ask, what is your current assessment of the likeliest way this war is actually going to end? AM: It’s incredibly tough to say when you’re dealing with unpredictable actors on multiple sides, but I think something that’s missing from the conversation is the prospect that the war will not end. This is actually just backed up by data. Most wars over the past 80 years do not end. Less than 20 percent end in a decisive military victory; less than 20 percent end in a negotiated settlement; and over 60 percent simply do not end. They settle into a kind of cold peace that can often be quite exacting for all the parties involved and breed continued conflicts across the region. And I think we’re gearing toward a situation where the U.S.-Iran conflict could settle into something that looks a lot like that. RA: That’s such a terrifying thing that you’re putting on the table here. What does this cold peace even look like? AM: I think it means the Strait of Hormuz being compromised for the foreseeable future. This gets to the recent article I wrote in Foreign Policy about Gulf countries trying to find workable solutions around continued instability in the Strait of Hormuz. The idea that the strait will return to prewar levels is just highly unlikely at this point. I think we will see potentially some increase in traffic but not a full prewar level. The prospects for a negotiated settlement that is blessed by Tehran, Washington, and the international community is appearing increasingly unlikely. My hope is that that status quo can mean some traffic through the strait and that it results in very limited or none of the attacks on the Gulf that we have been seeing, whether they’re from Iran directly or from Iranian-backed groups and have some degree of plausible deniability. But regardless, there will be economic consequences for the Gulf, Washington, and the broader global economy. RA: So, in your base case scenario where we don’t truly end the war and there’s some sort of uneasy peace that we’re living with, how do Gulf countries even begin to rethink their strategies? AM: You’re completely right. And I think the Gulf’s solution will be to diversify as much as possible. There’s no single industry that is resilient against continued disruptions from Iran, whether it be attacks on the Gulf or disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. The unfortunate thing about warfare today is that it doesn’t take a catastrophic attack with advanced weapons to have those consequences. Even just errant strikes of low-cost drones can overwhelm Gulf air defenses, disrupt investor confidence, dissuade tourists, and threaten critical infrastructure, including energy and digital infrastructure. So the best that Gulf countries can do is to diversify across as many sectors as possible with as many partners as possible and try to ride out that instability. This is something that Gulf countries have been doing for some time. We’ve seen most Gulf countries shift so that most of their GDP is actually no longer coming from the hydrocarbon sector. That’s not across the board but has been the trend line. I think that that will only continue. We’ve seen the Saudis really try to present themselves as a new logistics hub, taking advantage of the disruption of Hormuz to present their ports on the Red Sea as a new center of global commerce because the Middle East is a keystone between major markets in Asia and Europe, and there’s no way around that. You’ll see more of that kind of opportunism. You’ll see Gulf countries have significant capital, so they can be on the cutting edge of counterdrone technology and initiatives to make things like data centers resilient against drone warfare. You’ll see a lot of investments, perhaps even furthering some innovation in these sectors in ways that could be interesting. But there will be no perfect solution. The results of prolonged conflict with Iran will be higher risk premiums, decreased investor interest, and costs for all Gulf countries across multiple domains. item.title: The Regional Order Iran Wanted Is Taking Shape Without It
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.49
The Regional Order Iran Wanted Is Taking Shape Without It Tehran has long called for greater cooperation among Muslim states. The Mecca pact is not what it had in mind. For years, Iran has told its neighbors that the Middle East should rely less on the United States for its security. On Aug. 7, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan took a step toward doing just that. Iran, however, was not included. The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, under which an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan later compared the provision to NATO’s Article 5. The pact will have a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia. For years, Iran has told its neighbors that the Middle East should rely less on the United States for its security. On Aug. 7, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan took a step toward doing just that. Iran, however, was not included. The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, under which an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan later compared the provision to NATO’s Article 5. The pact will have a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia. Just how effective this new agreement proves and how ready its members are to come to one another’s defense remain to be seen. Iran may be tempted to put this to the test in the hopes of revealing the pact’s weakness. But there is a real risk that doing so would only deepen its regional isolation. When Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a defense agreement in September 2025, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian welcomed it as the beginning of a “comprehensive regional security system” among Muslim countries. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made a similar case in May 2025. In an article for the Tehran Dialogue Forum, he argued that regional states should build their own security arrangements rather than depend on outside powers. “Lasting peace in West Asia can only be achieved by empowering its regional actors,” he wrote. “Iran has consistently called for inclusive, homegrown mechanisms to address regional challenges.” In fact, Iran had initially hoped that the restoration of diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia in 2023 could offer a foundation for such a mechanism. But the rapprochement remained mostly a way to manage tensions between the two countries. It did not produce a common security system. In February, the outbreak of war made the issue more urgent for Tehran. Iran attacked U.S. military facilities across the Persian Gulf, and it also struck territory belonging to Arab states with missiles and drones. At the same time, Persian Gulf governments kept channels with Tehran open and tried to prevent Washington from widening the war. In this context, Iran renewed its call for regional security. On June 28, Araghchi said that the Persian Gulf’s security architecture should be reconsidered and called for a new framework that would include all regional states while excluding the presence or interference of extra-regional powers. Yet Iran’s neighbors drew a different lesson from the war. Instead of embracing a security architecture with Tehran, they sought out their own alignment. To be clear, the Mecca pact is not simply an anti-Iran alliance. Fidan has said that it is not directed against Iran or any other specific country, and negotiations had been underway for almost three years. Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia also have concerns about Israel and doubts about the future of U.S. security commitments. Still, there is no denying that this alliance has been driven, in part, by concerns over Iran’s activities. While Iran sees much of its military posture as protection against the United States and Israel, its neighbors, not surprisingly, see the same missiles and proxies as threats to their own security. Saudi Arabia has been hit by Iranian missiles and now faces a renewed Iranian-backed threat in the Red Sea. The question now is how Tehran will respond. The day the pact was signed Araghchi again called for Muslim unity and greater regional self-reliance. However, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, was more directly critical, arguing that a “paper agreement” with Turkey and Pakistan would not bring Saudi Arabia security. Indeed, the pact’s history and language suggest that there is some ambiguity over just how strong its mutual defense provisions are. Tehran may well seek to test that ambiguity. Fidan has already said the three countries would consult after an attack and decide the “degree, form, and format” of support that each would provide. That could mean direct military action, but it could also mean air defense, intelligence, weapons, or troop deployments. Pakistan’s earlier agreement with Saudi Arabia offers a precedent. This agreement left open whether Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent could extend to Saudi Arabia, something that Islamabad has never fully clarified. When Iran struck Saudi Arabia, Pakistan did not directly enter the war, but it did send thousands of troops, fighter aircraft, drones, and air-defense systems to the kingdom. If fighting with the United States resumes and Iran strikes Saudi Arabia again, the response from Turkey and Pakistan will be an early indicator of the pact’s strength. Likewise, renewed Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia would force Turkey and Pakistan to decide not only what form of support to offer but how directly to hold Iran accountable. The risk for Tehran is that, even if the combined response is underwhelming, testing the pact could ultimately strengthen and expand it. Turkey is already calling for it to expand, and Egypt has been discussed as a possible future member. The more Iran’s neighbors feel threatened, the more Iran will end up isolated. For Tehran, pursuing detente with Riyadh could prove a more useful strategy. Relations with Saudi Arabia have improved since 2023, and even during the war, Riyadh kept diplomatic channels open. A senior Saudi official said this week that contacts with Iran and mediation efforts were moving “in the right direction,” even as the kingdom prepared for possible new attacks. Iran also has room to work with Turkey and Pakistan. Both have close political and economic ties with Iran, and both have played important roles in mediation during the war. Their interests and threat perceptions are not identical to Saudi Arabia’s. Iran can use those relationships to try and prevent the pact from developing into a broader alignment centered on containing Iran. The path that Iran chooses may hinge on a broader policy debate taking place in the country. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of Iran’s parliament, has argued that the war has changed regional relations and that Iran should respond by strengthening ties with its neighbors. In a March interview with the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, he said Tehran was ready for “lasting security agreements” with regional countries and repeated that regional security should be provided without foreign interference. Amir-Hossein Sabeti, a hard-line lawmaker closely associated with Saeed Jalili, represents a different view of how Iran should secure itself. He described the June agreement with Washington as the result of a “miscalculation” by Iranian officials and argued that relying on diplomacy with the United States will neither prevent another war nor guarantee Iran’s security. He called for strengthening Iran’s military leverage and the “resistance front,” warning that otherwise “more and more severe wars” will follow. The Mecca pact may never become a Middle East NATO, and its first real crisis could expose serious limits. But Iran does not need to wait for that test to see what has changed. The country’s leaders spent years asking regional states to take more responsibility for their own security. They are beginning to do so. Whether the system they build eventually includes Iran, or increasingly serves to protect them from it, will depend in large part on what Tehran does next. item.title: The Middle East Tries Its Hand at a NATO-Style Pact
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.19
The Middle East Tries Its Hand at a NATO-Style Pact Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey pledge mutual defense in the face of aggressive Iranian and Israeli operations. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at military commitments for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey; a mass shooting in Thailand; and Colombia’s new right-wing president. Mutual Defense Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey inked a joint defense pact on Friday, concluding nearly a year of negotiations aimed at countering aggressive military posturing in the Middle East. Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the alliance will act as a NATO-style mutual defense pact that consolidates the power and influence of three regional heavyweights. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at military commitments for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey; a mass shooting in Thailand; and Colombia’s new right-wing president. Mutual Defense Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey inked a joint defense pact on Friday, concluding nearly a year of negotiations aimed at countering aggressive military posturing in the Middle East. Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the alliance will act as a NATO-style mutual defense pact that consolidates the power and influence of three regional heavyweights. According to a trilateral statement, “the agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” Although Egypt participated in early talks, Cairo was not mentioned as a participant in Friday’s deal. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan all attended the signing in Mecca, Saudi Arabia—Islam’s holiest city. Military cooperation among the three Sunni Muslim-majority nations is nothing new. For decades, Pakistan has provided Saudi forces with training and technical aid, Islamabad and Ankara have previously exchanged warships and training aircraft, and Riyadh has repeatedly purchased Turkish drones. Last month, Pakistan and Turkey also backed a Saudi-proposed maritime defense coalition that would help protect regional shipping routes and prevent global supply chains from being held hostage during war. But just how far the joint defense pact will go remains unclear. The three nations do not have a history of eagerly providing military support; last September, Pakistan signed a mutual defense deal with Saudi Arabia. However, Islamabad has not responded militarily to Iran’s recent attacks on the kingdom, and it has downplayed suggestions that its nuclear capabilities might be extended to allies. Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation in the world, but it is not the only one bringing something to the table. Turkey has NATO’s second-largest military and is known for its extensive (and profitable) defense industry. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s top oil exporters and recently signed a pact with the United States to begin development of a civilian nuclear program. All three regional powers are expected to leverage these assets to counter worsening security in the Middle East. Erdogan stressed on Friday that the pact is not aimed at one particular country, and Riyadh expressed similarly placatory sentiments. Friday’s agreement “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc. Nor is it linked to any nuclear ambitions or arms race, rather it is focused on building sustainable capabilities,” Rayed Krimly, Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, posted on X. But experts suspect that the deal is likely a direct response to Iranian and Israeli military maneuvers. Until now, Turkey and Pakistan have avoided getting directly involved in the Iran war despite both sharing land borders with Iran. Saudi Arabia also initially sought non-involvement; however, long-standing tensions with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen drew the kingdom into active conflict, and in late July, Saudi and U.S. forces launched joint strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. In public, Iranian officials appear unimpressed. “The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking by the Americans did not bring them security,” Ebrahim Rezaei, an Iranian politician, wrote on X. “Change your policies so that you do not have to #BegForSecurity from others.” Turkey and Israel, meanwhile, have increasingly found themselves in each other’s rhetorical crosshairs. In July, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described Israel as a “burden that humanity can no longer bear”—remarks that Israeli officials interpreted as a call for genocide. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other prominent political figures in the country have painted Turkey as the new Iran and warned of an “emerging radical Sunni axis.” This new defense pact is likely to further inflame such fears. Israel has yet to respond to Friday’s signing. Today’s Most Read - Why the United States Keeps Losing Wars by Stephen M. Walt - The Saudis Are the Architects of Their Own Misfortune by Steven A. Cook - Hamas Agreed to Disarm. Why Did Israel Reject the Deal? by John Haltiwanger What We’re Following Deadly school shooting. A mass shooting at a high school in Thailand on Friday killed at least six people and injured more than 20 others, with nine in critical condition. The youngest victim was 12 years old. Earlier that morning, the suspected shooter, age 14, also killed his grandparents in their home. Local officials confirmed that the perpetrator killed himself before authorities could apprehend him and that the situation is “now under control.” Thailand has one of the highest gun ownership rates in Asia, second only to Pakistan. In 2017, more than 10.3 million firearms were owned by civilians (or around 15 guns per every 100 people). The country also has the second-highest rate of gun homicides in Southeast Asia after the Philippines. Thailand’s deadliest mass shooting occurred in 2022, when 36 people—including 24 children—were killed at a childcare center. “When I became prime minister, one of my to-do things was to issue a new law regarding weapons, and it is still in the process,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters on Friday, adding that “the new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns.” Thai government officials and law enforcement are allowed to buy as many firearms as they want at a discounted rate, and few regulations are in place to prevent individuals from then selling those weapons on the black market. Colombia’s new leader. Conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia’s new president on Friday. Rather than hold the ceremony in Bogotá, though, de la Espriella chose to be inaugurated in the southwestern city of Cali, symbolizing his hard-line approach to crime. Cali has become known for its high homicide rate, rampant gang violence, and drug-trafficking networks. One of the key pledges of de la Espriella’s campaign was to tackle violent crime. He criticized outgoing President Gustavo Petro’s policy of negotiating with armed groups, and he dismissed the efficacy of a previous peace agreement with the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). Dissident rebel groups have emerged in the vacuum left by FARC, particularly the National Liberation Army, which has seized on FARC’s absence to fight for greater territorial control. Among de la Espriella’s other ambitions, the right-wing businessman and lawyer aims to revive the country’s oil and gas sector, build mega-prisons, eliminate wealth taxes, and roll back many benefits established under the previous administration. He is the latest in a slew of far-right leaders to clinch electoral victories across Latin America, several of whom attended de la Espriella’s inauguration. Ebola infections. The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo surpassed 4,000 for the first, according to government data, with deaths exceeding 1,850 individuals. Experts believe that the epidemic, which has been recorded in five Congolese provinces, is the second-largest and fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record. A Science report published last month estimated that the virus broke out at least four months before it was officially detected. Ebola is “spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate,” Doctors Without Borders said in a statement this week. And the response “is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains.” On Wednesday, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged local authorities to prioritize support for health care responders. The largest Ebola outbreak occurred between 2014 and 2016, when more than 28,000 cases and around 11,000 deaths were detected across West Africa. Health officials believe that the current outbreak is being exacerbated by poor infrastructure in rural communities, mining-related movement, and rebel conflict. Odds and Ends Several capybaras strolled into a legislative building in Cuiabá, Brazil, last week, surprising lawmakers preparing for a scheduled vote. The adorable rodents, known for their sociability and chill demeanor, are native to South America, with many living in the wildlife park located next to the Cuiabá facility. “They show up here quite often, so we’ve gotten used to seeing them,” staffer Nayara Bueno said. Unlike their human counterparts, they’re usually not visiting lawmakers to file a complaint. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Russia and Ukraine Are Mutually Shutting Down the Black Sea
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.18
Russia and Ukraine Are Mutually Shutting Down the Black Sea Strikes on ports and ships could portend another global food shortage. The Black Sea’s trade corridors are at the center of the Russia-Ukraine war again, as they were from 2022 to 2023, when a Russian naval blockade stopped Ukrainian maritime exports and shook agricultural markets worldwide. The current crisis looks similar, but it’s unique in important ways, as are the alternatives to resolve it. On July 23, Ukraine announced that maritime transport to and from its three unoccupied Black Sea ports was effectively frozen. Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone targeted 57 Ukrainian and foreign-flagged merchant ships in ports and at sea, including Golden Leo, a Turkish-owned bulk cargo carrier sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau. Three Russian missiles struck it in open water off the coast of Odesa on July 19, killing 10 people; the ship sank on July 27. By then, this year’s strikes had already cut Ukraine’s grain exports by roughly a third and doubled shipping freight costs into and out of the country. The Black Sea’s trade corridors are at the center of the Russia-Ukraine war again, as they were from 2022 to 2023, when a Russian naval blockade stopped Ukrainian maritime exports and shook agricultural markets worldwide. The current crisis looks similar, but it’s unique in important ways, as are the alternatives to resolve it. On July 23, Ukraine announced that maritime transport to and from its three unoccupied Black Sea ports was effectively frozen. Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone targeted 57 Ukrainian and foreign-flagged merchant ships in ports and at sea, including Golden Leo, a Turkish-owned bulk cargo carrier sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau. Three Russian missiles struck it in open water off the coast of Odesa on July 19, killing 10 people; the ship sank on July 27. By then, this year’s strikes had already cut Ukraine’s grain exports by roughly a third and doubled shipping freight costs into and out of the country. As in 2022-2023, when a Russian naval blockade trapped millions of tons of Ukrainian grain and sparked a global food crisis, Ukraine’s Black Sea ports are out of business due to the attacks, even if most of the facilities are still operable. Agricultural stocks are piling up, and global grain markets are tightening. Ukraine’s agricultural sector is staring at a direct loss in export revenue between $1.5 billion and $3 billion this year, according to its agriculture minister. Ukraine’s Black Sea maritime corridors handle approximately 90 percent of the country’s agricultural exports, along with the lion’s share of its mining and steel products. These sectors account for three-quarters of Ukraine’s foreign-currency earnings. This is why Ukraine urged the United Nations on July 27 to help facilitate safe transit through the Black Sea, as the U.N. temporarily succeeded in doing in 2022. Ukrainian officials accused Russia of war crimes and economic terror over attacks on civilian cargo ships and grain terminals. They argued that Russia is holding global food security hostage, just as it did four years ago. They compared Russia’s actions against food supply chains to disruptions of energy routes in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that developing nations could face hunger and rising prices. But the current crisis is different from the previous one in key respects. The 2022-2023 events involved Russian warships imposing a classic blockade on Ukraine’s ports, forming a cordon around the Odesa coast with vessels and mines that prevented the entry and exit of Ukrainian and foreign ships. The blockade began in late 2022, just as Ukraine was processing a record agricultural harvest from the previous year. Ukrainian silos were full, and roughly 20 million tons of grain ended up stranded. The crisis reverberated around the world, including to Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, where dozens of low-income countries rely on Ukrainian grain. Prices shot up, and although the shortage did not lead to famine, it caused hardship and food instability. The European Union came to Ukraine’s rescue by opening maritime passages through Danube ports in Romania and Bulgaria, and by offering rail and road access to international markets through Central Europe. The deal threw a lifeline to Ukraine by enabling it to sell its goods in EU markets, including Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia. But domestic farmers in those countries struggled to compete with the sudden influx of Ukrainian produce and grains, and they protested vigorously. Politicians responded by slapping embargoes on Ukrainian agricultural goods despite EU policy to the contrary. In July 2022, the U.N. brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, a safe maritime corridor for food and fertilizer exports, in exchange for easing Western sanctions on Russian food and fertilizer exports. (Russia broke the agreement less than a year later and has since regularly targeted and harassed shipping in the Black Sea corridors.) In appealing to the U.N. again in July, Ukraine clearly hoped for a repeat intervention and used the same language. But this crisis, thus far, hasn’t triggered anything like the food market turmoil of four years ago—yet. “In February 2022, agricultural stocks in Ukraine were full,” Oleg Nivievskyi, of the Kyiv School of Economics, explained. “That’s why the impact was so heavy.” This time, however, Ukraine had already shipped its recent harvest before Russia shut down the ports, and global grain markets are relatively flush, he said. Moreover, the impediment this time around is not a physical blockade. Russia is not obstructing ships but rather striking them, their crews, and their cargo directly. That makes the financial risk so great that merchant vessels won’t make the trip. War-risk premiums on freight rates and shipping insurance have spiked, if the latter is even available from underwriters. As a result, ship owners are citing force majeure to walk away from charters. Grain isn’t moving despite an open corridor. This is a market collapse driven by cost and risk, not a siege. That points to possible remedies: affordable war-risk insurance—through state-backed damage compensation, for example. But the logic of this hard-nosed financial calculus raises serious ethical questions, as a similar paradigm does in the Strait of Hormuz. War-risk insurance compensates for financial loss: the vessel, the cargo, and liability payouts if crew are killed or injured. This is compensation, not protection. The insurance makes the voyage financially viable for the owner; it does nothing to reduce the physical risk to the people actually on the ship. In the Gulf, after hostilities knocked out commercial war-risk coverage starting in March 2026 and premiums spiked fivefold, the United States set up a $20 billion maritime reinsurance plan that covered hull, cargo, war protection, and indemnity. It’s still operating, but it hasn’t fully worked: Most shippers are still steering clear of the Gulf. The backstop solved the insurability problem without solving the risk-to-life problem. Stephen Cotton of the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) summed it up: “These are not accidents, not collateral damage, these are deliberate acts against civilian workers who have no part in this conflict and no power to escape it.” No cargo, no contract, no commercial pressure is worth a seafarer’s life, the ITF underscored. “Until there is genuine, guaranteed safety, no vessel should be transiting this war zone with civilian crew aboard.” The go-to option is the alternative routes and markets provided in 2022-2023. Some of the load can be shifted to Danube River routes in the autumn (once water levels rise from their current historic lows) and overland through Central Europe. This, of course, assumes that Central Europeans will play ball—and that is in no way assured. This time, there is no discussion of completely reopening EU markets like in 2022. Moreover, even given good will, these corridors simply can’t absorb the roughly 2.5 to 3.5 million tons a month of capacity that Ukraine has lost from its deepwater ports. River exports on the Danube currently move around 100,000 tons a month. Truck exports, roughly, can handle another 100,000 tons a month, and rail to the western border tops out at 300,000 to 400,000 tons, according to Ukrainian sources. European ports already have their own exports to store and ship, and it’s not clear how much spare capacity they have. “In the longer term, Ukraine has no viable substitute for its Black Sea ports,” Slawomir Matuszak, of the Warsaw-based Center for Eastern Studies, said. The Danube ports, he argued, are very small and could handle half of the Black Sea ports’ monthly capacity at best. The roads and railways through Central Europe are underprepared for Ukraine’s prodigious loads. Together, they could handle half of the Black Sea ports’ monthly capacity at best, and the alternative routes would cost Ukrainian exporters an additional $45 to $50 per ton, according to Reuters. The picture is further complicated by Ukraine’s own strikes on Russian shipping in the Sea of Azov using one-way aerial and maritime drones. On July 10, Russia halted Kerch Strait transit after drone attacks had hit more than 100 vessels in the area, and it exported just 1.8 million metric tons of wheat in July—down around 830 percent from the same month in 2025. Russia’s busiest seaport—Novorossiysk on the Black Sea’s northeast coast—is virtually idle. Ukraine may be inflicting economic damage on Russia, but it’s also straining global grain supplies itself, even as it asks the U.N. to force Russia to stand down on humanitarian grounds—a contradiction that Kyiv didn’t acknowledge in New York. Russia’s main grain lobby group complained on July 31, apparently with a straight face, that Ukrainian strikes on its transports could result in hunger in Africa and the Middle East. Global grain markets are jittery but functional for now. “In September and October, however, there’ll be a new harvest,” Nivievskyi said. Come autumn, the world could face a food crisis every bit as severe as the one in 2022. Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Here’s What Middle Powers Can Actually Do
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.03
Here’s What Middle Powers Can Actually Do Mark Carney’s vision has gone unrealized, but that doesn’t mean states should give up. In his landmark speech at the World Economic Forum in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called on “middle powers” to jointly invigorate the international system. Such nations, he ventured, “have the capacity to build a new order that encompasses our values, such as respect for human rights, sustainable development, solidarity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the various states.” Champions of international order cheered his vision of a unified bloc able to offset great-power competition and counter the bellicose, norm-wrecking U.S. President Donald Trump. In the ensuing eight months, Carney’s vision for middle powers—countries with notable economic and military strengths that are smaller than the world’s hegemons—has gone unrealized. Due to a confluence of factors, including divergent priorities and limited leverage, these countries have confronted hard truths about their ability to call the shots. In his landmark speech at the World Economic Forum in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called on “middle powers” to jointly invigorate the international system. Such nations, he ventured, “have the capacity to build a new order that encompasses our values, such as respect for human rights, sustainable development, solidarity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the various states.” Champions of international order cheered his vision of a unified bloc able to offset great-power competition and counter the bellicose, norm-wrecking U.S. President Donald Trump. In the ensuing eight months, Carney’s vision for middle powers—countries with notable economic and military strengths that are smaller than the world’s hegemons—has gone unrealized. Due to a confluence of factors, including divergent priorities and limited leverage, these countries have confronted hard truths about their ability to call the shots. While Carney was right that the U.S. turnabout made cooperation among middle powers more necessary, it has also forced each of them to concentrate, above all, on their own exposure to political upheaval and economic shocks. Efforts to create a new order have been sidelined by the imperative of surviving the old one’s demise. Trump’s undersecretary of defense for policy, Elbridge Colby, brought this issue back into the spotlight last month on X, when he dismissed the “hubbub about a collective ‘middle powers’ strategy.” He claimed that Washington sees no sign that allies are diversifying away from technological or military reliance on the United States, adding that middle powers lack the coherence to align. While Colby is in denial about the scale of global hedging taking place, he is not wrong that middle powers lack the common ground for sustained collective action. Broad visions of a new system birthed by middle powers are, at least for now, farfetched. But even as they navigate an unstable world, these countries can still lay the groundwork for the international system to survive long enough to be reinvented. Middle powers and those who vest hopes in them should take a hard look at how the current imperatives of national self-preservation can contribute to, rather than detract from, the prospect of an orderly global future. That Carney has not made good on his conception of a new world order is unsurprising. At various points, Trump has threatened tariffs of up to 100 percent on Canadian goods. Faced with a suddenly hostile neighbor that accounted for 76 percent of his nation’s merchandise exports, 96 percent of its crude oil exports, and virtually all of its natural gas exports, Carney was in no position to go big on international architecture. Instead, it became a national emergency to lessen Washington’s leverage over Canadian jobs, revenues, energy, and security—never mind rallying the national spirit against a turncoat neighbor threatening to render Canada as the 51st U.S. state. Carney has tried to do this by concentrating Canada’s resources on strategic autonomy: rearmament, strengthening domestic industry, and cultivating international partnerships in search of new avenues for minerals, energy, defense, and trade. Canada’s recent moves to deepen relations with China, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia are motivated by the drive to diversify dependence, not by shared values. The closest thing to order that Ottawa has forged is a handful of new arrangements focused on specific sectors, including a tech partnership with Australia and India and a nine-nation Defense, Security, and Resilience Bank to finance national armaments. Carney’s inward turn forms part of a broader pattern of U.S. allies retreating into self-preservation. Although Carney said in his speech that “a world of fortresses will be poorer, more fragile, and less sustainable,” governments that once relied on the United States as a guarantor of security and prosperity—including Canada, Germany, Japan, Korea, and Poland—have hardened their defenses, secured new markets, and reduced dependencies on other states. These moves have consumed money, political attention, and diplomatic energy that Carney might have hoped would go into reimagining the global system. Even when middle powers have attempted to shore up the international order at various points, they have bumped up against fractured interests. For instance, the European Union’s plan last year to channel roughly $160 billion in frozen Russian assets to Ukraine faltered because most of the money sat in Belgium, leaving Brussels disproportionately exposed to Russian retaliation. Another example came after the United States intervened in Venezuela in January, capturing President Nicolás Maduro. Brazil convened an emergency meeting of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States to form a regional consensus on how to approach the operation. Yet the 33-member organization became paralyzed when some governments condemned Washington’s ouster of Maduro while others welcomed it. Middle powers often recognize their common predicament, but national exposure, domestic politics, and conflicting threat assessments prevent them from converting that recognition into collective power. Even when middle powers manage to convene imaginative coalitions, they often lack the leverage to alter the conduct of states that control the battlefields and chokepoints. In April, the United Kingdom and France brought together 51 countries to plan for a defensive maritime mission in the Strait of Hormuz. Yet while the coalition could prepare to secure the waterway in the event of its reopening, it could not compel Iran or the United States to end the conflict that had closed it in the first place. A U.K.- and French-led coalition has likewise assembled 30-plus countries behind post-ceasefire security guarantees for Ukraine but cannot produce the truce itself. Still, there are concrete steps that internationalist nations can take to staunch the erosion of global norms and set the stage for a stronger future. First, middle powers should pool capabilities across defense, energy, and advanced manufacturing. Currently, they are scrambling to reduce security dependency on Washington through a patchwork of national programs that are often disjointed, duplicative, and wasteful. Europe’s air defenses illustrate the continuing cost of atomized rearmament. Since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the continent has increased defense spending and cooperation through joint purchases and initiatives such as the European Sky Shield. Yet major acquisitions still reflect national requirements and industrial preferences. Governments continue to buy different systems for similar missions, creating separate command arrangements, maintenance chains, and training programs. The European Defence Agency has warned that national preferences produce shorter production runs, higher costs, slower delivery, and overall weaker defense. Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi’s concept of “allied scale”—which proposes that the United States must approach military, technology, and industrial competition with China by partnering closely with allies—offers a useful touchpoint. In areas where the United States is retreating, coordinated strategies among middle powers are even more imperative. Pooled orders, common command systems, shared inventories, and agreed divisions of production could support quicker and more cost-effective rearmament. Countries will only enter such arrangements if access remains dependable in a crisis, so they will require stronger commitments than commercial supply contracts, including treaty-backed delivery obligations. Measures such as prohibiting unilateral export suspensions and ensuring shared reserves across jurisdictions will also be important. None of this has to be at odds with domestic industrial interests. Governments can distribute employment and technical capacity across participating countries. Canada’s recent decision to turn to the German-Norwegian Type 212CD submarine for its new fleet offers a model for this: All three countries will share training, maintenance, parts, and technology, and Canadian industry will be involved in production. Pooling would carry not just material benefits but also political ones. Participating countries could make transparency, lawful procurement, labor rights, data protection, and accountable governance conditions of membership and access to these arrangements. The resulting networks would fortify shared norms through daily economic and security practice. They would also deepen relationships among rights-respecting countries and potentially build the confidence required for more ambitious collective action later. Second, middle powers should approach coalition-building as a way to further broaden international cooperation. Small, flexible, and temporary coalitions are increasingly defining the global system. But a world organized through shifting clubs—what Carney and others call “variable geometry”—can easily tip into one where norms have limited force and countries outside the most powerful coalitions lose both voice and protection. Yet variable geometry can reinforce—or at least prevent the further erosion of—global order if designed carefully. New informal coalitions could do this by anchoring their actions in international law, publishing their standards and decisions, establishing objective membership criteria, and remaining open to states willing to meet them. They should also report to relevant global bodies and cooperate with established institutions for technical expertise and coordination. The interim appeals mechanism created after the United States blocked appointments to the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Appellate Body in 2019 illustrates the approach. Led by Canada and the European Union, the improvised arrangement uses an existing provision of WTO law to offer appellate review for trade disputes among participating countries. It remains open to every WTO member and presents itself as a bridge to restoration of the full dispute-settlement system. Ultimately, it works around institutional blockage while preserving the WTO’s procedures and authority. Other coalitions should reinforce the same discipline. Partnerships on critical minerals should commit to uphold international labor, environmental, and human rights standards rather than creating closed purchasing clubs. Maritime coalitions should ground their mandates in the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. Groups supporting Ukraine should continue to root their work in the U.N. Charter and preserve transparent rules governing weapons and civilian protection. These measures can help prevent cooperation from accelerating the splintering of international relations into rival blocs. Finally, middle powers must protect the existing international machinery. It would be virtually impossible to replicate the global field networks, accumulated expertise, and convening authority of the United Nations and its related institutions for humanitarian relief, refugees, disease surveillance, food security, peacekeeping, and technical standard-setting. Even Trump has continued to rely on parts of this apparatus while attacking and abandoning others, exposing a gap between political hostility toward multilateralism and practical dependence on its capabilities. Yet several traditional defenders of international order are retreating from the system in its time of need. Countries including Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, and the U.K. are cutting aid and support for U.N. development programs in order to finance military buildups. Although their security concerns are real, these governments should not lose sight of the powerful stake they have in keeping the multilateral system afloat. Likewise, middle powers should aim to make existing institutions more relevant, authoritative, and useful. When the U.N. Security Council is blocked, they should use the U.N. General Assembly to affirm legal principles, create fact-finding commissions, and condemn countries that defy norms. They should collectively protect courts, investigators, and officials from sanctions and intimidation while treating the selection of the next secretary-general and the current U.N. reform process as major diplomatic priorities. These three approaches—pooling efforts to achieve allied scale, grounding ad hoc coalitions in the global system, and reinforcing the buckling rules-based system itself—could gradually create the conditions for broader renewal. Although these measures would fall well short of Carney’s proposed new order, they could strengthen multilateral relationships, preserve the foundations of a global system, and give middle powers important tools to work with when a wider opening for reinvention arrives. Suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. item.title: MagnaCut’s Inventor Made a New Super Steel That May Usurp the EDC Knife Throne
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.47
For the past few years, MagnaCut steel has had a stranglehold on the knifemaking industry. Often referred to as a “super steel,” it is beloved for its unique blend of performance, reliability, durability, strength, corrosion resistance and more. But for 2026, MagnaCut’s inventor has finally launched a potential successor. Called MagnaMax, it had been quietly teased by brands and artisans at shows and conventions before its official unveiling this year. In fact, it’s already available in quite a few knives from some noteworthy brands. What is MagnaMax, exactly? Like its predecessor, MagnaCut, MagnaMax is a CPM (Crucible Particle Metallurgy) steel. This means that, unlike traditional steel crafted from melted-down ingots, it’s created from an atomized powdered spray. This creates a microscopic, even structure that offers generally higher toughness, wear resistance and fewer weak points. Both of these steels were developed by the same person, Dr. Larrin Thomas, a master metallurgist and, understandably, an absolute legend in the knifemaking community.

item.title: Patagonia Reworks Its Modern Mountain Icon into an Everyday Jacket with Mil-Spec Styling
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.38
Retro-X. R1. The Houdini. Patagonia’s archive is full of iconic jackets for use on and off the mountain. But when it comes to modern technical performance, the Nano-Air ranks damn near the peak. In Gear Patrol‘s original review back in 2014, we asserted, “The Nano-Air represents the future of protective outwear: a mixed bag of breathability, temperature regulation and comfort.” It was a technical breakthrough in its debut, giving rise to a new category of versatile midlayers for high-output activities, and it continues to set the bar for active insulation more than a decade later. Turns out, it also doubles as a killer urban jacket. Like some of its Patagonia siblings, such as the Nano Puff and Synchilla Snap-T, the Nano-Air has long straddled the divide between mountainwear and urban aesthetics. However, a new entry into Patagonia’s catalog puts the pioneering technology squarely into the latter category.

item.title: Apple Is Quietly Making It Even Easier to Use Your Current AirPods
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.10
Most people never dive into their AirPods settings. They simply pop the AirPods in their ears, which automatically pair to their iPhone, and (boom!) they’re listening to music. That’s the beauty of AirPods: It’s easy, and they just work. But for “more advanced” users, Apple provides numerous ways to customize the AirPods experience. A better AirPods experience When paired and in AirPods Settings, you tweak the on-stem controls for switching between listening modes, answering calls and activating Siri. And you can customize these controls for the left and right AirPods. Depending on the model of AirPods you have, you may have access to customize more advanced controls, such as head gestures, sleep detection and using your AirPods as an iPhone camera remote. And that’s really just scratching the surface.

item.title: Casio Transforms Its Iconic F-91W into a Hiking Watch with One Small Change
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.03
Casio’s F-91W has been in production since 1989 and remains one of the best-selling watches ever made. Its beauty is found in its simplicity. Housed in a lightweight resin case, the timepiece offers basic water resistance and a host of useful features, all in one of the most GADA-friendly packages you’ll ever find in budget watchmaking. However, there’s always been one hitch in its theoretical perfection: the strap. Since the beginning, the standard F-91W has been paired with a resin strap, which works fine for everyday wear but feels less at home when you’re trekking outdoors. But now, after nearly 40 years of existence, Casio has given the F-91W a trail-ready upgrade. New strap, new personality If you’ve ever wanted to take the F-91W into the backcountry without the plastic strap building up sweat or looking out of place, Casio now has you covered. Introducing the F-91WF, a fabric-strap variant of its most iconic digital watch, giving hikers a more practical alternative to the original resin. Swapping resin for woven fabric sounds minor, but it significantly changes how the F-91WF breathes on the wrist during long days on the trail.

item.title: You’re (Probably) Using Screwdrivers All Wrong
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.97
Since it arrived in the 1930s, the Phillips head has established itself as a staple bit standard of the fastener world, and for good reason. As an improvement on the basic slotted screw and driver, the crosshair cut allowed for easy centering with much more stable engagement. Though it allowed for more torque, it also had the unintended benefit of “camming out” under too much pressure, thereby preventing damage. If you’ve ever stripped a screw, it might be because of this design bug feature. However, it could actually be because you’re mixing standards altogether. Not long after the Phillips head, the Japanese Industrial Standard (JIS) arrived in the 1950s. Eventually, Phillips worked with GKN Screws and Fasteners to create the Pozidriv standard for its own improved design.

item.title: Unimatic’s New $740 UT1-PD Merges Its Toolwatch and ProDiver Lines for the First Time
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.91
Over the past couple of years, Unimatic has amassed more hype than any other young, independent watch brand through its staggering amount of collaborations. However, the brand remains anchored in its pragmatic, high-performance tool watches with minimalist, mid-century aesthetics. Two primary branches of that core catalog, the Toolwatch and ProDiver collections, come together for the first time in the new Modello Uno UT1-PD. The UT1-PD is a limited edition Unimatic hybrid that combines the Toolwatch internal architecture with the ProDiver case and bezel. It features a brushed 40mm stainless steel case that overlaps both collections. Visually, the dial blends the classic printed triangle-dot-dash hour markers of the ProDiver line with the Toolwatch “ghost ladder” handset and dash minutes track. The 41.5mm coin-edge overhanging bezel looks very similar to that of the Toolwatch. However, the 60-minute track is reversed, counting up rather than down to conform to diving standards. It is also accented with an orange triangle on the pip.

item.title: Barbour’s New Bedale Jacket Restores a Rare Detail from Vintage Examples
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.87
The Barbour Bedale might be the brand’s most recognizable jacket, worn by everyone from the British royal family to that stylish dude at your local coffee shop. But the version hanging on the rack is not the one that necessarily built its reputation as the brand’s definitive style. Decades ago, Barbour traded two of the original’s four flap pockets for slanted hand warmers you see on current production models. A new collaboration between Barbour and Japanese retailer Journal Standard reverses that decision, reviving the four-flap-pocket configuration of the OG Bedale and pairing it with some modern adjustments in terms of fit and finish. The Bedale’s original design Barbour introduced the Bedale as a British equestrian jacket: short enough to clear a saddle, with a two-way zip and enough structure to handle wet weather. Since then, it’s become the template for waxed-cotton field jackets.

item.title: 22 New Watches You Might’ve Missed from Seiko, Casio, Breitling, Audemars Piguet and More
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.75
If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more From afar, the watch industry may seem unhurried. But every passing day brings about new timepieces from brands big, small, new and old. Below, find 22 new releases from the likes of affordable brands like Casio and Seiko, luxury legends such as Breitling and Audemars Piguet, and enthusiast favorites like Unimatic and Christopher Ward. Together, they show an industry that never stops ticking — and, centuries later, can still find the time to surprise you. Best New Gear: This article is part of an ongoing series collecting the most important new watches, gadgets, pocket knives and more. Catch up on other releases. Unimatic Modello Uno UT1-PD Limited Edition – ProDiver Unimatic combines its Toolwatch and ProDiver collections for the first time to offer the ultimate GADA watch. The 40mm ProDiver stainless steel case is equipped with the Toolwatch 360 Protection System, packing 300m water resistance and a Seiko smooth-sweeping quartz movement. It comes on Unimatic’s quick-release TPU pin buckle strap and is limited to 250 pieces. Christopher Ward’s Trident 30×30 limited-edition version of its flagship dive watch features a special wave-textured dial in teal with a matching bezel and rubber strap, along with a red coral seconds hand. The color scheme is a nod to the tropical parrotfish, which plays a key role in maintaining coral reef ecosystems. Proceeds of the watch’s sales will go to the Blue Marine Foundation’s ocean conservation efforts. Timex’s Q Marbella sports watch pays clear tribute to the legendary Gérald Genta with a design heavily inspired by his IWC Ingenieur. In addition to borrowing the Ingenieur’s bolted-on round bezel and integrated H-link bracelet, the Marbella also includes nods to Genta’s other most famous designs, the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Audemars Piguet Royal Oak. Seiko’s 145th Anniversary Limited Edition “Edo purple” collection includes the affordable solar quartz version of the Prospex Speedtimer. The “Edo purple” dial features a radiant sunburst finish with black subdials and gold plating on the hands and applied indices. The fixed bezel features a purple segment on the black aluminum bezel insert, marked with a tachymeter scale. It comes on a stainless steel three-link bracelet with a folding clasp. Part of Seiko’s third series of 145th-anniversary releases, the Alpinist gets an “Edo purple” dial, named after the distinctive hue that represented Tokyo’s original formation. It otherwise retains all the same details from the collection’s 2025 revision, including an internal rotating compass bezel, “cyclops” date magnifier, gold accents and the stylized Alpinist logo that dates back to 1959. It is a limited edition of 7,000 pieces, slated for an October release. The Navy SEAL 3550 reimagines one of Luminox’s most iconic tactical watches with a slimmer, more ergonomic 44mm Carbonox case that’s no less formidable than those that came before it. A Swiss Ronda 515 quartz movement powers the watch, while 16 Luminox Light Technology tubes deliver constant, self-powered illumination for up to 25 years. Add a screw-down crown, anti-reflective sapphire crystal, unidirectional rotating bezel and 200m water resistance, and this is a serious tool watch for divers and military enthusiasts alike. Casio’s new MTP-E740 borrows the looks of Seiko’s Time Sonar. It won’t be an exact dupe of the ’70s icon, but you still get the same transparent dial (and in five colors) and bilingual day-date wheel. What’s more, these can be yours at around one-fourth of the price. Trafford Watch Co., founded in Austin in 2023, releases its first regular production lineup, the Core Collection. It includes the Touring GMT, one of the brand’s most popular one-off releases. The Core version features a fully lumed dial, lumed hands and lumed date wheel seen at 6:00. It is a “true” GMT, powered by the well-respected Miyota Caliber 9075 automatic movement, regulated in-house to +/- 10 seconds per day. Originally launched in 2018 as a reimagining of the brand’s 1980s military prototypes, Timex’s Mk1 Chronograph has become a fan favorite, thanks to its archival history and timeless styling. While these additions to the lineup retain the watch’s overall styling and functionality, including its reliable quartz movement, they get a big upgrade in the form of a sunray finish on the dials — a seemingly simple change that adds overall refinement. Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Selfwinding Flying Tourbillon ‘Bleu Nuit, Nuage 50’ Ceramic AP’s second try at making a Royal Oak in full ‘Bleu Nuit, Nuage 50’ ceramic, which is the same shade of blue as the most iconic Royal Oak dial, adds a flying tourbillon at 6:00 courtesy of the brand’s Calibre 2950 automatic movement. The “open-heart” version of Orient’s modern sports watch is having its last hurrah. The current lineup was introduced in 2024 and got a final limited-edition restock, according to the brand. It’s 41mm stainless steel case holds a small seconds dial with a round aperture exposing the balance wheel below, available in crimson, sky blue, green and pearly white with a gold-tone case and bracelet. G-Shock Mudmaster Master of Horizon Gold GG-B100XMH-5A G-Shock debuts its Master of Horizon Gold collection, highlighted by this stunning new Mudmaster. The rugged adventure watch complements its 200m of water resistance and extreme shock and mud resistance with a yellow gold ion-plated bezel inspired by the look of the horizon where the earth meets the sky. Not long after reviving the 1976 Lexington with a gold-tone case, which promptly sold out, Timex followed it up with a polished-steel variation. The two-hand, time-only dial features the same brushed metal plate with a black printed “Tank” track, but the hands are updated with a blue finish. It comes on a brown embossed alligator leather strap with a steel pin buckle. Timex throws back to the ’80s with its new Retroware Digital. This completely original watch isn’t a reissue but pays homage to old-school digital sports watches like the Ironman and Triathlon. It features a large, quirky time display that takes up most of the dial. Meanwhile, underneath sits a full calendar readout. The timepiece also has chronograph, timer and alarm functions as well, all backed by Indiglo for nighttime visibility. Seiko links up with Honda for this 5 Sports Field tribute to the 1980s Motocompo folding scooter. The watch features numerous nods to the bike, including the yellow dial color, Honda-branded horizontal bar, dot-style typeface and much more. This year marks the 50th anniversary of Shelby’s iconic Aluminum Edition Daytona Coupe. In honor of the monumental occasion, the legendary motorsports outfit has teamed up with one of the most storied American watchmaking brands to build the chromed-out Bulova Shelby Racer Chronograph. A more traditional alternative to the brand’s 150th edition Shelby Racer Chronograph, this one gets a high-polish stainless steel case (with a matching bracelet and a leather alternative strap), mirror-polished chronograph dial, a high-precision quartz movement and subtle co-branding. Breitling Professional Endurance Pro 44 Ironman World Championship 2026 Breitling continues its partnership with the Ironman triathlon with this limited-edition Endurance Pro chronograph featuring a titanium case, a SuperQuartz movement and a turquoise color scheme inspired by the Ironman Championship’s Hawaiian setting. Panerai gives the Luminor an advanced new build while retaining its classic look. The case, siganture crown lock and fixed bezel are made of the proprietary Carbotech, a carbon fiber and polymer compound that is 64 percent lighter than titanium and highly corrosion-resistant. It retains the black 3-6-9-12 sandwich dial with pencil hands and a small seconds at 9:00. It comes on a brown leather strap with contrast box stitching and a titanium pin buckle, along with a black rubber pin buckle strap. Seiko draws inspiration from Austria’s Lake Hallstatt for this limited-edition, European-exclusive dive watch. The resultant sunburst green dial with gold accents is reminiscent of Seiko’s iconic alpine-inspired watch, the Alpinist. Casio updates its affordable MRW dive watch series with the 240H. Compared to the outgoing model (230H), the new quartz timepiece makes subtle changes, swapping the day-date window with only a date display and changing the dial text from “WR 100M” to “WR 100BAR.” It’s available in three stealthy new resin colorways as well and still features its 60-minute graduated bezel. Unimatic X San Francisco Market Modello Uno U1-SFM The Italian watchmaker teamed up with the Korean retailer San Francisco Market to design a galvanic dial where no two examples are identical. An electrochemical process creates a glittering speckled arrangement over a radiant navy blue background, mimicking stars in a clear night sky. The time-only dive watch is powered by a Seiko Caliber NH35A automatic movement, and comes on a navy blue leather pin buckle strap, with a navy blue TPU pin buckle strap provided as well. It is a limited edition of 111 pieces. The Pro Trek PRJ-B001EX-1 is the most distinctive entry yet in Casio’s Hiker Line. Its reversible cloth strap flips into a soft-shell pouch, complete with a built-in pocket for a key, coins or folded cash. It also features a carabiner loop for clipping to a tent or pack. A rotary guard bezel locks the side buttons against accidental presses on the trail. Tough Solar charging and Bluetooth round out the package, housed in a 50.3 x 46mm biomass-resin case rated to 100 meters of water resistance.
