item.title: Physicists Made 10,000 Particles Defy Newton’s Third Law for an Hour. Here’s How
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 7.33
Some laws of physics are so fundamental that theyâve served as the baseline for science for centuries. But with technological advancements, physicists canâalbeit temporarilyâcreate small worlds that evade these laws. And when they do, strange things occur. In a recent study published in Physical Review Letters, Japanese physicists created a system of more than 10,000 particles that defied Newtonâs third law of motion for an hour. According to this law, passive particles exert equal forces on each other, so none can just suddenly push itself along on its own. But in devising this system, the team subjected particles to an alternating electric field that caused passive particles to spontaneously form pairs and âchaseâ each other in a liquid environment. âThis research demonstrates that the breaking of action-reaction symmetry is a fundamental principle that generates new collective motions and self-organization of matter,â Yutaka Sumino, the studyâs co-author and a physicist at the Tokyo University of Science in Japan, said in a statement. A physical standstill To quote Isaac Newton himself, the third law of motion mandates that âmutual actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal and directed to contrary parts.â The key here is symmetryâa reciprocal relationship between action and reaction. Scientists have also found ways to engineer this principle to their benefit. For instance, the thrust of a rocket engine comes from the action of the hot gas flowing out from the back, which produces a reaction in thrusting force in the opposite direction. Beyond the norms More recently, researchers have been looking into systems that break this symmetry, according to the paper. For the latest study, the team suspended microscopic colloidal particles in water, then confined them between specially fabricated electrodes. Then, the researchers applied an alternating electric field. Initially, the larger particles developed a larger electrical flow, attracting the smaller particles. This introduced an imbalance that led the particles to move as self-propelled units through the suspension, the team explained in the paper. For comparison, the team tried something similar for suspensions containing particles of only one size. However, the results were very different, as the particles exhibited reciprocal interactions and gradually organized into a crystal. âTo put it more simply, particles that attract each other, such as sand, powder, or raindrops, generally continue to gather over time, growing into larger clumps,â Sumino said. The system with differing sizes, on the other hand, did cluster but never clumped together permanently, âinstead gathering and then splitting,” he added. The team suspects that similar interactions take place in biological systems, such as cell colonies and animal groups. If true, the mechanism studied here could even inspire programmable materials and microrobotic systems, it noted.

item.title: Archaeologists Thought a Mass Grave of 79 Shackled Men Held Foreign Invaders. They Were Wrong
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.46
In 2016, archaeologists in Athens uncovered an Ancient Greek mass grave full of men buried in a heartbreakingly vulnerable position: with their wrists shackled and raised over their heads. We now have a better sense of who they were.Â Â Researchers conducted isotopic analyses on 66 men from the so-called Esplanada grave, which dates back to the Archaic Period (~700 to 460 BCE), and discovered something surprisingâmost were from the surrounding region of Attica. In other words, they were locals, according to a study published last month in the Journal of Archaeological Science. The findings shed light on the identities of the victims but also hold broader implications for our understanding of the political and societal dynamics taking place in Athens right before ancient Greeceâs famous Classical Period (479-323 BCE).Â Local or foreign victims? All the major themes related to the Classical Periodâsuch as, most famously, democracyâactually develop out of the Archaic Period. âThatâs the first time democracy takes place in Athens,â Julianne Stamer, a bioarchaeologist at Arizona State University and lead author of the study, told Gizmodo. But not everyone agreed with this form of rule, and archaic Athens saw intense disagreement over whether the future city-state should be presided over by an aristocratic tyrant or the public. Still, when the Esplanada grave came to light with its 79 men arranged in three parallel rows, researchers werenât sure what to make of it. Were they victims of these domestic conflicts? Or perhaps defeated foreign invaders? To settle the matter, Stamer and her colleagues turned to radiogenic strontium analysis.Â âStrontum is an element that is found in the ground in relative abundance based on how old the rocks are and what kind of rocks they are,â Stamer explained. âBecause strontium isotopes get into our water and into our food, we all have some strontium isotopes in our teeth and bones,â she added. By measuring those isotopes, âwe can tell where people are from based on the geology of the surrounding area.âÂ Very few outsiders The team conducted radiogenic strontium analysis on 66 of the Esplanada men as well as 97 other people from the broader Phaleron burial ground that includes the mass grave. Their work revealed that the vast majority of them were locals. Among the men in the mass grave specifically, the analyses identified only two of them as outsiders.Â âWe found that most people have a strontium isotope signature that appears to be from the wider Attica region,â said Stamer, bolstering the theory of them being victims of internal political violence. Still, âwe were very surprised about that because in this period, Athens and Greece in general are becoming more interconnected. We have a lot more trade going on.â This dynamic is, once again, a precursor to the sort of connections that later contribute to making Athens a mighty Classical power.Â The Archaic burial ground itself is strongly associated with trade and travel. The Phaleron burial ground is right next to Athensâ ancient port, Phaleron, from which it takes its name. And yet the people buried there donât represent the sort of diversity one would expect from the years leading up to Athensâ extremely well-connected Classical Period.Â Archaic dynamics Not that Classical Athenians particularly liked diversity, either. In fact, they had very strict citizenship laws, but historians donât know if this was true during the previous Archaic Period, too. The isotopic analyses indicate that Attica might not have received many immigrants during this period. Perhaps this represents a dislike of foreigners during the Archaic Period that continues into the Classical Period despite the intense trade going on.Â Moving forward, Stamer and the team are taking an even deeper dive into the identities of those buried at Phaleron, including what they ate.Â By revealing where the Esplanada men were from, the recent study provides additional clues about what social and political life in Athens might have been like in the centuries preceding its most famous time period. And itâs pretty clear that it had some seriously dark moments whether or not you were an immigrant.Â

item.title: This Satellite Will Literally Breathe Air to Stay in Orbit
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.03
A new type of propulsion system could allow satellites to fly closer to Earth than ever before without being dragged down by the planet’s atmosphere. Spanish startup Kreios Space developed an air-breathing electric propulsion system that collects residual gases from the atmosphere, like oxygen and nitrogen, and uses them as propellant for a satellite’s thrusters. The new technology would allow satellites to stay in very low Earth orbit (VLEO), circling our planet at roughly 60 miles to 250 miles (100 to 400 kilometers) above the surface. The air-breathing system will be put to its first test in space during an upcoming mission in 2028, Kreios recently announced. Breathe in, breathe out Satellites flying in very low Earth orbit face severe atmospheric drag, rapidly decaying their orbit and pulling them down to a fiery death. For satellites to remain in VLEO, their propulsion systems would require large amounts of propellant to counter atmospheric drag. That’s not ideal for space missions, as it creates a satellite that is too heavy and expensive to launch. For Kreios’ air-breathing electric propulsion, the idea is to maintain that low altitude without the need for any propellant on board the satellite. Instead, the propulsion system scoops up air from Earth’s upper atmosphere, heats it up to ionize it, and expels it to generate thrust. The company has tested a prototype of its new propulsion system in a lab in 2021. For its first in-orbit demonstration, Kreios is using a microsatellite bus by Lithuania-based Kongsberg NanoAvionics to carry the air-breathing propulsion system to space. The upcoming mission is designed to validate the new technology, take measurements of the surrounding environment, and capture sub-meter resolution images in the visible and near-infrared (VNIR) spectral range. How low There are several advantages to satellites flying in VLEO as they can gather sharper, higher-resolution images of Earth, offer stronger signals, and require smaller parts for the same level of performance as those operating in low Earth orbit. VLEO is also significantly less crowded than low Earth orbit, with fewer satellites and less space debris zipping around at high speeds. âKreios is building the satellites that make sustained operations in Very Low Earth Orbit possible,” AdriÃ¡n Senar, CEO of Kreios Space, said in a statement. “By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer, and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications, more responsive and accurate missions, and a more sustainable orbital infrastructure.” China has also shown recent interest in VLEO, establishing a national industry alliance designed to demonstrate sustainable operations of satellites closer to Earth.

item.title: Suunto’s New Smartwatch Can Warn You About Incoming Storms
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.95
Suunto’s niche, streamlined watches have enough smart features to improve your next backpacking trip, setting them apart from smartwatches from the likes of Apple and Samsung. The newly announced Suunto Core 2 is an ABC (altimeter, barometer, and compass) watch that should not only make navigating the backcountry easier but also warn you about incoming storms. The original Suunto Core was released in 2007, so Suunto is revisiting the ABC watch concept with several improvements in tow. While the basic rugged design of the watch is similar to its predecessor, the company says it should feel more comfortable to wear, and its LED dot-matrix display is 40% brighter whether you’re using the built-in green or red backlights. The watch is also more durable. The Core 2 is water resistant to 10 ATM (around 100 meters), a big jump up from the original’s 3 meters of resistance. It’s also built to MIL-STD-810H military standards for maximum reliability and has a battery life of up to 15 months (with support for user-replaceable coin cell batteries). Unlike GPS-enabled smartwatches from Garmin, the Suunto Core 2 is deliberately less capable. The watch can replace a compass and even automatically account for the difference between true north and magnetic north, but it won’t map your location or navigate to your next destination. Still, Suunto has included some novel features: Besides tools like a step counter, the digital compass, and the altimeter, the Core 2’s barometer can detect changes in pressure and warn you of oncoming storms. The watch doesn’t offer the same connectivity as even Wear OS models that Suunto has experimented with in the past, but its new support for Bluetooth does mean Suunto can update it over time. The Suunto Core 2 makes less sense for a professional runner than it does an avid hiker, but at $179, it seems like a relatively affordable upgrade over a standard digital watch. And one that could theoretically improve over time.

item.title: Sonos Could Drop New Wireless Headphones Soon
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.93
Sonos had its first big hardware release since 2024 this year, launching a new Bluetooth speaker, the Playâbut apparently the company’s not done cooking yet. According to Federal Communications Commission (FCC) filings first spotted by Janko RÃ¶ttgers at Lowpass, Sonos is gearing up to launch the Ace Ultra, a new pair of wireless headphones. There’s not a ton of information in the filingsâmuch of the documents is redactedâbut there are a few details, including the existence of several colors, potentially five altogether. Among them are light gray, black, “Agave,” “Blush,” and “Sand.” The company’s last pair of headphones, the Sonos Ace, were only available in white or black, much like the recently released Play Bluetooth speaker and the Era 100 SL. More intriguing than new colors are hints at support for voice commands, which is something the first generation of headphones didn’t have. As Bloomberg notes, the addition of voice commands with the Sonos Ace Ultra would fit into previous clues about the company’s general direction, particularly its interest in AI and pushing further into the smart home category. Recently, Sonos expanded the ability of Sonos Voice Control to encompass some smart home controls, including support for Philips Hue products, so users can control their lights. The company has also partnered with Amazon to offer Alexa through its speakers instead of Sonos’ own voice assistant. Whether the Ace Ultra will expand those smart home abilities remains to be seen, but Sonos does have a tendency to tightly integrate its hardware, and there is evidence that Sonos Ace Ultra may include support for Bluetooth as well as Wi-Fi connectivity. Its last wireless headphones, for example, had a Wi-Fi feature called TV Audio Swap that allowed anyone with a Sonos Beam soundbar to switch seamlessly from listening out loud to listening inside its wireless headphones. No matter what Sonos does with the Ace Ultra, it’ll definitely look to avoid the same fate as its last pair of Ace wireless headphones, which were far from a commercial success. We may not have to wait long to find out more, as Sonos CEO Tom Conrad said there’s an event slated for September that could very well act as the launch for the Ace Ultra.

item.title: Watch China’s Workhorse Rocket Explode in a Massive Fireball During Launch
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.86
A Chinese rocket went up in flames less than two minutes after launch, triggering a huge explosion in the skies above the island of Hainan. China’s Long March 7A rocket launched on Monday from the Wenchang Space Launch Site. Around 85 seconds after liftoff, the rocket erupted in a massive fireball that left a thick trail of smoke and debris across the sky. Waking up to see the loss of a Long March 7A. Really unexpected. pic.twitter.com/XnU8WveWYS — CNSPACE (@CNSpaceflight) August 10, 2026 The incident was captured on video and shared online. Chinese state media later confirmed that the rocket experienced an unidentified anomaly during flight and that an investigation into the failure was underway, the Associated Press reported. Unusual failure Monday’s explosion marked the Long March 7A’s first reported failure since the rocket’s debut more than six years ago. On March 16, 2020, China’s medium-lift vehicle experienced an engine malfunction shortly after stage separation and its inaugural flight ended in failure. A year later, Long March 7A sent a classified, experimental payload into geosynchronous transfer orbit for its first successful mission. Since then, the rocket has completed more than a dozen missions without a hitch. The recent failure ended that long-running lucky streak. The Long March 7A is capable of delivering up to 7 metric tons of payload to geosynchronous transfer orbit, a temporary, highly elliptical path satellites take to reach a geostationary orbit high above the Earth. This makes the Long March 7A crucial for China’s specialized, high-orbit satellite missions. The rocket can also be used for deep space missions and to send spacecraft to the Moon, according to the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology. Rocket, interrupted During its most recent launch, the rocket was carrying the ChinaSat 4B satellite, a geostationary communications satellite designed to provide internet and broadcasting services to users. The explosion not only led to the loss of the payload but also reportedly delayed the long-anticipated launch of another rocket. Zhuque-3, developed by Chinese startup LandSpace, was scheduled for liftoff on Tuesday from the Jiuquan satellite launching station but its mission was pushed back, according to CNN. The partially reusable rocket is crucial to China’s efforts to compete with industry giants like SpaceX. Earlier in July, a Long March 10B launched on its maiden flight and its first stage was caught by a net-like grid system at sea, marking China’s first recovery of a rocket booster. China has been making significant progress with its rocket industry, but as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk points out, “Rockets are insanely hard,” he wrote on X in response to the Long March 7A failure.

item.title: This Deadly Drug-Resistant Fungus Can Lurk in Your Skin. Scientists Just Discovered How
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.83
The fungus Candida auris is one of the scarier emerging diseases out there, but scientists may have just uncovered a key secret to its survival that could allow us to fight back. Researchers at the University of California-San Francisco studied how the fungal pathogen behaved on the skin of mice. Compared to other related fungi, C. auris triggered a distinct response from the skin’s immune cells, they foundâone that enabled it to easily hunker down in hair follicles. The discovery could lead to new treatments that can clear the fungus from our skin before it becomes a life-threatening problem, the researchers say. “These results suggest that C. auris exploits a distinctive immune axis to persist,” the researchers wrote in their paper, published last week in the journal Science. The resistant, deadly fungus Doctors in Japan first discovered C. auris inside a personâs ear in 2009. Since then, it’s become one of the most urgent superbug threats in the world, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The fungus is uniquely adept at evolving resistance to the most common medications used to treat fungal infections; some strains have even been pan-resistant to every type of antifungal we have available today. Another insidious feature of C. auris is its ability to easily colonize the skin of healthy people, something that isn’t normally seen with other Candida species. Though most people carrying C. auris on the skin will never fall ill as a result, the fungus can cause problematic and often life-threatening bloodstream infections when a person’s immune system weakens. Carriers can also spread the fungus within hospitals or other places occuped by medically vulnerable individuals, such as nursing homes (this can happen through direct contact or even just shared medical equipment and room surfaces). The UCSF researchers were hoping to find out how and why C. auris can survive so well on skin, so they conducted experiments in the lab and with mice. They compared C. auris to its cousin Candida albicans, a species that can also cause human fungal infections but isn’t quite talented at persisting on skin. For starters, they found that C. auris loves to colonize hair follicles in particular. What’s more, theseÂ two fungi generated two very different kinds of immune responses from the mice. C. albicans tended to trigger higher levels of interleukin-17 (IL-17), a protein known for its role in tamping down fungal infections.Â C. auris, however, triggered the release of interferon gamma, which is typically used to help fight off viral infections. This wayward response not only blocked the release of IL-17, but it also appeared to slow down the replacement of hair follicle cells, both of which allowed C. auris to make itself nice and cozy in its hiding spot. Further experiments found evidence that C. auris triggers interferon gamma by changing its outer cell walls to expose more chitin, a tough sugar-based molecule commonly seen in fungi as well as the shells of insects and other invertebrates. “Our study helps explain why, once C. auris colonizes the skin, it can be so difficult to eliminate: the fungus senses cues from the skin environment and responds by remodeling itself in ways that favor survival, including reshaping the local immune response to promote its persistence within the skin and hair follicles,” lead study author Dean Merrill, a dermatologist and professor at UCSF, told Gizmodo. How this might help fight the superbug Merill is careful to note that C. auris poses little threat to the vast majority of people carrying it on their skin. That said, though still rare in general, annual C. auris infections have steadily climbed. This year so far, there have been more than 3,400 cases reported in the U.S., putting it on pace to surpass last year’s total. Should the team’s research be further validated (including studies in people), it could provide some important insights into the hardy fungus. While many scientists are actively working to develop new antifungals and vaccines that can treat or prevent invasive infections from C. auris and other fungi, we need all the help we can get. So the UCSF team is hopeful their work can eventually spur research into other strategies for fending off these superbugs. “Understanding these adaptations gives us new potential targets for developing better ways to clear C. auris from the skin and prevent its spread,” said Merill. It might be possible to develop proactive interventions that can nudge our skin’s defense toward the right immune response, for instance, or to otherwise prevent C. auris from tricking the immune system. And simply studying C. auris more might help us learn how to suppress its transformation from a harmless skin passenger to a killer drug-resistant germ, the researchers say.

item.title: Spotify Will Start Labeling AI Artists on Its Platform Next Month
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.82
A lack of regulation in the U.S. surrounding the use of deepfakes has led to a wave of AI artists washing over streaming platforms, but on Tuesday, Spotify announced it was taking a new step to give users some clarity around whether an artist is an actual human being, or a human-like character created by an algorithm. Starting in mid-September, the company will begin applying an âAI Personaâ label to the latter category. âListeners have been clear in telling us that they donât like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated,â the company wrote in its announcement. The new label âsignals to listeners that an artistâs identity may be AI-generated and does not represent a real person.â Spotify added in its announcement that the human creators behind AI personas on the platform will have an opportunity to self-disclose through Spotify for Artists. A similar voluntary labeling system was proposed last month by a group of organizations representing musicians and record labels.Â But the company will also run a review process for suspicious-looking profiles that havenât self-disclosed, beginning âwith artists who have met defined audience thresholds, so the labels cover the vast majority of artist profiles that users visit,â Spotify wrote, without specifying exactly what that threshold would be. âAI Personasâ wonât be recommended by default Artists that have been labeled as AI Personas will also no longer appear in Spotifyâs algorithmic recommendations, unless a user already follows an AI-generated artist. The labels will appear in artist banners and âAboutâ sections, in Spotifyâs search feature, and next to tracks from AI-generated artists in playlists.Â Presumably as an incentive not to try to evade the new system, users will be able to click on the label and see if the creator behind the AI persona self-disclosed or had to be discovered by Spotify. The streaming platform also introduced “AI credits” earlier this year, through which artists can disclose if the technology was used in various parts of a song’s production, such as writing lyrics.Â “With AI credits, we have seen that people are eager to take the opportunity to be transparent and share how they used AI as part of their songâs creative process,” Spotify wrote in its announcement on Tuesday. “Weâre hoping for a similar level of self disclosure for AI Personas.” AIâs place in the music industry AI is a touchy subject among musicians.Â Many will tell you itâs a scourge for their industry, a technology built using copyrighted material without compensation for the artists who created it, and a source of soulless musical slop. Others might be open to experimenting with AI without handing their entire creative process over to a machine. And for the small minority of people making huge profits streaming AI-generated tracks fronted by completely fictitious artists, itâs obviously been an enormous blessing.Â The âartistâ Enlly Blue, for example, currently has just shy of 168,700 followers on Spotify, and a profile picture that looks like a heavily airbrushed photo of Marilyn Monroe. Blueâs most popular song, âThrough My Soul,â debuted at #44 on Billboardâs âEmerging Artistsâ chart in October.Â Blue is an AI-generated persona, though, a project launched by a songwriter named Thong Viet, according to Billboard: a very profitable one at that. âThrough My Soul,â has been streamed well over 29 million times (and counting), meaning that track alone has earned more than $145,000.

item.title: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Director Says It Is to ‘Looney Tunes’ What ‘Iron Man’ Is to ‘The Avengers’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.76
After an underdog storyÂ of being shelved and then getting a theatrical release three years later, CoyoteÂ vs. Acme is poised to hit theaters as a loony courtroom misadventure for the ages, answering a question that’s long been running in the back of folks’ minds: what would happen if Wile E. Coyote sued Acme? To answer that, he’ll have to team up with Will Forte and Lana Condor to wrestle John Cena in a court of law to find out in a hybrid live-action animated movie later this month.Â This isn’t the first time Looney Tunes has jumped into a hybrid animated-live-action film. Pepperidge Farm remembers the Brendan Fraser-led Looney Tunes: Back in Action. Likewise, every project in the genre still lives in the long shadow of Who Framed Roger Rabbit. With Coyote vs. Acme adding its own ledger to the court records, io9 spoke with director Dave Green and longtime Looney Tunes voice actor Eric Bauza about how their underdog film stands apart from past Looney Tunes adventures and holds its own in a summer stackedÂ with blockbuster heavyweights. While there’s been much ado about how Coyote vs. Acme went from being the movie Warner Bros. didn’t want folks to see to reclaiming that narrative in its own advertisements as a court drama “Acme” doesn’t want viewers to see, Green says the movie folks will see in theaters is “100 percent” untouched since Ketchup Entertainment purchased the distribution rights. Though, if they could have their way, Bauza and Green joked about adding puppets tot he movie in post to really go wild with it. Still, the fact that the movie faced an uphill battle hasn’t led the pair to lose faith that Coyote vs. Acme isÂ a tale worth telling in theaters. “Most of the Looney Tunes movies that’ve been made to this date have been ensemble pictures. Coyote vs. Acme is very much the Iron Man to the Avengers. It is a character study of Wile E. Coyote and what his wants, needs, and obstacles are. He’s got such a singular want. He wakes up every single day expecting and hoping to catch the Roadrunner and eat Roadrunner stew that night,” Green said. “In this way, Wile E. is such an incredible optimist. In getting to feature him in that way as a star of this movie, we really get to know him in a much deeper way that I think audiences haven’t seen him before.” It’s certainly no small feat to have a main character who speaks through pantomiming and cue cards stand his ground in a courtroom where the sunset he hopes to ride off into could very well be painted on a brick wall. To make sure his journey is worthy of both Wile E.’s plight as the cartoon medium’s stalwart Sisyphus and die-hard Looney Tunes fans’ price of admission, Bauza teased “cameos galore” that serve the purpose of the plot over being arbitrary fan service. “I think that’s very unique,” Bauza said. “They’re not just slapped on there just to go, ‘Oh, look at that! I remember that!’ There’s importance and a reason why characters appear in the film the way that they do.” In order to discern how to add the pantheon of Looney Tunes characters into Coyote vs. Acme without going too far into cloying reference fodder, Green says they looked outside Bugs Bunny’s domain to The Muppets for inspiration. “When you watch a Muppets movie, they’re never talking about the group of Muppets as ‘the Muppets.’ [Coyote vs Acme] characters are hopping into roles and cameo appearances that reallyâhopefullyâsupport the story and the plot,” he said. That’s not to say that The Muppets were the only source of inspiration for how Green helmed Coyote vs Acme. He also did his homework with a media cocktail of classic cartoons and lawyer shows to find the pocket in the otherwise disparate Venn diagram he wanted the film to sit in. “Obviously, Roger Rabbit is a masterpiece. It’s a huge tonal imprint on the movie and a huge inspiration. But as well as that, I was watching courtroom dramas and thrillers like Erin Brockovich, A Few Good Men, andÂ The Verdict. Even a movie like The InsiderÂ was a huge inspiration for me here becauseâin all of those moviesâwe are telling great stories where we really care about our heroes. We care about what they want and what they’re fighting for. And that’s what was a north star for [screenwriter] Samy Burch and me in designing the screenplay.” Audiences can look forward to seeing how things pan out for Wile E. Coyote when Coyote vs. AcmeÂ hits theaters on August 28. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, whatâs next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: inReach Messenger Plus: Photo & Voice Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 6.26
Garmin inReach Messenger Plus Review Updated August 2026 Jump to a section The inReach for phone-first users, with up to 600 hours of battery life against the Mini 3 Plus’s 350. Cumbersome to use without a phone. The first inReach with Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) that gives you 1,600-character messages, voice notes, and photos. Performance was top-notch, even in dense Redwood canopy. But typing on the device with its small screen and minimal buttons is slow, so plan on using the Garmin Messenger app for almost everything. If you want a device that works well with or without an app, get the Mini 3 Plus Video Here’s a video I made using the Messenger Plus out on the trail so you can see how it works in real-world conditions. vs. Messenger Should you upgrade from the original inReach Messenger? Not unless you specifically need images or voice notes. | Feature | Messenger Plus | Messenger | |---|---|---| | Price | $499 | $299 | | Messaging System | Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) | Short Burst Data (SBD) | | Voice Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Photo Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Message Length | Up to 1600 characters | Up to 160 characters | | App Compatibility | Messenger & Explore | Messenger only | | Battery Life | Up to 600 hours | Up to 672 hours | | Subscription Rates | Higher for image/voice | Standard | Features The Messenger Plus is built around Garmin’s switch from Iridium’s older Short Burst Data (SBD) protocol to Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT), which is faster and supports larger payloads. In practice, that enables: - Photo and voice messaging: Record a voice note or send a photo via satellite when paired to a phone. Garmin Response can receive both in an SOS. - 1,600-character messages: The old 160-character limit is gone. Longer messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus device. - Tapbacks and emojis: Standard smartphone messaging tools, no message credit cost for tapbacks. - Garmin Explore compatibility: Unlike the original Messenger, the Plus works with Garmin Explore for offline maps, routes, and waypoints via phone. Speed - Messenger Plus was about 20-30% faster overall, but not dramatically so. - Both devices sent standard messages in under 2 minutes in most conditions. - Photo messages sometimes took 10 minutes or longer in dense forest. The 10+ minute figure was under heavy Redwood tree cover, which is a good stress test for satellite signal. Under normal conditions, open sky or light cover, Garmin specs and other testers put typical photo or voice send time closer to 1-2 minutes. If your trips are mostly above treeline or in open terrain, you’ll see much faster results than my worst-case numbers. Messaging - 1,600-character messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus. Sent to a traditional inReach like a Mini 2 or GPSMAP 67i, they break into 160-character chunks, each counting as a separate message on the receiving end. - Voice messages are useful. Record in the app, it sends as an audio file. The limit is 30 seconds, short enough that some people are caught off guard. Voice notes can’t be sent to older inReach models. - Photos are compressed but clear enough for trail documentation and emergency use. One thing nobody mentions upfront: recipients need the Garmin Messenger app installed to receive photos and voice messages. Standard SMS contacts get text only. If your emergency contacts or family don’t have the app, they won’t receive anything beyond a text message, worth sorting out before you leave the trailhead. Emergency - SOS still routes through Garmin Response, which can now receive voice notes and photos from the Plus. - Being able to send an image of an injury or describe a situation by voice instead of typing is a real upgrade in a serious emergency. Navigation - Connecting to Garmin Explore unlocks offline maps, routes, and waypoints, but the app uses your phone’s GPS rather than the device’s. The Plus has onboard GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou, but no multi-band. - Trackback functionality had bugs at launch but has been addressed in firmware. - If navigation matters, this isn’t the device. Use the GPSMAP 67i or pair your phone with an inReach Mini 3. Battery The new Certus protocol can burn more battery depending on how you use it. Garmin offers two modes: - Performance mode maintains a near-constant satellite link for fast back-and-forth messaging. Battery drains fast, especially in heavy cover where the signal is intermittent. - Low power mode checks for messages roughly once an hour, similar to older inReach models. Battery life improves dramatically. Real-world battery was more variable than older inReach devices. Garmin specs performance mode at up to 110 hours with 10-minute tracking and no media, but that’s a light-use baseline. In heavy tree cover using performance mode with several images and messages sent, I was tracking around 22 hours. That’s a stress test, not typical use. In open sky on low power mode with 10-minute location tracking, the battery barely moved over a 5-hour hike. Default to low power mode unless you’re expecting active back-and-forth communication.

item.title: South Kaibab Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.64
South Kaibab Trail Updated July 2026 Jump to a section Grand Canyon views hit you immediately on South Kaibab, a ridge trail with zero water or shade. Three natural turnaround points at 1.8, 3, or 6 miles let you dial in your distance, but most day hikers stop at Skeleton Point where the exposure gets serious. - Distance - 1.8–6 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 600–2200 ft - Time - 1–5 hrs Video Options - You can choose how far you want to hike down the South Kaibab Trail. Simply turn around and hike back up from the destination that you’re hiking to. - Cedar Ridge is the farthest the National Park Service recommends going on a summer day hike. - Similarly, they also don’t recommend continuing past Skeleton Point as a day hike outside of summer without consulting with a park ranger. Info Kaibab is a word of Southern Paiute origin meaning “mountain lying down,” aka inverted mountain. Difficulty Overall the South Kaibab Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. - When people get into trouble on the South Kaibab Trail, it’s usually because of the heat. The trail is totally exposed with no shade, so in hot weather it can be brutal. Even in the shade, summer temperatures often exceed 100F (38C). Check the weather and park alerts regarding the heat. - The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. - Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. - Outside of the trailhead and Colorado River, there is no water anywhere on the South Kaibab Trail. You have to carry all the water you need, and in summer that can mean several liters per person. - The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. But people have also died after getting too close to the edge (taking pictures). Be conservative. - Mules also use the trail, so be ready to step aside in safe areas when they pass. Trailhead The road to the South Kaibab Trailhead (Yaki Point Road) is closed to vehicles. Here’s what I would recommend. - Take the free Orange shuttle bus from the Visitor Center. This is by far the easiest way to get back and forth to the trail. If you want to get an early start, take the Hiker’s Express Shuttle, which is set up for long distance hikers but can be used by anyone. Getting an early start is a smart way to beat the crowds and see the sunrise in the canyon. - You can also walk from the Visitor Center along the wide and easy Rim Trail. It’s about 2.2 miles and takes most folks around 40-60 minutes. - There’s a very small parking lot along Desert View Drive, not intended for hikers but rather as a turn-off for drivers. From here you can walk about 0.5 miles to the Rim Trail and then to the South Kaibab trailhead. Trailhead Address: South Kaibab Trailhead, Grand Canyon Village, AZ 86023 Fees: Park Entrance Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) Gear - As I mentioned earlier, you need to bring your water with you. To Ooh Ahh Point, 1L is fine. To Cedar Ridge or Skeleton Point, bring 2L or 3L when it’s hot. Better to have more water than you need. Bring a backpack to carry it along with sun protection. - The hiking community has generally moved from hiking boots to trail runners. Overall you want your feet to be comfortable, especially if you’re not used to hiking this far. If you don’t have trail runners, wear sneakers. - Some hikers like trekking poles, and they can be helpful for stability, knee protection (on the downhill), and climbing on the way back out. - Don’t count on cellular service. If you need to call for help, having a satellite-enabled phone or satellite communicator can help. The trail is busy, so even if you don’t have satellite communications, you’re likely to see someone who might. - It can help to have a snack and/or electrolyte drink for the way back up if you’re doing one of the longer options. Maps Directions Trailhead to Ooh Ahh Point Info The South Kaibab Trail was built by engineers in 1924-25 to create a smooth and direct route down to the river. It has been described as “a trail in a hurry to get to the river.” Info At the bottom of the canyon, the layers date back 1.84 BILLION years! To put that in perspective, the Earth is 4.543 billion years old. Info If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Ooh Ahh Point to Cedar Ridge Info While Cedar Ridge seems open and a great place to camp, no camping is allowed along the South Kaibab Trail. If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Cedar Ridge to Skeleton Point Info The South Kaibab Trail is part of the Arizona Trail (AZT), which stretches about 800 miles from Mexico to Utah.

item.title: Bright Angel Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.58
Start near Bright Angel Lodge with water stations, multiple turnaround points, and the gentlest descent into the Grand Canyon. The 4,000-foot climb out will still humble you. Distance 3–12 mi Difficulty Hard Total Climbing 1100–3060 ft Time 2–8 hrs Who It's ForReasonably fit hikers. Well-maintained trail, clear signs, water stations make it the most forgiving canyon hike. Biggest RiskHeat and overexertion, especially on uphill return. Winter snow/ice on upper sections, mornings. When to GoYear-round. Start at sunrise in summer. Winter, check for ice near rim. You can choose how far you want to hike down the Bright Angel Trail. Simply turn around and hike back up from the destination that you’re hiking to. The National Park Service doesn’t recommend continuing below Havasupai Gardens as a day hike for most hikers. Warning When you’re figuring out which option is right for you, know that 2,640 feet of climbing is 0.5 miles straight uphill and fairly tough for most folks. It’s not just the distance. Difficulty Overall the Bright Angel Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. As you descend 1000 feet, the temperature will rise around 3.5°F to 5.5°F. So if you descend to Havasupai Gardens, the temperature could be somewhere around 18.5°F hotter than where you started. And the temperature will continue to rise until mid-afternoon. There are some shaded parts of the trail but not much, it can get very hot. You need to check park alerts and weather for the heat and plan accordingly. Leaving at sunrise is a great way to beat the heat and the crowds at the same time. The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. An advantage of the Bright Angel Trail is that it follows the water pipeline. You should still carry water with you, and you can refill along the way. Check the park page before you go, the water is sometimes turned off in places. The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. Info Want to camp on the Bright Angel Trail? You can book a tent site at Havasupai Garden on Recreation.gov (Backcountry Permit > Classic GC Hike South Rim > Havasupai Gardens Campground). Fees: Park Entrance Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) The closest parking is in the lot right next to the trailhead, which is next to the Bright Angel Lodge. I’ve had success here or on the street nearby when arriving early. The biggest lot nearby is Parking Lot D by the Backcountry Information Center. It’s a 5-10 minute walk to the trailhead from here and there are usually spots open. Alternatively you can take free shuttles from a bigger parking area like the Visitor Center to the stop for Bright Angel Lodge. Gear Even though there’s water on the trail, bring some with you, you’ll need it. Bring a backpack to carry it along with sun protection. The hiking community has generally moved from hiking boots to trail runners. Overall you want your feet to be comfortable, especially if you’re not used to hiking this far. If you don’t have trail runners, wear sneakers. Some hikers like trekking poles, and they can be helpful for stability, knee protection (on the downhill), and climbing on the way back out. Don’t count on cellular service. If you need to call for help, having a satellite-enabled phone or satellite communicator can help. The trail is busy, so even if you don’t have satellite communications, you’re likely to see someone who might. Bring a snack and/or electrolyte drink for the way back up. Tip See all the gear I use on hikes like this on my gear page. Did you know that the Bright Angel Trail used to be private and cost $1 (about $40 today) to hike? The path was used by Havasupai for hundreds of years but in the 1890s a settler claimed this land and started charging visitors to hike. Even after the Grand Canyon became a park in 1919 it was still private. The National Park Service was able to end private control by 1927. Hiking to 1.5 Mile Resthouse Info Pictographs = painted, Petroglyphs = carved Info These rest houses were built in 1935-1936 by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). Hiking to 3 Mile Resthouse Hiking to Havasupai Garden Info Havasupai Gardens was formerly known as “Indian Garden” and you may see some references to that on maps or signs. Info Theodore Roosevelt (who rode down the Bright Angel Trail on a horse) ordered the Havasupai who lived here to leave in 1901 in order to make way for the park. Some left and some stayed, but in 1928 the Parks Service forced the last Havasupai out of the Bright Angel area and onto a 518-acre reservation in Havasu Canyon. Info The fertile land at Havasupai Garden (around Garden Creek) has been cultivated since 300AD. Western tourists starting arriving in the 1890s and as you know, the last natives were moved out of here in 1928. Today there is a ranger station, toilets, picnic areas, a campground, and water. Info Havasupai means “people of the blue-green waters,” referring to the color of the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon. In the early 1900s they worked as laborers here and created much of what you see at Grand Canyon National Park. Hiking to Plateau Point Hiking Back To the South Rim The downhill is over, the hard part is yet to come. Unless you’re going to float down the river, you’ll have to walk back up to leave the inside of the Canyon.

item.title: ZOLEO Review: Still Worth It?
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.48
ZOLEO Review Updated August 2026 Jump to a section Inexpensive hardware, same Iridium network as Garmin, and the most seamless satellite messaging I’ve tested. If your phone is already how you navigate, this is worth a serious look. I’ve used the ZOLEO over the years on backcountry trips. At $149 upfront, the hardware is less expensive than any comparable inReach, and depending on your messaging volume the monthly cost can land lower too. It runs on the same Iridium network as Garmin. The Wi-Fi/cellular/satellite switching is the best implementation I’ve tested: one app, automatic handoff, no thinking required. The trade-offs are zero navigation and total phone dependence for anything beyond check-ins and SOS. The only reason to spend more on a Garmin inReach is if you want standalone navigation or you’re already deep in the Garmin ecosystem. For phone-first hikers, ZOLEO is the right call. Video Features The ZOLEO is a satellite messenger designed to work with your smartphone. Unlike Garmin’s inReach devices, there’s no screen or full interface on the unit itself. You pair it with the ZOLEO app via Bluetooth, and that’s where you handle messaging, weather forecasts, and settings. Without your phone, the ZOLEO still works for the essentials. Physical buttons handle SOS, check-in, and location sharing. LED indicators tell you what’s happening: green means it worked, red means it didn’t. What it does: - Two-way messaging (through the app) via satellite, Wi-Fi, or cell, whichever is available - Unlimited check-in messages with “I’m OK” and a map link to your GPS location - Breadcrumb trail location sharing with your contacts (optional $6/month add-on) - Weather reports for your current or custom locations - SOS with 24/7 emergency response coordination through GlobalRescue - Medical Assist messaging with health professionals (included on all plans) The biggest weakness is clear: you’re depending on your phone for the advanced functionality. If your phone dies, breaks, or loses Bluetooth, you’re limited to one-way SOS and check-ins. Advantages - Seamless messaging: ZOLEO gives you a real phone number and email address. You message with the same app whether you’re on Wi-Fi, cellular, or satellite, and it switches automatically. Garmin units don’t have their own number. - $4/month suspend: Garmin now offers 12 months of free suspension with SOS still active during that window. ZOLEO’s $4/month suspend doesn’t get you SOS you don’t already have, but it keeps your phone number and email live while paused, which Garmin’s suspension doesn’t. Garmin’s lowest active plan is $7.99/month for SOS only. - Medical Assist included: Contact a medical professional for advice before triggering SOS. Smart middle ground when something feels off but isn’t a clear emergency. - Rescue insurance available: Optional rescue insurance for around $40 covers the cost of an actual rescue. You can also sign up for the Overwatch & Rescue subscription, which is like AAA for the backcountry. - Proven durability: I’ve used mine in dust, rain, snow, and it’s taken some hits. It’s not flashy, but it works. Performance Across every trip I’ve used it on, messaging has been seamless and works exactly as advertised: you move between Wi-Fi, cell, and satellite without thinking about it. It just sends. The GPS does take longer to lock than my Garmin devices, which means check-ins sometimes take a minute or two longer to go out. I’ve had the occasional failed send too, but that’s become less common over time. Nothing that’s made me want to stop using it, and nothing that’s left me stranded. Subscriptions Both brands charge a $39.99 activation fee on first sign-up. After that, the monthly costs diverge. ZOLEO Plans | Plan | Monthly | Satellite Messages | Overage | Tracking | |---|---|---|---|---| | Basic | $20 | 75 | $0.50/msg | +$6/mo | | In Touch | $35 | 300 | $0.50/msg | +$6/mo | | Unlimited | $50 | Unlimited | Free | +$6/mo | All ZOLEO plans include unlimited check-ins, unlimited SOS, and Medical Assist. Suspend for $4/month; your phone number and email address stay active while suspended. Garmin inReach Plans | Plan | Monthly | Satellite Messages | Tracking | |---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | Pay-per-use ($0.50/msg) | $0.10/point | | Essential | $14.95 | 50 | $0.10/point | | Standard | $29.99 | 150 | Unlimited (10 min) | | Premium | $49.99 | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min) | All Garmin plans include unlimited SOS. Suspend free for up to 12 months, and SOS stays active during suspension, though messaging requires an active plan. No reactivation fee. The key difference: ZOLEO’s cheapest full-messaging plan ($20) gets you 75 messages and unlimited check-ins. Garmin’s Enabled plan ($7.99) gives you SOS and pay-per-use everything else. If you send more than a handful of messages per trip, ZOLEO’s $20 Basic is a better value than Garmin’s Enabled tier. If you primarily need SOS and check-ins with occasional messaging, Garmin’s Enabled plan is hard to beat at $7.99. Battery Advertised at 200+ hours with message checks every 12 minutes. Real-world numbers from my testing: - 12-minute message checks + 12-minute location shares: 88 hours - 12-minute message checks + 1-hour location shares: 140 hours - 12-minute message checks only: 190 hours Those numbers hold up on backpacking trips and thru-hikes. Increase check intervals and turn off location sharing to extend further. vs. inReach The inReach Messenger is the closest Garmin competitor. Both use Iridium, both rely on your smartphone for messaging, both include SOS. The differences come down to navigation, battery, and ecosystem. | Feature | ZOLEO | inReach Messenger | |---|---|---| | Price | $149 | $299 | | Coverage | Iridium global | Iridium global | | App Experience | Comparable | Comparable | | Location Sharing | Good | Better | | GPS Chipset | GPS/GLONASS | GPS/Galileo/QZSS/BeiDou | | Navigation | None | Very limited | | Battery Life | 200+ hours | 672 hours | | Connector | Micro USB | USB-C | | Weight | 150g (5.3 oz) | 114g (4.0 oz) | | Suspend | $4/month | 12 months free | | Activation Fee | $39.99 | $39.99 | The inReach Messenger wins on battery life (672 vs 200+ hours), weight (36g lighter), USB-C, multi-GNSS, and free 12-month suspension. The ZOLEO wins on device price ($150 cheaper), having a real phone number, and $4/month suspend that keeps your number and email active. If you’re in the Garmin ecosystem with watches and handhelds, the Messenger makes more sense. If you want lower hardware cost and seamless messaging on Iridium, ZOLEO is the right call.

item.title: Mount Perry Hike from Dante's Ridge Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.44
Mount Perry Hike from Dante's Ridge (Death Valley) Updated July 2026 Jump to a section Follow Dante’s Ridge 9 miles across the widest panorama in Death Valley, walking the spine of the Black Mountains 5,000 feet above Badwater Basin with views stretching to the Sierra Nevada. Almost nobody else attempts this point-to-point hike, stick to cooler months. Distance 9 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 2100 ft Time 4–5 hrs Who It's ForModerate hikers, 9 miles, 1,400 ft gain from 5,475 ft. Ridge walk, unmarked sections need navigation skills. Biggest RiskUnmarked route requires navigation. Significant wind exposure on ridge. Do not hike summer. When to GoOctober through May. Summer temperatures extreme even at elevation. This is a rugged and fairly remote hike. Don’t expect to see others and prepare for the conditions, which are often windy and exposed. Even though it’s cooler at this altitude than lower in Badwater Basin, it can still get extremely hot here. In the winter it can be freezing but don’t expect snow. In the summer, temperatures can be deadly. Checking the weather and conditions before you do this hike is critical. Bring at least 3L of water when it’s warm out. The trail is rocky and overall in good condition. Trail runners are a good choice for footwear. There is intermittent cellular service along the route but nothing dependable. If you have a satellite messenger, I’d bring it. Tip See all the gear I use on hikes like this on my gear page. Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America at -282 feet. During the last Ice Age there was a massive lake there called Lake Manly. The water dried up about 10,000 years ago but occasionally heavy rains will create mini-lakes in the basin.

item.description:

Grand Canyon National Park Hermit Trail to Santa Maria Spring Updated July 2026
Jump to a section
Follow the original 1911 sandstone-paved route down to a remote canyon shelter with views into Hermit Canyon. At 4.5 miles with shuttle access, you’ll have the trail nearly to yourself, making this one of the quietest ways into the Grand Canyon.
- Distance - 4.5 mi

Trailhead

This is a backcountry hike and you should prepare accordingly. - The Grand Canyon is a place of extremes. Prepare accordingly by checking the weather. If it’s hot out, skip the hike or leave before sunrise when temperatures are cooler. - When it’s hot, I bring 2L of water.
