item.title: How to Find the Right MSI Gaming Desktop for Your Setup
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.54
Shopping for a gaming desktop can easily turn into a spec-sheet spiral—an agonizing exercise in weighing wattages, chipsets, fan counts, memory, cooling systems, and a number of other variables. On their own, none of these figures explain which machine is a good bet for how you like to play. That’s the crux of what most gamers are really after when browsing for a new setup: a system that fits their space and budget, with room to grow and tinker as time goes on. MSI won top honors for Gaming Desktops for the third year running at the most recent PCMag Reader's Choice awards, winning the Graphic Card category for the third year in a row as well as the Motherboard category. Maybe that's because the company's most popular lineups are organized around how people actually play and make the choice feel less like a hardware audit. Here are four to know about, organized by gaming style. Key Takeaways - MSI's gaming desktops span four distinct series, with each one offering a unique value proposition for different player priorities - The Codex series is the approachable entry point, with an upgrade-friendly design ideal for newbie gamers or first-time builders looking to make the leap from console - The Aegis series is built for stability and suited for competitive players and streamers, with intelligent cooling and AI features that hold consistent frame rates - The Infinite series targets enthusiasts who want easy power upgrades, featuring top-tier components with the cooling and headroom for streaming and content creation - The Vision series is the flagship that pairs premium design with AI-enhanced features like the AI HMI touchscreen, great for design-conscious buyers or high-end creators To explore the full desktop lineup and self-select your ideal hardware path, check out the official MSI gaming desktops selection guide. The MSI Codex Series: Setting the Foundation In publishing terms, a codex is a book of fundamentals or a compendium. That’s the inspiration behind the Codex series, MSI’s dedicated entry-point gaming PC line. Desktops in this lineup arrive ready to play out of the box, which makes them a practical choice for any gamer making their first foray into the PC space from a console. It offers all the essentials for PC gaming, without the steep learning curve or complexity of building a rig from the ground up. Specs-wise, the Codex R2 AI 2nd (one of the latest models in the line) pairs an Intel Core Ultra processor with NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50 Series graphics and ships fully assembled with Windows 11. A mesh front panel keeps air moving, and MSI's Frozr AI Cooling adjusts fan speed as gameplay intensity fluctuates. These features handle the games most hobbyist gamers play regularly, from competitive shooters to sprawling open worlds. The Codex is an easily upgradable desktop PC that can grow alongside your rig enthusiasm. When you're ready, you can add storage, increase memory, or swap out the graphics card. The MSI Aegis Series: Engineered for Stability In Greek mythology, the aegis was a shield, an emblem carried by Zeus and Athena that represented defense and resilience. MSI's Aegis series brings that protective symbolism to a tower that stays steady even as gameplay heats up, making it a great choice for anyone seeking a lag-free streaming setup. The Aegis series meets just about any challenge with its advanced cooling systems: Higher configurations ship with a 360mm liquid cooler, and an intelligent architecture pairs multiple intake and exhaust fans with Frozr AI Cooling, which reads system temperature and automatically adjusts fan curves to keep components in their comfort zone. Under the hood, recent Aegis models run Intel Core Ultra or AMD Ryzen processors alongside RTX 50 Series graphics, so there's real headroom behind that stability. The MSI Infinite Series: Scalability and Toolless Upgradability The Infinite series is for players who'd rather not think about limits at all. The name alludes to boundless potential, and the series is built for enthusiasts who aren't afraid to tinker with upgrades. For the gamer chasing every last frame in a high-refresh shooter, or the creator rendering video between matches, these desktops pack plenty of power in reserve. At the top, an Infinite configuration can run an Intel Core Ultra 9 processor with a GeForce RTX 5090, fed by a power supply up to 1300W and cooled by a 360mm liquid loop. PCIe Gen 5 storage keeps load times short and snappy. Scalability is built in here, too. The larger Infinite houses its components in a roomy MEG PROSPECT case with several ARGB fans and space for up to ten, plus dual-hinged doors that make accessing the internals painless. Standardized parts mean the system scales with your skills, while the toolless design takes the headache out of making upgrades. The MSI Vision Series: Premium Design Meets AI-Enhanced Features The Vision series boasts an eye-catching design you’ll want to display for all to see, complete with AI-enhanced desktop features. It’s a statement piece that both aesthetics-conscious buyers and high-end creators will appreciate every time they walk by their setup. Behind the tempered-glass panel, forward-looking PC design shows up in details such as: - A cable-hiding motherboard for a clean interior - Silent Storm Cooling AI that monitors component temperatures and automatically adjusts fan speeds to match the workload at hand The flagship machine, the MEG Vision X AI, boasts AI HMI, a front-mounted touchscreen that works as an AI control center for system monitoring and quick settings adjustments, as well as a compartmentalized airflow layout that gives the CPU, GPU, and power supply their own thermal chambers. Configurations reach an Intel Core Ultra processor with up to a GeForce RTX 5090 and thousands of TOPS of combined AI performance, so the Vision series backs up its looks with the power to handle even the most demanding games or creative projects. How to Choose an MSI Series Here's a quick reference guide to how the four series stack up. Whether you’re setting up your first rig with a Codex, guarding your rank with an Aegis, chasing the ceiling with an Infinite, or making a statement with a Vision, the right MSI desktop is the one built for how you actually live and play. Explore the MSI desktop family today to choose your path and elevate your interactive experience. Which MSI gaming desktop is good for beginners? The Codex series is an approachable entry point into high-performance PC gaming. It features modern visuals and facilitates smooth gameplay out of the box, while intentionally offering an easily upgradable design so users can confidently expand their hardware footprint as they grow comfortable with PC components. Can I upgrade the components in the MSI Codex series later? Yes, easy upgradability is a core feature of the Codex series design layout. The chassis and internal organization are structured to allow straightforward access, giving first-time buyers and students room to grow by swapping out parts as their performance demands change over time. What features make the Aegis series reliable for competitive gaming? The Aegis series is engineered around defense and stability. It features an intelligent cooling architecture designed to maintain consistent frame rates and optimal thermal regulation under pressure, acting as a technical shield against the lag and stuttering that can disrupt competitive play or live content creation. How does the Infinite series handle demanding AAA gaming titles? The Infinite series is built for uncompromised power and scalability. It provides the necessary hardware headroom and high-refresh capabilities required to smoothly run demanding AAA titles, heavy streaming software, and complex media editing workloads simultaneously. What distinguishes the Vision series from other desktop lines? The Vision series represents the cutting edge of design and technology within the lineup. It blends flagship performance with premium aesthetics, refined craftsmanship, and forward-looking AI-enhanced features, making it a distinct statement piece for design-conscious buyers and advanced creators.

item.title: Have You Set Up Your Digital ID Yet? How to Add Your Driver’s License and Passport to Your Phone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.42
From credit cards and car keys to event tickets and transit passes, your phone can now hold all the physical objects you once crammed inside a pocket, wallet, or purse. But did you also know you can add your state-issued driver's license and passport? Several states let you quickly store digital versions of your identification on the Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, or Samsung Wallet app to get through TSA checkpoints a little faster. Certain states also have third-party ID apps. Here's what you need to know before you add your own. Which US States Support Digital Driver's Licenses? There are 21 states and territories that allow digital IDs. In total, 15 are compatible with Apple Wallet, 11 with Google Wallet, eight with Samsung Wallet, and five only use a state-developed third-party app. Your digital ID is not intended to replace physical credentials, but it can be used to quickly move through supported TSA checkpoints at airports (with a Real ID) and other locations. - Apple Wallet: Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Puerto Rico, and West Virginia. - Google Wallet: Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, and Puerto Rico. - Samsung Wallet: Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado (Galaxy Watch support), Georgia (Galaxy Watch support), Iowa, Maryland, North Dakota, and West Virginia. - Third-Party app: Alaska (Mobile ID only), Arkansas (Mobile ID), California (DMV Wallet), Iowa (Mobile ID), Louisiana (LA Wallet only), Kentucky (KY Mobile ID only), New York (NY MiD only), Utah (GET Mobile only), Virginia (VA MiD only), and West Virginia (WV MiD). - Unspported States: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Washington, Washington, D.C., Wisconsin, Wyoming How to Add an ID or Passport to Your Wallet App To add your Driver's License or passport to your phone, you'll need to set it up in your Wallet app. The exact steps are different with each app, though the process is similar: - Apple Wallet: Tap the Add Card (+) button, then Driver's License or ID Cards. Select Driver's License to add your state-issued ID or Digital ID to add your passport. You'll also have the option to add the ID to a connected Apple Watch. - Google Wallet: Tap Add to Wallet > ID, then Driver's license or state ID to add your state-issued ID. You can also tap ID Pass to create a digital version of your passport. You can also enroll in TSA PreCheck Touchless ID. - Samsung Wallet: Open the Quick access tab, then tap the plus (+) sign, and choose Digital IDs. From here, you can add your driver's license or select Samsung ID with Clear to add your passport. Once you've made your selections, follow the instructions through the process. You'll be asked to scan the official documents. For a state-issued ID, this will include the front and back of the physical card. For a passport, you're asked to scan the document's chip. Next, you'll need to verify your identity to the ID issuer by taking a series of photos or videos of your face. This process isn't instantaneous. Once finished, you'll need to wait for confirmation from the ID issuer that you've been approved. You should get a notification on your phone. If your application is rejected, you can try again. The California Department of Motor Vehicles recommends a number of practical adjustments, such as taking the photo on a plain background, using consistent and ample lighting, and making sure your phone isn't in low power mode. Which Phones Support Digital IDs? In order to add an ID or passport to your phone, you'll need to meet a few requirements. Take note that more devices support a driver's license than passports: - iOS: For an ID, you'll need an iPhone 8 or later, or an Apple Watch Series 4 or later. If you want to save your passport, it will require an iPhone 11 or later, or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later. - Android: For Android devices, you need to be running Android 9 or higher. Samsung specifically calls out the S20 or newer, Z Flip and Z Fold 5G or newer, the A53 or A54, or Watch 6 series paired to a device running Android 15 or higher. Samsung ID with CLEAR requires Android 14 or higher, and works on the S21 or newer, Z Flip 3 and Fold 3 or newer, and A53, A54. The Galaxy Watch is not supported. What Can You Do With a Digital ID? For now, the practical uses for a digital driver’s license or passport on your phone are a bit limited. Apple, Google, and Samsung bill these features as quick and easy ways to verify your age or identity through an app or at more than 250 supported TSA checkpoints. However, you are still expected to carry your physical documents on your person. It's also crucial to note that this is not a replacement for a Real ID, which is now required to board domestic flights in the United States. The actual benefits will vary on where you live. In California, for instance, you can only use it at select airports, like LAX and SFO, so if you're due to fly out from another location, this won't be of much help. You also won't find much support for digital passports outside the United States, with only Google Wallet listing support for additional regions (Brazil, Singapore, Taiwan, UK) Are Digital Driver's Licenses and Passports Safe? A digital driver's license is convenient, but is it safe? As one Redditor asked about Connecticut's digital ID effort: "Why would you want to give your unlocked phone to a cop?" Everyone's comfort level is different, but as the video above demonstrates, you scan or tap your own phone at a TSA checkpoint, so you shouldn't have to hand over your phone. Since you're still expected to carry your physical ID, you can always just present that instead if you're concerned about mobile security. Apple, Google, and Samsung make note that your digital ID is not tracked by these companies, and no data leaves your device without your consent. That means neither the company nor any local government can see when or where you share your information. You will also be required to set up some kind of security measure on your phone. On iPhone, that means Face ID or Touch ID, and two-factor authentication for your Apple account. Android phones require at least a PIN. About Our Expert I’ve contributed to PCMag since 2019, covering Apple, electric vehicles, and lots of other consumer electronics. If a gadget plugs into a wall or uses a battery, there’s a good chance I’ve tested it and have some thoughts about its place in our daily lives. I write featured articles, how-to guides, and daily news. I got my first taste of writing about technology for Fast Company in 2013, mostly how it intersected with the music industry. Since then I’ve written for dozens of publications and explored all other facets of service journalism, from reviews to buying guides. At one point, I took a break from journalism for a few years to work at a technology startup and then an industry Goliath, both valuable experiences in understanding how the business of tech works from top to bottom.

item.title: Live in One of These States? Your Computer Might Require an Age Check Soon
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.40
Age verification laws have moved beyond social media and porn. Three US states have passed laws requiring your operating system to collect your age, and Congress is discussing the same at the federal level. One day soon, verification requirements could require you to upload a photo ID to prove you're a legal adult before you can use your computer. This new front in the age verification battle comes after more than two dozen states passed laws targeting adult websites like PornHub, and Utah started cracking down on VPNs. Major OS developers aren't pushing back, but the open-source community has been vocal about the risks to your online privacy and the future of the web. Why Is This Suddenly an Issue? Starting in 2027, California's Digital Age Assurance Act will require operating systems, including Windows, macOS, Android, ChromeOS, and Linux distributions, to ask users for their age during device setup and share an age range with apps. Depending on how future laws evolve, that process could eventually involve government IDs, credit cards, or biometric verification. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, warns the effects won't stop at California’s borders. Because tech companies rarely build separate operating systems for different states, he says these systems will likely be rolled out "for everyone who uses [operating systems], including the billions of folks outside of California." Colorado followed California by passing a similar law, and Illinois followed. The three states are unlikely to remain alone for long. Similar bills are advancing in other states, while the proposed federal Parents Decide Act would expand age verification at the operating system level nationwide if passed. At WWDC 2026, Apple discussed age-based content restrictions across apps and websites for child accounts, which are mandatory for users 13 years old and under. You might have to prove your age to avoid this requirement, too. Apple recently introduced mandatory age verification for new accounts in Texas, and more states are likely to follow. Privacy advocates, open-source developers, and lawmakers are now battling over a question that could reshape the future of computing: Should your computer know your age before you can use it? Here's what you need to know so far. Which States Have OS Age Verification Laws in the US? As of this writing, three states have OS age verification laws: - California has the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It applies to Linux distributions as well as to closed-source operating systems such as macOS and Windows. However, state legislators are discussing amending the law to exempt open-source operating systems. - Colorado has bill SB26-051, which takes effect on July 1, 2028. It exempts open-source operating systems, such as Linux. - Illinois has the Children's Online Social Media Safety Act (HB5511), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2028. It applies to both closed- and open-source operating systems. California’s law is the first and serves as a model for other states. It requires that operating systems ask for your age when you set them up. Your OS must then share an age bracket signal with the applications running on your computer. Applications will see one of the following age ranges: under 13, 13-16, 16-18, or over 18. Application developers are then “deemed to have actual knowledge of the age range of the user.” They would have a legal duty to comply with any laws requiring different treatment of minors and could not plead ignorance of the device user's age. An application might need to restrict access or features for users under 18 under other laws, including the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA), which requires online services to handle the personal information of users under the age of 13 differently. This could affect dating, gaming, and social media apps, for example. California’s law doesn’t affect websites. However, a proposed California law would extend the age signal to the web. How Will Your OS Verify Your Age? Under California’s law, as written, your operating system must ask for your age during the device setup process. Your operating system will accept that age without requiring identification. Attestation—in other words, simply declaring your age—is sufficient proof. Nichole Rocha, a data privacy attorney who represents Children Now, a California-based organization that backs the law, tells me that California’s bill was designed to protect privacy. “There’s no requirement for the uploading of a government ID, and that was intentional on the part of the author, [California state assembly member] Buffy Wicks,” she says. “I think the bill strikes an appropriate balance. You see other states requiring the uploading of government IDs, and that’s incredibly invasive,” says Rocha. She argues that research shows parents set up devices for minors and will enter a child's age accurately at that time. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification."
However, the EFF believes operating system providers like Apple, Google, and Microsoft will require more personal information. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification,” Mackey says. He points out that there are fines and legal consequences if minors bypass age checks, and that companies will want to prevent minors from lying. “That involves more invasive forms of age verification that adult websites implement,” he says. That could mean providing a credit card, a facial scan, or a government ID during OS setup to verify that an adult was involved in the process. What Similar Laws Are Advancing in the US? On the federal level, the Parents Decide Act, introduced in Congress in April, would require OS-level age checks in all states if it passes. Specifically, the proposed law says operating system providers must "require any user of the operating system to provide the date of birth of the user" to set up an account or use the OS. Adults would also have to provide their date of birth. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would also need to “issue regulations on how operating system providers can… verify the date of birth of a parent or legal guardian” if a minor is setting up a device. This could potentially include government identification checks upon device setup; the implementation details would be up to the FTC. Similar language appears in other proposed bills. The Kids Online Safety Act, introduced in the Senate in 2025, would require the Secretary of Commerce to "conduct a study evaluating the most technologically feasible methods... to verify age at the device or operating system level." "I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states.”
Rocha doesn’t expect the federal government to take action. “Every year, things pop up in Congress that never get signed, right?” she says. “We just haven’t seen anything meaningful happen at the federal level in this space since the mid-1990s.” The EFF is concerned about the current legislative environment, however. "This is a trend we're seeing," says Mackey. "Lawmakers don't understand the technology, and they don't understand that these proposals are unpopular." Other states followed California and Colorado. As mentioned, Illinois legislators passed the Children’s Online Social Media Safety Act, HB5511. It requires the person setting up a device to declare only an age, without requiring proof of identity. “I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states,” says Rocha. Some states might require more personal identification. New York’s senate, for example, is discussing Bill 8102, which will require operating systems to determine user ages via “commercially reasonable age assurance methods.” How Will Apps Get Your Age From Your OS? Apps will get your age range from your operating system using an application programming interface (API). In other words, they’ll ask the operating system for your age range and get a response. Major operating system vendors are already implementing compliant APIs. Google has the Play Age Signals API for Android apps from Google Play, while Apple has the Declared Age Range API in iOS and macOS. A Microsoft spokesperson tells me that Windows will also offer an age range API and that the company will have more to share in the future. The system software that many Linux distributions use now has an age field for user accounts, too. How Is This Different From App or Website Age Checks? The legislation discussed above moves age verification from the application or website layer to the device or operating system level. PornHub has urged Apple, Google, and Microsoft to implement OS-level age verification. With OS-level age verification, adult online services like PornHub would not need to confirm visitors' ages by collecting documentation themselves. Instead, the operating system would have that obligation. PornHub is already using signals in Apple's iOS to check the age of visitors in the UK. However, as mentioned, California’s law does not require that the operating system pass age signals from the web browser to a website. That’s surprising, given that age-verification laws in many states have targeted adult websites. Rocha says California’s lawmakers were trying to address the web in the original law, but “ran out of time.” California's Bill AB 1856, which hasn’t passed yet, would extend the age verification requirement to web browsers and websites. Web browser developers are already working on age-verification standards. Google’s Chromium and Apple’s Safari both support the Digital Credentials API to share government identification information with websites. If you save a driver's license or other government ID to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet on your phone, you can securely share your credentials with websites. Theoretically, you could use the same process to share an age you provided to your desktop operating system with a website, too. What About Linux and Other Open-Source Software? In addition to affecting Apple’s iOS and macOS, Google’s Android and ChromeOS, and Microsoft's Windows, these laws impact smaller open-source community operating systems, including Linux distributions. “I think the open-source community is rightly very concerned about what’s happening here,” Mackey says. He adds that the law doesn’t regulate people who contribute to open-source operating systems or host downloads of Linux distributions. However, he says the law may apply to hobbyists who create or mod open-source operating systems. “And if they don’t implement these systems, then in theory, the state of California can bring enforcement action against them," he says. "And I think that is very scary.” Mackey points out that many open-source operating systems prioritize privacy and don’t want to collect user data or engage in surveillance. “There are lots of folks who have talked to lawmakers about this problem with the open-source system," he says. "It’s just that lawmakers are not hearing them and not responding to address those concerns." Rocha disagrees. She says she’s met with members of the Linux community, and that lawmakers are listening and considering changes to the law. ”We are actively trying to figure out how to solve for the problem of open-source without undermining the protections in the bill,” she says. Colorado's bill SB26-051, signed into law on June 4, 2026, exempts Linux distributions and other open-source software. Specifically, the law says it doesn't apply to "an operating system provider... that distributes an operating system... under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software." California lawmakers may also exempt Linux and other open-source operating systems before the law takes effect. Assembly Bill 1856, currently under discussion in the California legislature, would change the law to exempt operating systems distributed "under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software." The EFF is pleased with this proposed change, writing that "The bill is narrower now than it was before, and lawmakers clearly responded to concerns raised by EFF and the broader open-source community." It still takes issue with the concept of age-gating, however. How Are Open-Source Projects Responding? The open-source community is discussing age verification laws, and some projects have already commented publicly. GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused Android fork, has announced its intention to “remain usable by anyone around the world without requiring personal information, identification, or an account.” The project adds, “If GrapheneOS devices can't be sold in a region due to their regulations, so be it." Mackey says what California is doing to privacy-centric operating systems that don’t want to collect data on their users is tragic. “They’re envisioning an internet and mobile operating systems… without the surveillance, and we’re actually shutting them out of this and potentially creating liability for them," he says. MidnightBSD, an open-source operating system based on FreeBSD, once banned residents of jurisdictions with age verification laws from downloading its software on its download page. “We are working on a plan to try to implement functionality to comply with California, Colorado, and Illinois laws, but will never be able to comply with Brazil or New York. We are not a company and don't have revenue to pay for verification services,” read MidnightBSD’s statement. (Brazil’s ECA Digital law requires operating systems to verify user ages with “reliable” methods.) The project has since removed this language and now says that it "may provide optional tools, including aged(8), that users can configure for their own compliance purposes" but also that "MidnightBSD Project does not represent or warrant that use of any such tool satisfies the laws or regulations of any jurisdiction." Other projects are deciding how to proceed. “There are currently no concrete plans on how, or even whether, Ubuntu will change in response,” writes Jon Seager, vice president of engineering at Canonical, in response to the passage of the California law. Canonical is the company that manages Ubuntu, Will These Laws Affect VPNs? California’s law doesn’t mention VPNs. However, under other laws or regulations, a VPN application might need to block access based on OS-level age signals. Or applications and websites might legally need to check the OS-level age signal to confirm user ages. What Do These Laws Mean for the Future of Computing? Although I spoke to lawyers for this piece, I’m not a lawyer. I’m a tech geek who’s been using computers and operating systems for decades. As far as I can see, there are two types of laws under discussion: those that ask for your age and those that require proof of your age. California’s law, as well as the laws passed in Colorado and Illinois, accept whatever you provide during device setup. This puts additional legal requirements on operating system providers, including open-source communities, to design operating system interfaces that collect user ages. Rocha summarizes the California law’s approach: “We are going to try and protect as many children as possible in the most privacy-protecting way possible. And there will probably be some kids who get around the system, but the vast majority of kids will be protected by this.” “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely. It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws."
Legislation like the proposed bill in New York could require proving your age with a credit card, facial scan, government ID, or other method while setting up your device. A federal law could enforce this nationwide, depending on what the FTC requires. Future operating systems may require biometrics or identity document verification during device setup. I’m not a fan of either type of law. I don’t believe governments should require operating systems—especially small, open-source projects—to verify their users' personal information at the risk of legal liability. I want privacy-centric operating systems that don’t collect any user data to continue existing. “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely,” says Mackey. “It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws.” Mackey doesn’t think these laws are inevitable, though. “My hope is that people are energized by this [debate] and recognize the opportunity that we can push back,” he says. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: RTX GPUs Prices Jump 30% Overnight, With RTX 5070 Hitting $900
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.31
Prices for Nvidia graphics cards have jumped overnight at some retailers as regional pricing adjustments finally impact American buyers. Taking an average of recent Newegg prices, Tom's Hardware found that some card prices have increased by over 30%, with RTX 5070s now at a median price of $900; its launch price was $549. The RTX 5090 is up by 9% to $4,700. Gaming graphics card prices have been impacted by secondary demand several times over the past decade. But the AI-induced shortages are far worse than the cryptocurrency mining boom of years gone by. Many cards are now more than 50% more expensive than they're supposed to be, and in some cases, closing in on double their original launch price. The RTX 5090 blew through that milestone a long time ago and is now about 150% more expensive in 2026. The latest round of price increases has been hinted at for a few weeks. We'd heard rumors of price increases in Eastern markets like Japan and South Korea, but as stock of older cards dwindled, we're now seeing big price rises in the US too. Tom's Hardware's data is only from Newegg, so you can still find cheaper RTX cards elsewhere, but don't expect that to last more than a few days. The price adjustments at the time of writing are as follows: - RTX 5050 is now 5% more expensive, at $315. - RTX 5060 is now 27% more expensive, at $470. - RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is now 13% more expensive, at $530. - RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is up 39%, now averaging $805. - RTX 5070 is now 36% more expensive, at $900. - RTX 5070 Ti is the only card not to see a price increase, but it's still $1,100. - RTX 5080 is up 3%, now priced around $1,500. - RTX 5090 increased by 9%, with a median price of $4,700. There are cards that are more and less expensive; that's the median for you. But it shows how ridiculous prices are right now. The RTX 5060 is almost $100 more than the launch price of the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, and the 5060 Ti 16GB is almost $400 more than it cost when it launched just over a year ago. The RTX 5070 is $150 more than when the 5070 Ti debuted, and the 5070 Ti is $100 more than what the RTX 5080 launched at. None of these cards is more powerful than they were, but AI buyers and global shortages have pushed the prices far into extremes. Fortunately, AMD's GPUs are less affected. Though they are more expensive than they were and should be, you can still find a 9070 XT for under $800, making it now cheaper than a 5060 Ti, a card it absolutely runs rings around. You can get an even better deal with the RX 9070 GRE, which is roughly comparable to the RTX 5070 and yet costs less than $550. These prices are unlikely to last, so if you need an upgrade, think fast, but watch out for resellers and scammers. They love nothing more than a desperate buyer. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: US Drone Ban Explained: What You Can and Can't Buy in 2026
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.14
It's been months since the FCC took the unprecedented step of adding all foreign drones and handheld DJI camera gear to its Covered List, a registry of equipment that's not allowed to be sold in the US. We've already seen new releases like the waterproof HoverAir Aqua and the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P vlogging camera in other regions, but they haven't come to the US because of the FCC's decision. The drama is far from over, as DJI is suing to overturn the ban, and the FCC has retaliated by moving to revoke authorization for a brand that sells DJI clones and a handful of LiDAR-equipped drones previously allowed to be sold in the US. Meanwhile, the agency has added several other types of foreign tech to the Covered List, including Wi-Fi routers, portable power stations, and robot vacuums and lawn mowers. There's been some confusing reporting around what this means for creators who use camera drones, as well as DJI's line of cameras, microphones, and gimbals, as part of their workflows. Drone pros and content creators still aren't feeling the full impact, but that will change quickly if retroactive bans broaden. Drones have moving parts that can wear out over time; they don't last forever, and creators are already missing out on the latest innovations. If you have questions about the FCC's foreign drone ban and how it affects you, read on. Was There a Warning That a Drone Ban Was Coming? Yes. We knew the federal government was all but certain to add DJI's cameras and drones to the FCC's Covered List; the writing has been on the wall for months. The 2024 iteration of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a law that's updated annually in order to provide funding to the US military, included language that states that DJI and Autel drones, video surveillance, and communications equipment would be added to the FCC Covered List if it did not pass a security audit before Dec. 23, 2025. But as the deadline approached, it became clear that the government had little interest in actually performing the required audit. Will DJI Challenge the Drone Ban? Yes. DJI filed a lawsuit against the FCC in late February, two months after it was added to the Covered List. The suit accuses the FCC of violating the Fifth Amendment's due process clause, arguing that the FCC did not provide "the chance to provide information to address or refute any concerns." We'll have to wait and see how this plays out in the courts, but for now, it doesn't change the status quo. What Is the FCC Covered List? The Covered List is a registry of products and companies that are ineligible for use or sale in the United States. The FCC has to approve all devices with built-in wireless tech before they can be sold in the US, so being on the Covered List is a big deal for tech companies. Which Drones Are Banned Per the FCC Rules? All foreign-made drones that have not yet received FCC certification are now on its Covered List. Drones that have already gone through the FCC vetting process are exempt, but future releases are excluded from the US market. For all practical purposes, this applies to every consumer drone brand: Antigravity, DJI, Holy Stone, Hover, Potensic, and Ruko are all impacted. All additions are on a going-forward basis, so models that are already available in the US aren't affected. If you're looking for specifics, the DJI Lito 1 and Lito X1 drones, Osmo Pocket 4 and Pocket 4P vlogging cameras, HoverAir Aqua waterproof drone, and Potensic Atom 3 drone have all launched in other markets in 2026 but aren't allowed to be sold in the US. Wait, I Thought the FAA Regulated Drones? The FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) sets the rules for how and where you can fly drones, but the FCC (Federal Communications Commission) approves electronic devices. The FCC must approve nearly every consumer electronics device before it can be sold in the US. I Already Own a Drone, Can I Continue to Use It? Yes. You'll still need to follow all FAA rules for use, but so far, there are no restrictions on using older drones from DJI and other brands that previously received authorization. It's a good idea to follow the regulations, though, as the FAA has been more aggressive in fining pilots who violate Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) orders or otherwise skirt the rules in recent months. The New York Times reports that the FBI confiscated more than 700 drones that violated TFR orders that were in place during the World Cup, for instance. Are DJI’s Cameras and Gimbals Included in the Ban? Yes. The Covered List now includes "communications and video surveillance equipment and services listed in Section 1709(a)(1)" of the NDAA, and the language in that law applies to DJI's entire product line, not just its drones. A DJI spokesperson confirms that all of its products, including Ronin and Osmo, are now on the Covered List. Again, this only applies to products that have not yet received FCC approval. Older releases like the Osmo Action 5 Pro, Osmo Pocket 3, and RS 3 Mini aren't affected. But new releases, including the Osmo Pocket 4 and 4P, aren't allowed to be marketed in the US. The FCC has not yet moved to revoke authorization for older DJI camera equipment, but it has moved to stop sales of cameras from Xtra, a US-based company that specializes in what are best described as clones of DJI's action and vlogging camera line. What About Drones (and Cameras) That Were Previously Authorized? When the drone ban first took effect in December, it seemed that drones and DJI cameras previously vetted by the FCC were safe. Recent actions by the FCC have called that supposition into question. In late July, the FCC moved to revoke approvals for a number of DJI clones, including Skyrover drones and Xtra cameras, and, in August, followed with a similar motion to revoke approvals for Anzu Robotics, a US-based company that licenses DJI technology for its Raptor drone. The FCC is also seeking to pull authorization for "military-grade" drone hardware, including anything with integrated LiDAR tech, a thermal camera, spray capabilities, or with a takeoff weight greater than 55 pounds. Several consumer-grade DJI drones, including the Air 3S, Avata 360, Mini 5 Pro, and Neo 2, use LiDAR for obstacle avoidance and are likely to be affected. Likewise, DJI's Mavic 3T, an enterprise-class drone with a thermal camera used for industrial inspections and by first responders, its Agras farming drones, and its FlyCart delivery drones are also in danger of losing FCC certification. The FCC's final decision on this action is expected in the first week of September. All of these proposals are delayed for a period of public comment, but once that window closes, we expect Xtra cameras, several clone drone brands, including Anzu and Skyrover, and the aforementioned DJI models to disappear from retail in the US. We expect the decision on Xtra and Skyrover to drop within a couple of weeks, with Anzu following in early September. Note that you're still allowed to use these products if you already own them. There is an unknown here: It's unclear what the FAA will do if the FCC revokes authorization for drones that it previously approved. The FAA requires pilots to provide a serial number when registering a Remote ID-equipped drone for recreational or commercial use, and it matches that serial number against drones for which it has issued a Declaration of Compliance. We'll have a clearer answer to that question in early September when the comment period for the proposed LiDAR drone ban closes. I Still See Drones for Sale at Us Retailers. I Thought They Were Banned? The FCC Covered List drone ban applies to future models that have not yet been approved for sale in the US. Drones that have previously been certified for sale are not included in the ban unless the FCC undertakes specific action to revoke their status. Its rules state that it must revoke authorization on a case-by-case basis. I Want To Buy a Drone. Which One Should I Get Now? You can check out our list of the best drones for specific recommendations on drones I've tested, but the general rule of thumb is to get a DJI drone that fits your budget and needs. The safest bet for beginners is the DJI Flip or the Potensic Atom 2, while we recommend that experts consider the DJI Mavic 4 Pro. I'm a little less confident recommending a newer drone with LiDAR today on the outside chance that the FAA follows the FCC's lead and declares them military hardware. Recreational pilots don't have to register drones that weight 249g or less, so the DJI Mini 5 Pro and Neo 2 are still safe buys. The DJI Air 3S requires FAA registration for recreational flight, and owners face a potential headache if the FAA removes it from the Compliance List. Whether the FAA will start removing drones from its registry remains unknown at this point, but we should know more in September, when the comment period for the LiDAR drone ban ends. Can't I Just Import an Unapproved Drone or Osmo Pocket 4P? Technically, yes, but you may run into unexpected problems. If you're flying under recreational rules and pick a drone that weighs 249g or less, you don't have to register with the FAA, so you're not likely to run into any headaches. However, if you're a pro pilot or want a drone that's heavier than 249g, you may run into trouble with registration if your imported drone has built-in Remote ID. The FAA's system restricts which Remote ID drones can be registered and requires you to enter a valid serial number. Vlogging cameras like the banned Osmo Pocket 4P don't require any sort of federal registration, but there's been at least one instance of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) confiscating a Pocket 4P from a US resident who bought one abroad and tried to bring it home. There are plenty available on eBay if you don't mind taking a chance. Are There Any Drones Made in the US? Yes, there are a handful of drone makers manufacturing products stateside, but they are typically made for industry, agriculture, or the military. The Parrot Anafi USA, Hylio Ares, and Teal Black Widow are a few examples indicative of the types of drones made stateside. These are serious drones made for first responders, law enforcement, crop monitoring, industrial inspections, and the military—they are simply not consumer-grade and cost far more than standard camera drones. But almost every drone that's considered affordable is made in China. There's no US-made replacement for the camera drones that content creators, real estate photographers, and wedding videographers typically use. There's always the possibility a US company will try and enter the consumer market. I asked Hylio CEO Arthur Erickson when an American-made take on the DJI Mini 5 Pro could come to market and how much it would cost, and his answer is telling: "I think US companies in the next one to three years will come out with approximate DJI Mini equivalents around the $4,000 to $5,000 price point." That's some serious sticker shock, especially given that the Mini 5 Pro costs $759. Are Any Drones Exempted From the Covered List? Yes, but not consumer models. The FCC made additional changes to the Covered List on Jan. 7, carving out drones from the Department of Defense's Blue UAS Cleared List. These drones have been cleared for military use, and some are manufactured in other countries—specifically Denmark, France, Norway, Switzerland, and Taiwan. The change also removed drones that may contain foreign parts but have a high enough percentage of domestic components to qualify as US-made under the Buy American Standard. These amendments don't have any real-world implications for consumer drones; to date, none qualify for either exemption. The FCC has also exempted what it calls toy drones. It has a long list of restrictions that a drone must meet to qualify as a toy. The highlights include a maximum takeoff weight of 150 grams, a 300-foot altitude limit, a maximum battery life of 10 minutes, a dedicated remote that doesn't use Wi-Fi, a top speed of 22.4mph, and a complete lack of GPS and camera capabilities. Essentially, this is a carve-out for true toys that look like drones. I Saw a Headline Saying That the Drone Ban Was Dropped. Is That True? No. While it's true that the Commerce Department ended its efforts to restrict the import of DJI and other drones in January 2026, it did so only because it would be redundant in light of the FCC's actions. The Commerce Department is a separate entity from the FCC, and its proposed restrictions were never implemented. Some reports on the Commerce Department's decision have misleading headlines that could make you think the government did an about-face, so I don't blame you for being confused. If My Drone Breaks, Will I Be Able to Get Replacement Parts? Yes. I asked the FCC if the component ban applied retroactively, and a representative referred me to the agency's fact sheet, which states that the entirety of additions to the Covered List are on a "going forward basis." A DJI spokesperson also confirms that parts for drones already approved are unaffected. That means you should be able to pick up a fresh battery or replace a broken gimbal or a worn-out motor for the drone you already own, at least in the near future. Are Hasselblad Cameras Banned, Too? This is unclear. DJI entered into a strategic partnership with the legendary Swedish camera brand in 2015 and strengthened it with a cash injection in early 2017. The two brands are quite close these days, going as far as to share booth space at trade shows, though they are technically different companies. The language in the NDAA extends to DJI's "subsidiaries, affiliates, partners, joint ventures, and any entity to which they have a technology sharing or licensing agreement," and it's certainly possible that Hasselblad falls under that big umbrella. However, I've not been able to get the FCC to confirm this, so my guess is that Hasselblad won't face any future difficulties. Call that informed speculation; to know for sure, we'll have to wait and see what happens the next time Hasselblad submits a camera for FCC review. That could be a couple of years away as its X2D II 100C and 907X & CFV 100C are both fairly new. Does the Drone Ban Also Cover Model Aircraft? Yes. Remote-controlled airplanes predate drones by decades and are a staple at hobby shops nationwide. In recent years, they have been segmented into the same regulatory bucket as drones. The Academy of Model Aeronautics (AMA), the largest organization for model aircraft enthusiasts in the US, is tracking the situation via its blog. Stay Tuned DJI has taken its fight to remain in the US market to court, so I'll pay close attention to developments and update this story as news breaks. For now, the company and other foreign drone makers remain on the Covered List, so we'll have to wait and see whether it succeeds in its suit against the FCC. Keep your eyes peeled to PCMag for news and updates as the court battle proceeds. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Zoom Screen-Sharing Flaw Could Give Attackers Control of Participants' Devices
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.99
Researchers at A Security have discovered a critical bug in Zoom that allows attackers to assume full control of a participant’s device by exploiting a flawed screen-sharing function. The vulnerability exists in the Zoom Workspace app for Windows, Mac, iOS, Android, and Linux. When a user launches the annotation tool while sharing their screen, the bug allows attackers to remotely execute malicious code and access participants’ devices. The attack requires no action from a victim’s end and leaves no visible warning, A Security says in its blog post. The firm discovered the bug and developed a working exploit for it in just 24 hours. They did it using just 20 prompts on a publicly available AI model, highlighting how AI can make cyberattacks easier to carry out. “This class of capability would previously have only been available to nation-state threat actors, but the model requiring elite teams, months of effort, and weapons-grade budgets has collapsed,” A Security says. “Today, a single researcher was able to develop a nation-state-level exploit in less than a day.” A Security notified Zoom about the bug on June 10. Zoom acknowledged it the next day and deployed client-side and server-side fixes to mitigate the threat a few weeks later. The video-conferencing service also published security bulletins noting that the vulnerability exists across all Zoom Workplace platforms prior to versions 7.1.5 and 7.0.6. “Users can help keep themselves secure by applying the latest updates,” Zoom adds. This comes after Apple issued emergency macOS updates to fix a similar screen-sharing flaw that allowed attackers to view a user’s screen, open files, and launch apps. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Tesla Debuts Starlink On Cybercab as Elon Musk Eyes Industry Adoption
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.85
Tesla has started to officially incorporate Starlink into the company’s Cybercab. On Monday, the company showed off the satellite internet integration in an actual vehicle. In a tweet, the official Tesla Robotaxi account posted two photos, writing, “First Cybercab with Starlink integration.” The Starlink antenna has been built directly into the vehicle’s rear and occupies a rectangular compartment that hides the dish’s signature design. In seperate tweet on Sunday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk didn't stop at the Cybercab. He went even further and boldly claimed that “All cars will have Starlink in the future. It’s the only way to get super high bandwidth to billions of vehicles.” That said, Musk might be referring to the cellular-focused Starlink Mobile, which doesn't require a satellite dish, but can work over smartphones. In an earnings call last week, SpaceX strongly suggested that the next-gen Starlink Mobile will eventually compete with AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon. In contrast, the home broadband-focused Starlink requires the dish antenna. Telsa debuted the integration after first teasing the Starlink capability on a display at a company showroom in San Jose. The company then publicly tweeted an image of the display, not only confirming the capability, but also stating the Cybercabs will use the newly-launched V5 dish model, which is capable of download rates up to 375+ Mbps. The Cybercabs represent Tesla’s effort to create self-driving robotaxis with a new kind of vehicle that drops the traditional steering wheel or gas pedals; instead, the passenger is supposed to sit inside and let the car's onboard computer drive them to their destination. By tapping orbiting Starlink satellites, the Cybercab will also be able to receive high-speed internet no matter the location, including in cellular dead zones. “Watch 4K streaming video while Cybercab takes you anywhere you want,” Musk tweeted last month. In an earnings call last month, Musk added: “Starlink will be integrated into all our car vehicles, at least for markets that Starlink is active. Because for a Robotaxi situation, you need to have coverage everywhere. There are many places, even in Silicon Valley, where the cellular coverage is terrible or sometimes non-existent.” However, Tesla’s VP for AI software Ashok Elluswamy noted the Starlink integration isn’t required for safe operation of the vehicle. Connectivity is primarily meant for navigation, customer service and, in general, fleet management.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Spotify Will Now Flag 'AI Personas' and Stop Recommending Their Music
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.84
Is that a human artist or an AI persona? Spotify will soon make that distinction clearer with new “AI Persona” labels. The streamer introduced the label today and said that it will apply to artists’ profiles whose public identity, name, and imagery “represent photorealistic AI-generated identities.” You will begin seeing the label in search, artist profiles, and playlists starting in mid-September. Once an artist has been marked as an “AI Persona,” Spotify won’t include their songs in any editorial or algorithmic recommendations unless you follow the AI Persona. “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated,” Spotify says. “The badge signals to listeners that an artist’s identity may be AI-generated and does not represent a real person.” Artists can declare themselves as an AI Persona through the Spotify for Artists platform starting today. Spotify will also begin identifying and marking “Likely AI Personas” soon. If Spotify applies the label, the account holder will be notified and allowed to make a self-disclosure. They will also be allowed to appeal the label if it was applied in error. Spotify already has a Verified by Spotify badge for real, human artists, and an AI credits badge to indicate when part of a track is generated by AI. The new AI Persona label is meant to ensure that artists whose public image doesn’t suggest they are human are marked as such. “This badge is about the artist’s public identity, not about how the music was made,” Spotify said. The streamer also noted that while “all artists have creative choice in determining how they present themselves, Spotify’s programming is focused on elevating music from authentic artists building careers in music.” About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Your Claude-generated text will soon include AI watermarks
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.62
It’s about to get much easier to spot AI-generated text, with Anthropic announcing that invisible AI watermarks will soon be added to all Claude-created content. The new policy, which is mandated by the European Union’s AI Act, will apply to any text or files that were created or otherwise touched by Claude, including computer code, company reports, or cover letters to potential employers. In a recently published support page, Anthropic says that new Claude models launched in the EU on or after August 2, 2026 will support adding watermarks to the content they create or edit, and that it’s working to add watermarking abilities to previously launched Claude models. The watermarking mandate stems from the EU AI Act, which includes a provision boosting the transparency of content that was created or “processed” by AI. Anthropic says it will deploy Claude’s watermarking abilities worldwide and across all Claude products, including Claude Cowork, Claude Code, and the Claude API, to comply with the law. When it comes to marking text, Anthropic says a “supported” Claude model “weaves an imperceptible watermark into the text itself,” and that the mark will remain present after the text is copied and pasted, or even after “some” editing. Meanwhile, Claude will attach “provenance” metadata to certain files it creates, including SVG, PNG, and JPG files. Anthropic says it plans on releasing tools that allow anyone to detect the watermarks, with details on those tools slated to arrive in “forthcoming” announcements. The presence of a Claude watermark doesn’t necessarily mean the content was originally created by Claude, Anthropic points out. For example, human-written text that’s later edited by Claude will also get a watermark. There may also be cases where Claude-touched content isn’t watermarked, such as when the content is “heavily” edited, too short, or produced by a Claude model that doesn’t yet support watermarking. It’s worth noting that the EU AI Act applies to any AI providers operating in the European Union. Both Google and Meta have pledged to sign the act, while ChatGPT maker OpenAI says it will take a “layered approach” to the act’s transparency provisions. But while those companies have signaled their intentions to comply with the EU AI Act, they’ve stopped short of detailing their own watermarking plans for AI-generated text. In any event, news of Claude’s forthcoming watermarks means a) it will soon get much easier to detect Claude-created or “processed” text, and b) it will also be much easier for others to spot text that you’ve created with Claude. Food for thought.

item.title: There’s a one-click way to email an open Office file. Most people miss it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.40
Imagine you’re working on an Excel workbook and you want to quickly email it over to a colleague or friend. There’s actually a handy little trick you can use to get it done fast—and it also works in Word and PowerPoint. All you have to do is look at the Quick Access Toolbar and find the drop-down menu, represented by an icon with a small horizontal line and a downward-pointing arrow. Click it to open the menu of quick access actions and select Email. Joel Lee / Foundry By selecting Email, you’re enabling the action in the actual Quick Access Toolbar. Look to the left of the icon and you should now see an envelope icon. Clicking it will launch your system’s default email client, which is likely Outlook if you haven’t changed it—but more importantly, it’ll open with a new email draft and the Excel workbook attached. You can repeat these steps in both Word and PowerPoint, which will launch your system’s email app with a new draft and the current Word document and PowerPoint presentation attached, respectively. It’s such a quick and easy way to share what you’re working on with others, so be sure to add it to your Quick Access Toolbar soon. Further reading: 18 power shortcuts every Excel user should know

item.title: Breached: Valve warns Steam hardware buyers to watch for scams
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.73
In summary: - Valve has warned European Steam hardware customers that a data breach at CEVA Logistics exposed personal details including names, addresses, and phone numbers. - According to PCWorld, payment information and Steam account passwords were not affected, but scammers may use the stolen data for highly targeted phishing attacks. - Customers are advised to stay cautious of unexpected messages, even if they appear legitimate by referencing real personal details. The more a scammer knows about you, the more convincing the scam can become. They don’t need your most sensitive information to pull it off, either. A recent breach involving Steam hardware customers is a good example of this. First reported by Engadget, Valve recently warned European customers who purchased Steam hardware that some personal information might have been compromised. The breach happened occurred at Valve’s logistics partner, CEVA Logistics. The data includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and order details. Payment information and Steam account credentials weren’t affected, but Valve warned that the information could be used in fraudulent emails, texts, or phone calls. Valve states that it’s working with CEVA Logistics to figure out exactly what data was stolen. It has also notified European data protection authorities.

item.title: How to change up Windows 11’s Widgets panel—or disable it altogether
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.67
By default, Windows displays so-called widgets at the far left of the taskbar. These include, for example, current weather information or stock market prices. Clicking on the widget currently displayed opens a window where you can remove individual widgets from the selection by clicking on the three dots and selecting ‘Remove.’ Foundry Clicking the plus sign in the top right-hand corner, on the other hand, takes you to a list where you can add additional widgets. However, it’s also possible to disable the display of widgets completely. To do this, go to ‘Settings’ in Windows, click on ‘Personalisation > Taskbar’ and then toggle the switch next to ‘Widgets’ to ‘Off.’

item.title: Biggest 2D Map of the Universe Took 13 Years and 263,407 Photos to Make
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 8.67
Scientists have used a pair of NSF NOIRLab telescopes for 13 years to create the new DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys map. It is the largest 2D map ever of the Universe and covers three-quarters of the sky. The catalog has nearly four billion objects. Scientists used the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Mayall telescope and the NSF Blanco telescope, which houses the U.S. Department of Energy-fabricated Dark Energy Camera, a 570-megapixel wide-field camera. The telescopes captured nearly four billion celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, black holes, and even asteroids. Together, their photos have been used to build a 5.6-trillion-pixel map. Over 160 scientists contributed data to the new collection, and it comprises 263,407 telescope photos. This new map is available now to everyone and builds upon existing DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. So far, over 1,800 scientific papers have been published that reference Legacy Survey data. “It’s part of the fabric of astronomy research now,” says David Schlegel, co-lead of the Legacy Surveys and a scientist at the Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “When you’re working with astronomical objects today, you often start by pulling up the Legacy Imaging Viewer to see what you’re looking at.” With the latest data, scientists can look at about 75 percent of the sky in both visible and near-infrared light, the latter of which helps scientists see through the dust and stars of the Milky Way into the deep cosmos. Researchers believe this newly updated map will be the most comprehensive 2D map of the Universe for “years to come.” “Explorations of our Universe always start with images of the night sky. The DESI Imaging Legacy Surveys are just one step in this venerable human tradition,” adds Arjun Dey, NSF NOIRLab astronomer and co-lead of the Legacy Surveys. “For our team, these data are fundamental to the investigation of the expansion history of the Universe and the formation of our galaxy. But the skies belong to everyone, and this survey gives everyone the chance to marvel at their wonders.” The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys were originally performed to prepare for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey. The new 2D map is basically a “deep photograph of the sky,” as NOIRLab puts it. It shows where galaxies and stars are located and how bright they are. This is extremely important information for the DESI survey to select its targets and build a 3D map of the Universe. It will be the largest high-res 3D map of the cosmos ever, and will be used to investigate and track Dark Energy. DESI completed its mission ahead of schedule in April, mapping more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. Scientists are poring over the results now. Legacy Surveys will also prove to be a foundational reference for the next generation of telescopes, like the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory and its huge 3.2-gigapixel camera. Image creditsDESI Legacy Imaging Surveys/LBNL/DOE & KPNO/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Additional credits and image processing by M. Rodriguez (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab) & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab).
