item.title: CFTC warning on ‘American odds’ puts sports prediction market pricing in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 5.51
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has warned companies offering event-contract derivatives that presenting prices in sportsbook-style “American odds” could mislead consumers, a move that could have significant implications for sports-focused prediction market products offered or distributed by major betting brands. In an August 7 press release, the CFTC said its Division of Market Oversight and Market Participants Division had reminded regulated entities involved in listing, soliciting or accepting event contracts that they must provide “clear and accurate pricing information” and avoid misleading consumers. The underlying three-page staff letter goes further. CFTC staff said it was concerned about reports that some regulated event-contract products were being marketed using the “American odds” format associated with casino gambling bookmakers, rather than nominal or percentage pricing reflecting market prices. The warning represents the latest step in the CFTC’s increasingly active oversight of prediction markets. Earlier this year, the commission issued guidance stressing that event-contract exchanges are responsible for robust surveillance, contract design and market integrity as sports prediction markets continue to expand. The March advisory described exchanges as “front-line regulators” and stressed that event contracts should not be readily susceptible to manipulation. The CFTC views exchange-traded event contracts and traditional sportsbook wagers as fundamentally different pricing mechanisms. According to the letter, derivative contract prices are established through competitive bidding among market participants, with order books generally displaying real-time bids and offers. Prediction markets can therefore perform both price- and information-discovery functions. By comparison, the agency said displaying those contracts as bookmaker-style odds is “likely to mislead” customers about the transaction they are entering and could obscure information about market depth and the pricing impact of their trades. The CFTC also warned that confusion between exchange products and sportsbook bets could potentially be exploited to steer customers toward higher-margin, non-market-priced bookmaking products. The CFTC press release echoed that warning, saying regulated markets should present pricing in a way that makes clear to consumers that they are trading an event contract on a CFTC-regulated exchange rather than purchasing a sportsbook product. Warning draws attention from prediction market industry In an August 8 post on X, industry commentator Bill Speros called the CFTC guidance “a direct hit” on DraftKings, FanDuel, Novig, Underdog and Fanatics. He argued that their platforms had been designed to resemble sportsbooks and said platforms that did not mimic sportsbooks had “won big” from the guidance. That characterization is Speros’ interpretation, not the CFTC’s. Neither the agency’s press release nor its staff letter names DraftKings, FanDuel, Novig, Underdog or Fanatics. The CFTC instead addresses regulated entities, affiliates and other businesses or people involved in listing, marketing or accepting orders for event-contract derivatives generally. The letter is formally addressed to “CFTC-Regulated Entities and Affiliates.” The agency has issued an industry-wide regulatory warning rather than announcing an enforcement action against any of the companies named in Speros’ post. The CFTC grounded its warning in existing federal requirements. Its letter cites Section 9 of the Commodity Exchange Act and Commission Regulation 180.1, which prohibits intentionally or recklessly making materially untrue or misleading statements, omitting material facts or engaging in practices that operate as a fraud or deceit in connection with regulated products. The agency’s August 7 release similarly warned that misleading pricing information in connection with a regulated product risks violating federal prohibitions against manipulative devices. The warning also arrives against a backdrop of growing legal and political disputes over sports prediction markets. In July, a coalition of 44 state attorneys general urged the CFTC to withdraw its proposed prediction markets rule, arguing the commission was attempting to regulate sports betting without congressional authority. The group maintained that sports wagers are not financial derivatives, warned that the proposal would override state gambling laws and consumer protections, and accused the agency of expanding its jurisdiction beyond the Commodity Exchange Act. The CFTC, by contrast, has consistently maintained that qualifying event contracts traded on regulated exchanges fall within federal derivatives law. CFTC says sportsbook odds can mislead traders The two CFTC divisions said entities marketing and trading derivative products are expected to ensure that intermediaries, affiliates and partners also comply with regulatory standards. CFTC-regulated entities that list, solicit or accept orders for event-contract derivatives were asked to review their pricing displays, marketing materials and other consumer information — including information used by partners and affiliates — and confirm receipt of the letter by August 31, 2026. Introducing brokers and futures commission merchants involved with event contracts are instructed to confirm receipt with the Market Participants Division, while designated contract markets are directed to the Division of Market Oversight. The letter is signed by DJ Hennes, director of the Market Participants Division and acting director of the Division of Market Oversight. The CFTC’s position ultimately centers on what consumers believe they are buying. A sports event contract may look superficially similar to a sportsbook wager when both are tied to the outcome of the same game. But the regulator says a market-priced derivative should be presented as a market-priced derivative — not dressed up to look like a bookmaker’s bet. Featured image: Ajay Suresh via WikiCommons / CC BY 4.0

item.title: DraftKings revenue falls despite betting growth as Predictions expansion accelerates
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 5.26
DraftKings reported weaker second-quarter revenue even as more customers placed bets and used its platform. Favorable sports results for bettors and heavier promotional spending to attract new users reduced the online gambling company’s revenue and profitability during the quarter. The Boston-based operator posted revenue of $1.44 billion for the three months ended June 30, down 5% from $1.51 billion a year earlier. The company said bettor-friendly outcomes and increased promotional reinvestment tied to customer acquisition across its Sportsbook and Predictions products were the main reasons for the decline. Customer activity, however, continued moving higher. Sports Consumer Volume, which measures settled wagers and trades across Sportsbook and Prediction Markets, climbed 15% year over year to $13.1 billion from $11.5 billion. Monthly Unique Payers rose about 9% to 3.6 million, although average revenue per monthly payer dropped 13% to $132 because promotions and favorable betting outcomes reduced revenue generated from each customer. DraftKings doubles down on Predictions as second-quarter results show decline DraftKings also swung to a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $67.6 million after reporting net income of $157.9 million in the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA declined to $114.6 million from $300.6 million a year earlier. Across its business lines, sports revenue fell 10.6% to $891.9 million, while iGaming revenue increased 7.5% to $461.9 million. Other revenue rose 5.2% to $89.4 million, and the sports net revenue margin narrowed to 6.8% from 8.7%. “We delivered a strong second quarter and enter the back half of the year with real momentum, as our core business grew across handle, users, and engagement,” said Jason Robins, DraftKings’ Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder. “Our Super App is now live nationwide, and Predictions is already growing faster than we anticipated. The similarity of Predictions customer metrics to Sportsbook customer metrics, our advantaged LTV position, and our playbook to innovate on a leading Predictions offering all underpin our confidence that we can win the category this NFL season and beyond.” The emphasis on Predictions has grown steadily this year. In first-quarter results, DraftKings reported its first quarterly profit of 2026 and said stronger sportsbook margins were giving it room to invest in prediction markets while expanding its broader Super App strategy. Chief Financial Officer Alan Ellingson said the company continues to expect its core business to generate about $1 billion in adjusted EBITDA this year, giving it flexibility to invest in its Predictions business. “Our core business remains on track to generate approximately $1 billion of Adjusted EBITDA this year, providing us with financial flexibility to invest behind the significant opportunity that we are seeing in Predictions,” Ellingson said. “Therefore, we are maintaining our fiscal year 2026 guidance for revenue of $6.5 billion to $6.9 billion and Adjusted EBITDA of $700 million to $900 million.” The company left its full-year guidance unchanged. It has also continued expanding its federally regulated prediction markets business through Railbird Exchange, which recently filed sports event contract certifications with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. At the same time, the strategy faces legal scrutiny, with two proposed class-action lawsuits alleging the Predictions platform functions as an unlicensed sportsbook. DraftKings currently operates mobile sports betting in 27 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, while iGaming is available in five states and its Canadian business reaches provinces representing about 51% of the country’s population. Featured image: DraftKings

item.title: FanDuel pays Iowa $95K penalty after offering prohibited sports betting markets
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 5.10
FanDuel will pay Iowa regulators $95,000 after acknowledging that its sportsbook offered wagers the state had not approved. The Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission approved the stipulated agreement with Betfair Interactive US LLC, FanDuel Sportsbook’s operator. The case covers two compliance violations. During the period involved, Betfair held licenses for retail sports betting at Diamond Jo Dubuque and Diamond Jo Worth while also running FanDuel’s licensed online sportsbook in Iowa. FanDuel faces mounting scrutiny over Iowa betting compliance The larger penalty arose from wagers on the Philippines-based Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League. FanDuel told regulators on May 7, 2025, that it had offered MPBL betting from June 4, 2024, through April 2, 2025. Iowa permits wagering on international professional basketball leagues only when they are their country’s top tier and are sanctioned or recognized by FIBA. The MPBL did not qualify. Customers made 21,638 straight, parlay and round-robin bets containing MPBL selections, producing $1,189,640.93 in handle and an initial FanDuel profit of $60,692.19. FanDuel later reviewed its basketball offerings and strengthened its process for checking international leagues. The company refunded affected Iowa customers’ net losses while leaving winning payouts intact. On July 9, 2025, FanDuel returned $154,898.99 to 1,665 customers and adjusted its July revenue filing by negative $60,110.03. A separate commission review on July 8, 2025, found FanDuel’s Iowa retail sportsbooks had taken wagers involving yellow and red cards in international soccer. Iowa prohibits proposition bets tied to officiating decisions, including soccer cards. FanDuel pulled those markets and began changing its filtering process. They had not appeared on its Iowa mobile sportsbook. Regulators identified one affected $134.58 parlay. Because FanDuel could not identify the bettor, it surrendered $44.86 through Iowa’s unclaimed-property process. FanDuel stopped operating Iowa retail sportsbooks on April 15, 2026. The latest action follows a separate $125,000 Iowa penalty reported in July 2025 covering five counts involving unauthorized wagers and responsible-gambling requirements. Commission official Daryle Olsen said at that hearing: “Five counts within a very short period of time is just too much, you know, and so I know they’re dealing with a big volume. I believe FanDuel is our number two operator in the state. But we just expect more. “I think in fairness, the Commission has to look at how we treat our out-of-state operators versus our brick-and-mortar casinos, because we need to be consistent, and that’s all we’re trying to do. We expect more. “I think our job is to tell them what we expect, lay out the concerns, and then hopefully they go back and fix it, and we don’t have to deal with this again.” FanDuel spokesperson Ben Roth said then: “We take responsibility for the matters represented in the settlement before the Commission today and understand that we did not meet the high standard that we hold for ourselves. “In response to the issues before you today, FanDuel has worked to remediate the various root causes through a combination of manual remediation efforts. “That includes increased training, more detailed checklists and runbooks for the deployment of content, and of course, automation wherever possible to avoid the potential for manual error. “FanDuel has addressed each issue by ensuring that no impacted customer has been adversely affected by these issues, and FanDuel has disgorged itself of any resulting revenue as a result of these.” Under the new settlement, Betfair accepted a $50,000 penalty for the basketball violation and $45,000 for the soccer markets. The money goes to Iowa’s general fund. Betfair CFO David Jennings signed the agreement July 24, 2026, and commission Chair Amy Burkhart approved it July 27. Featured image: Canva

item.title: Tabcorp agrees $189M BetMakers takeover to accelerate global wagering technology
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.69
Tabcorp is moving to buy wagering technology provider BetMakers Technology Group in a deal with an enterprise value of about A$267 million ($189 million), which is said to be one of its biggest technology investments as the betting company pushes to modernize its operations and strengthen its international business-to-business offering. The companies have signed a binding scheme implementation deed under which Australia’s largest gambling firm will acquire all issued BetMakers shares through a scheme of arrangement. The offer values BetMakers at A$0.24 a share, placing the company’s fully diluted equity value at about A$283 million and its enterprise value at roughly A$267 million. The proposed price represents premiums of about 41%, 42% and 37% over BetMakers’ one-month, three-month and six-month volume-weighted average share prices, respectively, as of August 7. Tabcorp said bringing BetMakers into the business would help speed its transition to a cloud-based wagering technology platform. The company also expects lower technology costs, reduced capital spending and faster development and rollout of new wagering products. “The acquisition of BetMakers will accelerate our strategy across multiple areas. BetMakers has undergone a significant transformation over the past two years and built impressive wagering technology and a talented team,” Tabcorp Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer Gillon McLachlan said in a statement. “Accessing those advantages will uplift our own tech capability and fast track our product ambitions, particularly for our unique media and tote offering. Combining BetMakers’ business with our rights, content and customer relationships creates a differentiated offering that will unlock growth and deliver attractive financial returns. “Tabcorp is midway through its strategic transformation, with strong foundations established, and this acquisition provides us with an excellent opportunity to accelerate our ambitions.” Tabcorp bets on technology-led transformation with BetMakers takeover Tabcorp plans to pay the cash component using existing cash reserves and available debt facilities. BetMakers investors can choose to receive part of their consideration in newly issued Tabcorp shares, although stock will account for no more than 25% of the total consideration. The shares will be priced at the greater of A$1.00 each or Tabcorp’s five-day volume-weighted average price before the scheme record date. The company expects A$30 million in annual pre-tax operating cost savings by the end of its second year of ownership, with efficiencies coming from technology infrastructure, applications, contracts and support functions. Tabcorp also expects the transaction to become earnings per share accretive from the second year, with double-digit EPS accretion from year three. BetMakers would expand Tabcorp’s international B2B portfolio by adding wagering technology, racing data, media services, tote hosting, commingling and integrity services. “Having spent time with the Tabcorp team, it is clear we share a common purpose: to build a market-leading global wagering and media business,” BetMakers Chief Executive Officer, Jake Henson said. “Bringing together Tabcorp’s rights, content and relationships with BetMakers’ platforms, data and B2B wagering services will create a more complete and compelling global offering for our customers, and an exciting future for our people.” The acquisition comes as Tabcorp faces increased regulatory scrutiny. In July, Australia’s communications regulator fined the company more than A$2.7 million after investigations found widespread telemarketing and spam law breaches involving customers who had opted out of marketing. Tabcorp has also recently faced regulatory action over gambling compliance issues and has been drawn into wider parliamentary scrutiny of Australia’s wagering industry. BetMakers’ board has unanimously recommended the deal, which remains subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals, with completion targeted during the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Featured image: Tabcorp / Canva

item.title: The Istanbul Equation: Understanding the Hair Transplant Phenomenon in Turkey
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 5.45
In the arrivals hall of Istanbul Airport, it has become an unremarkable sight: men with heads wrapped in gauze, sometimes dotted with fresh blood, navigating their way to hotel shuttles. Far from being victims of an accident, they are medical tourists, part of a phenomenon that has cemented Turkey’s position as the global epicentre of hair restoration. With an industry generating an estimated US$1 billion annually and attracting over 500,000 medical tourists in the first half of 2022 alone, Istanbul’s rise to prominence is a story of economics, marketing, and a fundamental human desire to restore a youthful appearance. The primary driver of this trend is financial. The cost of a hair transplant in Turkey is remarkably lower than in Western Europe or the United States. In the UK, for instance, a single procedure can cost between £3,500 and £5,000, with a full course potentially exceeding £14,000. In contrast, a comparable package in Turkey often falls between €1,500 and €2,500, frequently including hotel accommodation, transportation, and even sightseeing tours. The devaluation of the Turkish Lira has only sharpened this price differential, making the country a highly competitive and cost-effective destination. For many, the savings justify the journey. As Servet Terziler, head of the Turkish Health Tourism Association, pointed out, hair loss treatments in Türkiye typically cost between €3,000 and €7,000, whereas in Europe, they can run from €8,000 to €10,000. However, low cost in a booming market often comes with a caveat. The industry is a complex landscape of high-volume clinics, often labelled "hair mills," and more established practices. An academic review published in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery described a regulatory environment that is permissive and lacks standardization, creating what it termed a "data black hole" regarding safety and complication rates. This variability poses significant risks for international patients who may struggle to verify the credentials and experience of the clinic and the technicians performing the surgery. Critics frequently point to the expanded role of unsupervised technicians performing the majority of the work, as well as "bait and switch" tactics where the doctor seen in consultations is not the one present during surgery. These concerns are magnified by aggressive digital marketing that often downplays potential complications, leaving patients vulnerable. Among the numerous clinics in Istanbul, Dr. Serkan Aygin’s clinic has garnered significant attention. Dr. Serkan Aygin graduated from Istanbul University's Çapa Faculty of Medicine and has been specializing in hair loss treatments since 1996. His clinic, established in 1996, employs a team of 51 to 200 people and positions itself as a specialist in hair restoration. The clinic's prominence is partly due to its strong digital presence and public endorsements. Notably, journalist Spencer Macnaughton documented his experience at the clinic for Business Insider, and Mexican YouTuber Victor Sales discovered the clinic through ChatGPT, a testament to its visibility in the modern, digital-first landscape of medical tourism. Such endorsements highlight a broader trend: many patients are drawn to clinics with established international reputations and clear patient journeys. When considering a transplant, potential patients are advised to look beyond price and evaluate the clinic's history, the experience of the medical team, and the clarity of their post-operative care plan. Turkey’s reign as the "hair transplant capital" is built on a powerful value proposition. For patients from high-cost Western nations, Istanbul offers a fast and affordable solution. Yet, the allure of the deal must be balanced against the inherent risks of medical tourism—a lack of regulatory oversight, variable quality of care, and a challenging legal framework if complications arise. For a successful outcome, patients need to move beyond price sensitivity and conduct thorough due diligence. Choosing an established clinic like Dr. Serkan Aygin’s, which has been operating for over two decades and has a track record of working with international patients, may offer a sense of security. However, the onus is always on the patient to ask the hard questions and ensure the chosen clinic prioritizes safety, transparency, and medical ethics. The journey to a new head of hair is significant, and the decision of where to undergo the procedure is as crucial as the procedure itself.

item.title: Review: Therm-a-Rest Parsec 20 Down Sleeping Bag
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 5.14
The Therm-a-Rest Parsec 20 is a high-quality sleeping bag filled with 900-fill hydrophobic duck down, ideal for three-season use. Its box-baffled construction keeps the down evenly distributed in individual pockets, preventing shifting, eliminating cold spots, and preserving maximum loft for consistent warmth. Combining sustainability, comfort, and packability, this bag offers outstanding performance at a competitive price.
- Weight: 1 lb 13 oz (820 g) – we measured 1 lb 14.4 o (862 g) - Packed Dimensions: 7 x 10.5 in (18 x 27 cm) - Insulation: 900-fill PFAS-Free Hydrophobic Duck Down, RDS-certified - Fill Weight: 17 oz (490 g) - Construction: Box Baffles - User Fit Length: 72 in (183 cm) - Bag Length: 80 in (203 cm) - Girth (Shoulder / Hip / Footbox): 62 / 57 / 46 in (157 / 145 / 117 cm) - EN Comfort Rating: 29 °F (-1 °C) - EN Limit Rating: 18 °F (-8 °C) - Shell Fabric: 100% Recycled 20D Nylon Ripstop with DWR finish - Lining: 20D Nylon Ripstop - Zipper: Left side - Compression Sack: Included Materials The Parsec 20 has a comfortable 20-denier nylon ripstop fabric for both the shell and lining. This fabric is lightweight yet durable, offering resistance to wear and tear while maintaining a soft hand feel. The durable water repellent (DWR) finish enhances resistance to moisture, helping the down insulation maintain loft even in damp conditions and dry faster. The insulation is premium 900-fill power hydrophobic duck down treated without PFAS chemicals, reducing environmental impact and potential health concerns. Duck down is just as warm as goose down with the same fill power rating, but it's less expensive for manufacturers to source, which is why the Parsec is more reasonably priced than other options. The down is also RDS-certified, meaning it comes from waterfowl that were raised and harvested humanely. With a generous fill weight of 17 oz (490 g), the insulation provides ample warmth for three-season use. Warmth and Temperature Ratings The Parsec 20 is rated with an EN Comfort temperature of 29 °F (-1 °C) and an EN Limit rating of 18 °F (-8 °C). This means most campers, including women and those of smaller stature, will feel comfortable at just above freezing temperatures, while the limit rating indicates the lowest temperature at which a larger person or your average man might be safe without additional insulation. To their credit, Therm-a-Rest was one of the main proponents of industry-wide temperature-rating standards testing for sleeping bags, but given that this bag is marketed as a unisex bag, I think it'd be more transparent if it were named the Parsec 30 rather than the Parsec 20. With 80 inches of length, a shoulder girth of 62 inches, and a footbox girth of 46 inches, the Parsec's dimensions allow for comfortable movement inside the bag without feeling overly snug. However, smaller individuals, including women, may feel colder because more body heat will be required to “heat the bag up” once it's zipped closed. Design Features and Comfort The Parsec’s design prioritizes warmth retention and comfort. The sleeping bag has a three-fourths length left-hand zipper with a YKK antisnag zipper and a second zipper slider so you can vent warmth on warm nights. The zipper is backed by a beefy draft tube full of down insulation to prevent cold air from leaking through the zipper teeth and has a zipper garage and snap at the top. This offloads pressure on the zipper and also lets you unzip it from the top to vent excess warmth. Between the top zipper and the bottom zipper slider, the venting options on the Parsec 20 are really great. The bag’s hood is cinchable to trap heat around the head effectively, an essential feature for maintaining warmth during cold nights. It has a 360-degree draft collar that surrounds the upper part of your chest and neck, preventing warm air from escaping when you wiggle at night. One of the distinctive features of the Parsec is its baffled insulated footbox, designed with extra down insulation to concentrate heat around your toes, a common area of heat loss. This ergonomic feature adds noticeable comfort in cool conditions. Finally, you’ll find a small stash pocket inside the sleeping bag that is ideal for storing small essentials like a headlamp or phone within easy reach. Packability and Weight At 1 lb 13 oz | 820 g (our sample was 1.4 ounces heavier), the Parsec 20 is impressively lightweight for a down sleeping bag with such generous insulation and interior room. It compresses down to a compact 7 x 10.5 inches (18 x 27 cm) in its included compression sack, making it a great choice for backpackers who want to minimize pack volume and use a smaller, lighter-weight backpack. While it’s not the absolute lightest bag in its class, the Parsec balances weight with durability and comfort features that justify the slight trade-off. Comparable ultralight 15 and 20-degree sleeping bags | Make / Model | Weight | Down Fill Power | Price (USD) | |---|---|---|---| | Hyperlite Mtn Gear 20-Degree | 26.52 oz | 1000 | $650 | | Western Mountaineering Ultralight 20 | 29 oz | 850 | $680 | | Western Mountaineerng Alpinlite 20 | 33 oz | 850 | $767 | | Rab Mythic 20 | 26.8 oz | 900 | $625 | | Sea-to-Summit Spark 15 | 25.7 oz | 850 | $549 | | Mountain Hardwear Phantom 15 | 32.6 oz | 800 | $680 | | Thermarest Parsec 20 | 29 oz | 900 | $470 | | REI Magma 15 | 35.6 oz | 850 | $399 | | Feathered Friends Swallow UL 20 | 26.6 oz | 950 | $659 | Recommendation The Therm-a-Rest Parsec 20 is a versatile and well-crafted sleeping bag ideal for three-season use. Its 900-fill hydrophobic duck down provides excellent warmth and loft retention, while the box-baffled construction prevents shifting and cold spots. With features like an insulated draft-tube zipper, cinchable hood, and extra-insulated foot box, it delivers consistent comfort throughout the night. The use of recycled nylon ripstop fabric with a durable water repellent finish enhances durability and moisture resistance without adding weight, making it both practical and environmentally friendly. While not the lightest option in its category, the Parsec 20 strikes a strong balance between warmth, comfort, and sustainability. Its generous internal dimensions offer ample space without sacrificing heat retention, although smaller individuals may need to consider fit carefully. The temperature ratings suit typical spring-to-fall camping conditions just above freezing, making it a reliable choice for most three-season outings. Disclosure: Therm-a-Rest donated a sleeping bag for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: Taiwan 'Throttles' Mobile Internet For First Time During Annual War Games
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 5.64
Taiwan deliberately throttled mobile internet across the Taichung area during its annual Han Kuang war games, "simulating communication disruption in the event of a Chinese attack or natural disaster," reports Reuters. The drill accompanied air-raid exercises and military rehearsals aimed at defending strategically important areas such as the Penghu Islands. From the report: Democratically governed Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory, has long lived with the threat of a Chinese invasion and holds air raid drills along with its war games every year, clearing people from the streets for 30 minutes. During the internet "throttling" drill, centered on Monday on the major central metropolis of Taichung, only basic mobile phone services worked, though other functions including ATMs, traffic signals, landlines and fixed internet services were not affected.
Air raid sirens rang out in Taichung "and people cleared the streets from 2:30 p.m. (0630 GMT) as the government sent simultaneous text messages in Chinese and English telling mobile phone users of "simulated air attacks on communication infrastructure." The government had widely flagged the drill ahead of time, including posting details on social media, and most people Reuters spoke to at the Taichung train station were prepared. [...] The same exercise will be repeated on Thursday in northern Taiwan, including the capital Taipei.

item.title: A Zoom Screen-Sharing Bug Let Anyone Take Over Other Devices On a Call
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 5.60
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: As AI models gain advanced capabilities to find vulnerabilities in software, develop ways to exploit them, and even carry out autonomous hacking sprees, researchers offered a sobering new example on Tuesday, disclosing vulnerabilities in the video conferencing platform Zoom that could have been exploited to take over targets' devices. Anyone on a call that involved screen sharing, whether participants or the host, would have been vulnerable to a silent attack that could be carried out with no indication and no interaction from the victim.
Researchers from the digital defense firm A Security say thebugwas discovered in early June using publicly available AI models, and that it took fewer than 20 prompts to uncover the vulnerabilities and create a working attack. Zoom issued a security advisory on Tuesday, including details about fixes the company has already begun rolling out to address the flaws, which affected devices running all operating systems that Zoom supports -- Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android.
The vulnerabilities were specifically in the protocol used to facilitate real-time annotation during screen sharing. The researchers say that their AI bug hunting systems specifically delved into this component because, like human bug hunters, they have been trained that convoluted and obscure functions often contain overlooked vulnerabilities. This is particularly true with proprietary, closed-source software. An established company like Zoom presumably does extensive code review and vetting on all components and functions, but without the benefit of public, open review, esoteric yet complex features like annotation are more likely to contain mistakes. The bugs are now patched, with Zoom issuing both server and client-side fixes—or patches for both Zoom's own servers and the applications that run on customer devices. But the researchers emphasize that it was alarming to contemplate bugs that could have been exploited to take over a target device simply by getting someone onto a Zoom call. "What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous is the democratization of these capabilities -- the barrier to entry is dropping rapidly," A Security cofounder Omer Gull told WIRED ahead of the disclosure. "Before it would have taken a team of five people maybe six months with a lot of refining and iteration to find this. Now people can reach the same results with under 20 prompts. And Zoom is an important type of target because people assume trust when using it. They don't see it as a threat."

item.title: Taxi Drivers Rarely Die of Alzheimer's
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 5.47
An anonymous reader shares a report from The Conversation, written by Hatim Sharif, a civil and environmental engineer who has "spent more than two decades staring at maps" and spatial data. Sharif finds one connection especially fascinating: the link between spatial reasoning and why taxi drivers seem to have lower rates of Alzheimer's. From the report: Taxi and ambulance drivers are less likely than workers in almost any other job to die of Alzheimer's disease. That was the surprising result of a 2024 study examining the death certificates of nearly 9 million people in the U.S. [...] Of the 9 million death certificates from January 2020 to December 2022 that researchers examined, taxi and ambulance drivers had the lowest risk of dying from Alzheimer's disease out of 443 occupations. After adjusting for age, sex, race, ethnicity and education, roughly 1 in 100 taxi and ambulance drivers died of Alzheimer's, compared with 1 in 60 people overall. This pattern did not extend to other driving jobs.
The researchers concluded that the key to reducing the risk of Alzheimer's was not driving itself but continuous real-time navigation: the constant work of locating yourself in space, tracking a destination and updating a mental map as conditions change. Drivers whose jobs relied on fixed or predetermined routes, like bus drivers and aircraft pilots, didn't seem to experience a similar advantage. Researchers believe the association between navigation-heavy work and lower Alzheimer's risk centers on the hippocampus, a part of the brain that governs memory and spatial navigation. It's one of the first brain regions that Alzheimer's damages: Problems with spatial navigation and orientation are among the earliest signs of the disease, sometimes surfacing before obvious memory loss.
In one landmark 2000 study, neuroscientists compared the brains of licensed London taxi drivers with those of people who did not drive cabs. Their findings provided the first evidence via structural imaging that regions of the adult brain can measurably change under sustained navigational demand. To earn a license, London cabbies must memorize more than 25,000 streets within a 6-mile radius of Charing Cross, a challenge known as "The Knowledge" that takes three to four years.
The researchers found that London taxi drivers had measurably more gray matter in the posterior hippocampus, a brain area tied to storing large-scale spatial maps. That volume tracked with experience: The longer someone had driven, the larger that part of the brain. The change was built through practice, not inherited. While people who are good at navigation might gravitate to this kind of job, the job itself does have an impact on the brain. Together, these two studies make a coherent case: Work that intensively exercises the hippocampus may reshape it, and that reshaping may protect against one of the most feared diseases of aging.

Do they die earlier, of stress? (Score:2) Or are they more mentally fit due to more social interactions and navigating a car? Any details on that? Re: (Score:3) Re:Do they die earlier, of stress? (Score:5, Informative) Main outcomes measures Among 443 occupations studied, percentage of deaths attributed to Alzheimer’s disease for taxi drivers and ambulance drivers and each of the remaining 441 occupations, adjusting for age at death and other sociodemographic factors. We then used multivariable logistic regression at the individual level to estimate risk adjusted percentages of deaths from Alzheimer’s disease for each occupation, adjusting for age at death (indicator variables for each year of age), sex (male or female), race and ethnic group (black, white, Hispanic, Asian or Pacific Islander, other race), and educational attainment (indicator variables for 8th grade, 9-12th grade, high school, college, master’s or doctorate). Mortality odds ratios from the multivariable model were also ranked from lowest to highest across occupations to facilitate identification of occupations with the lowest risk of death from Alzheimer’s disease; chief executive (occupation code: 0010) was arbitrarily chosen as the reference group in regression models. We performed four sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our comparisons... Would you look at that, Slashdot skeptic! From TFOriginalScientificArticle: "Additionally, death certificates included a field for reported usual occupation (the occupation in which the decedent spent most of their working life), generally completed by a funeral director with help from the decedent’s informant." How do they measure occupation [Re:Do they die...] (Score:3) It's a good question. Not enough information here. Alzheimer's disease starts slow, and progresses incrementally for years. My first hypothesis would be that taxi drivers in the early stages of Alzheimer's become unable to drive effectively, and hence leave the profession years before they are diagnosed with Alzheimer's; hence their death certificates don't list "taxi driver" as their occupation. But the observation that taxi drivers die an average of ten years earlier than other occupations also makes the ex Re: How do they measure occupation [Re:Do they die (Score:2) Very early symptoms could discourage the job well before obvious symptoms and inability surface. But I'll taking dying 10 years prior as a strong hint that driving cabs might not be a good choice. (There are some other aspects of cab driving, varying substantially over where you do it that should also be considered. It's not the same job in many respects in NY vs Toronto or LA.) C != C (Score:2) It could be a case of confusing correlation with causation. People who are easily confused and have trouble paying attention to the road will choose other professions. Re: (Score:2) It could be a case of confusing correlation with causation. People who are easily confused and have trouble paying attention to the road will choose other professions. Also, this is about the risk of dying from Alzheimer's. Depending on when we're talking about, it could be that they die from something else first, like secondhand smoke. Re: (Score:2) That's not a "could be". They *did* report that. And adjusted the statistics to handle that effect. There's a reasonable argument that "10 years earlier" is hard to adjust for", though. Re: (Score:2) Alzheimer's disease is not related to people who have trouble paying attention or who are "easily confused". Alzheimer's is not a personality flaw that somehow leads to dementia, it is a neurological condition that is physically visible in brain tissue. Re: (Score:2) Or are they less physically fit and dies from other diseases before Alzheimer's becomes an issue? Re: (Score:2) What about navigating PornHub? (Score:5, Funny) Just asking for a friend. fuck you google (Score:2) not content with stealing my data, now you're going to lure me with your amazing navigation and give me Alzheimers??? Can people with early alzheimers drive taxy? (Score:2) Sure, the study shows a connection. Or it kills them undiagnosed (Score:2, Funny) Re:Or it kills them undiagnosed (Score:5, Informative) Re: (Score:1) Perhaps taxi and ambulance drivers just get killed on the job in the early stages of the disease, causing the death to be attributed to anther cause? Or perhaps the study has controlled for that, as it clearly explains in the freely accessible text. Or perhaps the way they controlled for that was inadequate. If even ONE PERCENT of the deaths attributed to other causes was actually due to Alzheimers, that would swamp the observed effect. Can they say for sure that their method of controlling for other effects is better than 99% effective? Re: (Score:2) They die more often (and at a younger age) from gunshot wounds and traffic accidents. I kid, I kid... Re:Or it kills them undiagnosed (Score:4, Interesting) Re: (Score:2, Troll) I'm always baffled by what's going through your head, when someone like you posts something like this. Normally I don't bother following up, but this time, sure, why not. Several professional researchers spent months or years on this research. Several other professional researchers evaluated the results and concluded that they held together and convincingly supported their conclusions. And now you looked at the headline of an article quoting another article quoting the paper, spent fifteen seconds thinking a Re: (Score:2) Also I don't understand jokes either. Nope, the fellow doubled down in a reply. Anyways, you're not the person I was asking, but thanks for... that. Re: Or it kills them undiagnosed (Score:2) Many studies draw bullshit conclusions from inadequate data and are later invalidated, so skepticism is warranted. In this case there are numerous strong confounding factors which it really doesn't sound like they investigated, let alone addressed Re: Or it kills them undiagnosed (Score:2) Perhaps so. That's not what the person I was responding to was talking about, and it's not what I'm talking about. I tried to resist, but I am weak (Score:2) "Taxi Drivers Rarely Die of Alzheimer's" "It's usually the illegal left turns what does for 'em, guvnor!" So FSD will dumb me down... (Score:1) What about engineers? (Score:2) And I don't mean software developers but actual engineers that work with CAD and blueprints. I wonder whether that counts too. Have we compared? (Score:2) Too bad we killed off most of the taxi drivers (Score:3) Re: Too bad we killed off most of the taxi drivers (Score:2) Soft life, soft brain? It's interesting that a population with less cognitive load than ever before suffered conspicuously from memory degradation. I wonder if the findings generalize to "navigation" understood more broadly. For example, writers "navigate" through stories, maintaining a mental map of social relationships, plot points, and sometimes fictional geography. There are man Re: (Score:2) The rise of Alzheimer's disease in the late 20th century, at least in the U.S., coincided with the highest standard of living ever achieved by humans. It also coincides with an improved definition of Alzheimer's, and more effective detection and diagnosis. Re: (Score:2) This is what I was thinking. Might be interesting to compare the rates of people who hike frequently, or mountain bike (both require memorizing trail systems, somewhat similar to our species previous lifestyles.) Even FPS games like Doom might trigger this. I'm not super close with a lot of riders, but I ha Re: Soft life, soft brain? (Score:2) Re: Soft life, soft brain? item.title: Cyber Vulnerability Sweep Picks Up Royal Navy Drones Sending Data To China
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 5.05
A routine security assessment found that cameras aboard Royal Navy Kraken unmanned surface vessels were sending "heartbeat" signals to an IP address in China. "A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally," said a Ministry of Defense spokesperson. "Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment." The Register reports: According to reports, the talkative components were cameras sourced by Kraken from a third-party supplier. The incident raises questions about supply chains, audits, and cybersecurity in the British armed forces. The spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is national security, and we take the security of our equipment, networks, and data extremely seriously."
Raises questions? (Score:5, Insightful) Raises questions? No, boys and girls — who slept through the journalist lecturer's implorations against cliches — it does not raise questions. It provides clear and obvious answers... Re: (Score:3) It also provides a much needed laugh. Re: (Score:1) And then you think about Putin (and Trump and Greenland) and that laugh should die a pretty fast death Re: (Score:2) yup made me laugh Re: (Score:3) we take the security of our equipment, networks, and data extremely seriously which, as anyone who has been in IT for more than about ten minutes, knows is really: we really got caught with our pants down on this one Re: (Score:2) The question it raise is: why are we so incompetent? I think the West should stop preparing for war when it's questionable we could win one ever again. Re: (Score:1) The question it raise is: why are we so incompetent? This one is simple: Greedism and arrogance and a general disdain for actual experts. Because they tell you limits on what can be done and make you put in sound safety and security. Business graduates and politicians cannot stand that. And hence this decay. Also note that the largest NATO military power is now a Kakistocracy. It is really simple: Being good at something requires genuine humility, altruism and a strong connection to actual reality. These qualities are in short supply in the west these days. Al Re: (Score:1) I wouldn't base the ability to win a war on the Epstein-Iran war. If you put a bunch of dingbats in charge of powerful military, they can still screw it up. Re: (Score:2) it does not raise questions. It provides clear and obvious answers... Indeed, it does. About as clear as they can get. This is a failure on the side of procurement that could not be any more extreme. That there was not even an attack (and hence the camera vendor did not try to hide anything) makes this failure a lot worse. Gross insecurity by abject stupidity. Not that the UK Navy has a monopoly on that in any way. A lot of modern engineering is "experts only", on the evaluation side as well. If you do not have or use these experts, things will go sideways in surprising and e They Worry Too Much (Score:2) They need to stop worrying about this. Juts load Deep Seek into your autonomous marine drones and let 'er rip. Re: (Score:1) They need to stop worrying about this. Juts load Deep Seek into your autonomous marine drones and let 'er rip. DeepSeek is just a bag of weights. It does not phone home. Bah. (Score:2) It's just ET trying to phone home. Probably dialed the wrong number. Re: (Score:2) Back to China? Isn't that the "Wong" number then? But why did they have access to the Internet?! (Score:2) Re:But why did they have access to the Internet?! (Score:5, Insightful) Re: (Score:3) No, this is exceptionally serious. Because it means there is uncontrolled information flow to the world in a combat system. That there apparently is no attack in this case and it is only extremely gross negligence is besides the point. Re: (Score:2) Probably because that is how they are sending data and receiving instructions. This sounds a lot more serious than they are trying to make it. Potentially it means that an enemy (China) could locate your "stealthy" drones and destroy or mislead them. I'm sorry, your stealthy unmanned drone whose sketchily sourced webcam expects a wireless connection to the whole internet so that it can receive instructions to compromise the bespoke internal network This probably isn't the supply chain attack you're making it out to be, this is stuff you should expect and check for when sourcing components for the drone you're building in your garage, like the ea Re: (Score:2) My only explanation is that somebody classified these as dumb munitions and no IT security tests, evaluations, requirements, etc. were ever done. I.e. terminally incapable bureaucracy at work. Re: (Score:2) Did they have internet access? TFA isn't clear, but it could be that they were on a VPN connected to MoD systems and the pings just bounced off the firewall. Sounds like the contractor just used off-the-shelf cameras and they do periodic checks for firmware updates or cloud storage or something. No conspiracy, just a failure to properly specify and then audit the hardware. Re:But why did they have access to the Internet?! (Score:5, Interesting) Does it matter though? (Score:3) This sort of "phoning home" is common, not just in Chinese products, and no evidence of malicious intent. And its not like these systems are connected to the internet. Re: (Score:2) Re: (Score:2) overrated? Re:Does it matter though? (Score:5, Informative) You can piggy back on the civilian infrastructure without ever exposing devices - just require all devices to access anything beyond the local network via a specific router, which pushes all traffic over a VPN, and nothing goes out over the naked internet as its all dropped if its not going over the VPN. Then all you need to ensure are thoroughly audted and hardened are those routers - everything else cant hit the internet. Re: (Score:2) Re: (Score:2) 50+ percent of your bases belong to us? Re:Does it matter though? (Score:5, Insightful) It actually does. It does a few things. ( If the heart beats actually make it back to China. ) They would likely make it back since the devices would likely have redundant connection mechanisms. A lot of drones use starlink now and this is effectively public. The US has an early starshield capability. Not sure if this is shared with friendlies yet. 1. The device is alive. Meaning turned on and active. Meaning it is in use for an operation or training. 2. It's ping or latency time can be used to build a heat map of likely world wide locations. This used to be tricky not so much any more. 3. It's giving away at least part of the network path to the device. So basically it can tells China with this data what the theatre of operations likely is. Which destroys the element of surprise. If a bunch of English drones all of a sudden start showing up around Taiwan for example it's tells China a lot. This could and would compromise operational security and potentially lives. It would also raise tension levels between nations. If enough drones are doing the same thing then the data quality will improve. And at no time does the drone have to be hacked. No attempt to communicate with the drone needed. The simple fact that a phone home command is sent is enough to compromise safety. So it does matter. Re: (Score:2) But, if we (well, the Royal Navy) can get China to think the UK's drones will ping them, we can tie them in knots by pinging like crazy from Taiwan. Re: (Score:2) You can bet the UK is making sure that they can't get on the public net now. I'm fairly sure whether the pings got through or not would be a state secret. Now there are a lot of ways to implement a ping of sorts. - Advanced ones use an API to send back some telemetry. This could literally be anything in the payload. This is by far the most dangerous. - A subset would be some sort of REST API on a web service. This has a lot of advantages as you can do geo location tricks to place listeners So no firewalling? And no testing? (Score:2) Are these people bloody amateurs? Re: (Score:2) Pretty much. Apparently they mostly make sonars. Prior to the drone sales, which don't even show up on their web page, they were crowing about a tremendous $13 million in annual sales. https://www.krakenrobotics.com... [krakenrobotics.com] Re: (Score:2) Incredible. Re: (Score:2) At least someone realized that it would be a good idea to scan outgoing traffic. One hopes that the internal reaction amongst the leadership was more than just, "bloody hell." Re: (Score:2) Indeed. And there probably was some suspicion that things might be really fucked or this test (well, wireshark on a connection and somebody with a clue on the keyboard) would probably not have been done. Not making things is a strategic vulnerability (Score:5, Insightful) Seeing as it puts you at the mercy of the people who make your stuff for you. History, both recent and not so recent, repeats this lesson again and again. Re: (Score:2) No. Not even remotely. Not verifying the properties of what you buy is a really bad vulnerability. There is no possibility to make everything yourself. That ship has sailed a long time ago. For example, consider ASML. There is no other manufacturer of even remotely comparable equipment. And these machines need always active network connections home or they stop working. Even if the US throws everything it has at the problem, they are probably 20 years away to making a replacement, maybe longer. For other thi Re: (Score:2) Camera on a drone, but network? (Score:2) Re: (Score:2) It's almost certainly the latter. Manufacturer's engineers almost certainly said, "We need a camera capable of X, Y, and Z", and Purchasing found one in a catalog that checked off the boxes for a reasonable (or cheap) price. I'm fairly sure that most Western military robots are put together that way, after all profit is far more important than security. Re: (Score:2) i am sure some one consulted the approved vendor list Re: (Score:2) It actually makes some sense. Because it then could be operated detached from other components, in a low power mode "timed snapshot mode picture every And not to forget movement/feature detection by embeded algorithms, which is often found in these types of cameras. Those cameras often have - openly or hidden - GPIO interfaces, which then could be used to "re-energize" the whole system in a predefined event. low power mode -> enhanced Re: (Score:2) Why does a camera on a drone even has TCP/IP? Drones use off-the shelf components. But what else would you expect? CANBUS (like in your car) is used in tanks, but can it take video bandwidth? Many modern combat systems use tcp/ip for moving large amounts of data. Re: (Score:2) Because the camera comes by default with it. I have a few security cameras for $3 each, size of 2EUR coin, just a bit thicker, which open their own WLAN. You connect with an app via Wifi with them, and configure them and tell them into which WLAN they should connect. The camera they use is probably similar. Is connected with the ship computer via Ethernet and the boat itself connects via starling or similar to the home base. With "standard radio technology" you do not have the bandwidth to reasonable transmit v Re: (Score:2) Re: (Score:2) Or more to the point, why on the open internet? Put it on 10/8 or unallocated IPv6 somewhere and VPN it through the public internet if they must. That way, if the camera tries to phone home, it won't find a router willing to complete that call. Re: (Score:2) because everything is better on the cloud, how else will you manage these devices. Re: (Score:2) It's still a cloud, just one behind a military firewall. Re: (Score:2) This will be a camera module with an ethernet port. And TCP/IP on that because it is the only viable general networking standard. Re: (Score:2) Or was it just lazy Lego stick together by default manual, no brain participating? Well let's think about the brain for a moment. How do you get data from a to b? Using some protocol. What is TCP/IP? A protocol. As such the brain would very much look at two components, ask what protocol they both speak, and then use said protocol. There's no reason TCP/IP can't be used short distances point to point. In fact many industrial devices are shipped precisely in this way largely because virtually all underlying OSes have a fully functioning TCP/IP stack present and ready to use without having to Re: (Score:2) It was is all lazy lego stick together. Which I am not even sure is wrong entirely except for the lazy part. I have looks a number of larger drone systems land, sea, and air. The state of the art is mostly off the self components, especially where it comes to scientific equipment and sensors because redesign of that stuff would blow the budget out and modification would risk function and invalidation of a tested tool. So what you get is a drone with an Ethernet lan aboard along with the usual NAT router and Re: (Score:2) pervert glasses (Score:2) China finds that Meta Pervert Glasses send all data to IP addresses in the US, no matter who wears them or where. Re: (Score:2) made in china, so i doubt that is entirely true. Re: (Score:2) "IT Security is our highest priority!" (Score:2) Also, as seen here "We take IT security extremely serious!" and variations. That is a key-phrase that means "we have no (real) clue about IT security and we do not actually care that much". I have seen that one, for example, on the website of a major bank, 15 minutes before I found their online banking app did not even have basic security (no server certificate identity checks, a beginner's mistake, allows you to proxy the connection, which we did). Microsoft likes to use it whenever they have screwed up ex The bright side (Score:2) At least they're competent enough to have noticed. marxist (Score:1) A global device has to use a Chinese IP (Score:2) Imagine you've built a device that needs to know whether or not to run in offline mode. So you put in a heartbeat ping to a reliable IP address. But what IP addresses are reliable on both sides of China's firewall? Chinese ones. If your device is going to work worldwide, Chinese IP addresses are your best bet.

item.title: A Data Breach At Shipping Giant Ceva Logistics Is Rippling Across Banks, Retailers, Steam Gamers, and Beyond
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 4.95
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Ceva Logistics, one of the world's largest shipping and logistics giants, has been hacked. Several companies that rely on Ceva for shipping their products to their customers say that their personal information was also stolen in the breach. The cyberattack on Ceva is affecting at least eight warehouses across Europe used for shipping goods across the continent, the company told TechCrunch. Industry news site FreightWaves reports that the hack began on July 29 and is causing shipping delays for many of the goods in affected warehouses.
Ceva is a France-headquartered shipping and logistics giant that companies around the world rely on to deliver their goods from their assembly lines to customer homes. The company, which brought in $18.3 billion in revenue in 2025, has over a thousand warehouses across the world. [...] The hack at Ceva also resulted in a data breach, affecting a large amount of personal information belonging to retail customers that Ceva relies on for delivering goods to people's home addresses. Several companies reported that hackers took their customers' names, home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses used to place their orders from Ceva's systems.
Dutch online retail giant Bol said on its website that hackers gained access to systems of its warehousing partner, Ceva, and warned that their customers' data may have been taken. Bol also said that it expects delays and some customer orders to be canceled as a result of the incident. De Bijenkorf, another Dutch luxury retailer, similarly confirmed order delays following the theft of its customers' data, per local media. Football club Ajax, banking giant ING, and eyeglass maker Ace & Tate also reported that customers' shipping information was affected. Video game giant Valve told customers that it learned on August 7 that data was taken from Ceva's systems, and alerted customers who recently bought its Steam hardware that they had personal information taken in the incident. Valve said in its note to customers, posted to Reddit, that Ceva stores their shipping and delivery information for 90 days following their order. So far, Ceva says the agency has received data breach reports from 10 organizations in relation to the incident.

ChatGPT, everything is permitted (Score:4, Funny) Can you please figure out a way to pay for yourself? Why was all that in one database? (Score:3, Insightful) No business role needs all that info. Why was all of that in one place to steal? Huh? (Score:3) No business role needs all that info. Why was all of that in one place to steal? Perhaps I'm missing something? Name, address, phone number, and email address doesn't sound like a lot of information to store in a single database. Frankly it's just the customer table in many much larger databases that I've seen. Every internet order I've placed required that information for the order. Re: Huh? (Score:2) But do you need those data items for every single client all at once? Why not (weak example to make point) one login for customers A through M and another for N through Z? If someone breaks security for a system, they should not ever be staring at a database of *everything*. Maybe divide customers by region? Or class of freight? It is insane to me that any user's login carries the ability to see all the data downloaded in this attack. Re: Huh? (Score:4, Informative) They're a logistics company. They take in products that are to be shipped to people. Likely they come in as the orders happen. So it's likely just a simple FIFO queue - someone from Steam buys a Steam Controller and their details get entered into the shipping database in FIFO order. As people work to package and ship product, that order will come up and whoever's the lucky person takes a steam controller, puts it in a box and slaps a label on it, then enters in the tracking information and tosses it on the shipping pile. It's likely not ordered by anything - other than maybe the order the orders came in as. If someone else orders a widget after the guy orders a steam controller, the next person then gets to pick the widget, pack it into a box and then move on. The database in question only contains orders up to 100 days old, so it's likely just the active database containing the orders that need to be sent out and orders that were sent out. Anyone fulfilling orders will need access to it so they can see what product needs to be packed and where to send it off to. It's not a database of "every single client". It's a database of orders that have been shipped out and less than 100 days old and orders yet to shipped out because either they are being held for supply, or they just haven't gotten around to handling the order yet. The 100 day history is so if there is a problem, it can be traced - if a product doesn't arrive, they can look at the order and figure out tracking. Or if there's a problem and it needs to be returned, it can be traced to the original shipment for RMA. As far as it looks, other databases weren't compromised, which can include inventory information - what stock is on hand and where it is in the warehouse, or their customer information (as in who buys their services). The only thing compromised was the active order table which likely has lots of access out of necessity as people fulfilling orders need to read the database to get the orders, and backend systems like Valve need the ability to read, add and delete order entries to see what order status is, the ability to add an order, and the ability to cancel a shipment that hasn't gone out yet. It looks like a perfectly reasonable way to segregate the business. They aren't storing your name, address, phone and email, it's just information that's needed to fulfill the order and any post-shipping issues that might arise. And it looks like that database was compromised Re: (Score:1) Maybe this info needs to be stored in some kind of encrypted escrow format. The database, instead of having an address, would have a blob that decrypts to the address in the shipper's system. And maybe not the full address, but only just enough information for routing - when the shipper picks it up, if its local they get the full address, if its across the country they just get enough to get the nearest distribution center, which has a key to decrypt the recipient's distribution center, and so on. at each s Re: (Score:2) Rather than mess with their shipping procedures (which they won't want to do), some sort of rate limiting on database access would prevent any user from dumping the database and exfiltrating it, without causing any noticeable delay. Re: (Score:2) Re: Why was all that in one database? (Score:2) What person needs all the addresses *at once*? Why is there not separation by class of freight or by region? Why isn't there some requirement to query multiple databases that would set off alarms that someone is touching so many parts? Re: (Score:2) What person needs all the addresses *at once*? Why is there not separation by class of freight or by region? Why isn't there some requirement to query multiple databases that would set off alarms that someone is touching so many parts? Person? No one. Businesses, every one. You need to store data to meet regulatory requirements. You need to store data to meet proof of service requirements. You need to store data to meet customs requirements. And TFS says 90 days so it very much sounds like they were storing the information for the limited amount of time possible. Why is there not separation by class of freight or by region? Thought experiment: You order something from Germany. The logistics company is responsible for picking it up in Germany, Road transfer to the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Banks, Retailers, Steam Gamers (Score:3) One of these things is not like the other One of these things just doesn't belong Can you tell me which thing is not like the other Before I finish this song? item.title: Reddit Bans 11-Year Account for GPL Game Post, Testing the EU's DSA
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 4.88
Longtime Slashdot reader DF5JT writes: On July 26, I posted a single announcement in r/backgammon: GNU Backgammon for Android, GPLv3, the first standalone backgammon engine on F-Droid. Reddit's spam filter removed the post and permanently banned my 11-year, 30,000-karma account -- the result is publicly visible at reddit.com/user/OE1FEU. To this day, Reddit has given no reason whatsoever, although Article 17 of the EU's Digital Services Act makes a statement of reasons mandatory. The only appeal channel is a 250-character web form that sends no confirmation and has never been answered; Reddit's own help text admits: "you may not have received a message to your inbox." A GDPR export of 11 years of data came to 7.2 MB; every post was truncated after a few lines, with zero data about the ban decision.
So I spent one day escalating through every mechanism the EU provides: certified out-of-court dispute settlement at Austria's RTR, complaints with the Austrian and Dutch Digital Services Coordinators, the data protection authority (citing the ECJ's SCHUFA ruling on automated decisions), noyb, and Austria's consumer association. Bonus finding: the European Commission's DSA Transparency Database contains 14,067 Reddit statements of reasons for that week -- none for my ban -- and the Commission's own feedback form limits reports to 500 characters and crashed with a 500 Server Error. Is the DSA enforceable for ordinary users, or just paperwork?

item.title: Spotify Will Label 'AI Persona' Profiles, Exclude Their Music From Recommendations
item.description:
Source: Slashdot Score: 4.72
Spotify will begin labeling AI-generated artist identities with "AI Persona" badges and exclude their music from editorial, algorithmic, and personalized recommendations unless users explicitly follow them. The company says the designation applies to whether an artist profile represents a real person, not whether AI was used to make the music, and will allow appeals for mislabeling. TechCrunch reports: While Spotify will allow artists to identify themselves as AI Personas, the company says it won't rely on self-disclosure alone. It will also review artist profiles and identify those where the artist's name and imagery appear to represent photorealistic AI-generated identities. Spotify said it will begin its review with profiles that have met pre-defined audience thresholds to ensure the more listened-to artists are covered first.
Once labeled, the AI Persona badges will appear on the artist's profile in the banner and the About section, in Search, and on track rows across playlists. By default, Spotify won't include AI Personas in its editorial or algorithmic recommendations, nor will it add AI Personas' music to users' personalized recommendations -- unless they happen to follow an AI Persona. Only users can choose to follow an artist, so it's an explicit signal that the user wants to hear more music from that person or group. Spotify wrote in its announcement that, "while we believe all artists have creative choice in determining how they present themselves, Spotify's programming is focused on elevating music from authentic artists building careers in music."
"Although there's a broad spectrum in how artists use AI as a creative tool, the question of whether a profile represents an actual human is one where Spotify can help make a clear determination. This badge is about the artist's public identity, not about how the music was made," the company said.
